title: Problem 1.1
question: Which of these is a quantitative observation? A. The fluid draining from the wound is cloudy. B. The patient's respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute. C. The tablet tastes bitter. D. The gas in the flask is colorless.
answer: B. A quantitative observation is a measurement: a number with a unit. "18 breaths per minute" has both. A is qualitative: "cloudy" describes appearance with a word, not a number. C is qualitative: taste is described with a word. D is qualitative: "colorless" is a description, not a measurement.
hint: A quantitative observation has a number with a unit. Which choice gives a count or measurement rather than a description in words?

title: Problem 1.3
question: Which statement is a testable (falsifiable) hypothesis? A. Tule fog is the most beautiful weather in California. B. Sugar dissolves because it wants to be in water. C. Raising the water temperature from 20 °C to 40 °C makes sugar dissolve faster. D. Chemistry is more important than biology.
answer: C. You can test it: time how long the same amount of sugar takes to dissolve at each temperature, keeping everything else the same. If the 40 °C trial is not faster, the hypothesis is shown wrong, which is what makes it falsifiable. A is an opinion; no measurement could prove it wrong. B gives sugar a "want," which no experiment can measure. D is a value judgment, not a prediction about what will happen in an experiment.
hint: A hypothesis must be testable: could an experiment show it is wrong? Opinions and claims about what a substance "wants" cannot be tested.

title: Problem 1.8
question: Which statement about scientific theories is correct? A. A theory becomes a law once it has been proven. B. A theory is a well-tested explanation that can still be revised if new evidence requires it. C. A theory is the scientific word for a guess. D. Laws explain why things happen; theories only describe what happens.
answer: B. A theory explains why nature behaves as it does and is supported by many experiments, but it stays open to revision. A is wrong: theories and laws do different jobs (why versus what). A theory never "graduates" into a law. C is wrong: that is the everyday meaning of "theory." In science, a theory is the strongest kind of explanation there is. D has the two backwards: laws describe what happens; theories explain why.
hint: Laws and theories do different jobs: a law says what happens, a theory says why. Does a theory ever become "proven" and closed to new evidence?

title: Problem 1.29
question: Which of these is a compound? A. O 3 (ozone) B. N 2 C. NH 3 (ammonia) D. air
answer: C. NH 3 contains two different elements, nitrogen and hydrogen, bonded in a fixed 1:3 ratio. A is an element: every atom in O 3 is oxygen. A subscript does not make a compound. B is an element (one of the diatomic seven): only one kind of atom. D is a homogeneous mixture of several gases (mostly N 2 and O 2 ), not one substance.
hint: A compound has two or more different elements bonded together in a fixed ratio. A subscript alone does not make a compound, and a mixture is not a substance.

title: Problem 1.34
question: Which of these is a molecule but not a compound? A. H 2 O B. NaCl C. Br 2 D. CH 4 (methane)
answer: C. Br 2 is two atoms bonded together (a molecule), but both atoms are bromine, so it is an element, not a compound. A is both a molecule and a compound (H and O bonded). B is a compound, but it is made of Na + and Cl − ions in formula units, not molecules. It is the reverse case: a compound but not a molecule. D is both a molecule and a compound (C and H bonded).
hint: A molecule is atoms bonded together; a compound needs two or more different elements. Which choice has bonded atoms all of one element?

title: Problem 1.39
question: A sample keeps its own shape no matter what container it is placed in. Which description fits its particles? A. Far apart and moving fast in all directions B. Touching, but sliding past one another C. Closely packed and vibrating in place D. Closely packed and not moving at all
answer: C. A definite shape means a solid, and solid particles are packed closely and vibrate in fixed positions. A describes a gas, which fills its container and has no definite shape. B describes a liquid, which flows and takes the shape of its container. D is wrong because particles in a solid still vibrate; they just do not move out of place.
hint: A definite shape means a solid. Which description matches solid particles: packed closely, and doing what?

title: Problem 1.44
question: When you breathe in, your diaphragm (the dome-shaped muscle under your lungs) contracts and moves down, making the chest cavity larger. The air already in the lungs spreads out to fill the larger space. Which statement explains this? A. Gases have a definite volume, so the air keeps the same volume. B. Gases have no definite volume; their particles are far apart and move freely, so they spread to fill any space available. C. Gas particles are touching, so they push each other into the new space. D. The gas particles themselves get bigger when the lungs expand.
answer: B. A gas has no definite volume. Its fast-moving particles spread out to fill whatever space they have. A is wrong: a definite volume is a property of solids and liquids, not gases. C is wrong: gas particles are far apart, not touching. D is wrong: the particles do not change size; the space between them changes.
hint: Does a gas have a definite volume? Think about what gas particles do when more space becomes available.

title: Problem 1.45
question: Which pair of particles repels? A. Mg 2+ and Cl − B. a proton and an electron C. F − and O 2− D. Li + and Br −
answer: C. Both particles are negative, and like charges repel. (The sizes of the charges differ, but only the signs decide attract or repel.) A: positive and negative attract. B: a proton is positive and an electron is negative, so they attract. D: positive and negative attract.
hint: Only the signs decide attract or repel: opposite signs attract, like signs repel. Which pair has the same sign?

title: Problem 1.49
question: A Na + ion and a Cl − ion are a certain distance apart. Which single change makes the attraction between the two particles stronger? A. Move the two ions farther apart. B. Replace Na + with Mg 2+ , keeping the same distance. C. Replace Cl − with a second Na + . D. Replace both ions with neutral atoms.
answer: B. At the same distance, a larger charge gives a stronger attraction, and 2+ is larger than 1+. A weakens the attraction, because the force gets weaker as charges move apart. C gives two positive ions, which repel instead of attract. D removes the net charges, so there is no attraction between ions at all.
hint: At a fixed distance, larger charges attract more strongly; moving apart weakens the attraction. Which choice keeps opposite charges and makes one of them larger?
new_hint: Recall from 1.7 how the size of the charges and the distance between them affect attraction. For each change, ask whether the charges stay opposite and whether either one gets larger or smaller.

title: Problem 1.53
question: Which of these is a chemical property? A. Isopropyl alcohol evaporates quickly at room temperature. B. Iron tends to rust in moist air. C. Copper conducts electricity. D. Glucose dissolves in water.
answer: B. Rusting turns iron into a new substance (iron oxide), so the tendency to rust describes how iron changes into something else: a chemical property. A is a physical property: evaporating alcohol is still alcohol, now as a gas. C is a physical property: electricity passes through copper, and it is still copper afterward. D is a physical property: dissolving is a physical change, and evaporating the water gives the glucose back.
hint: A chemical property describes how a substance can change into a new substance. Which choice involves forming something new?

title: Problem 1.57
question: The large bubbles that rise in a pot of water at a full, rolling boil are mostly: A. hydrogen gas and oxygen gas B. air C. water vapor D. heat
answer: C. Boiling is vaporization: liquid water turns into gaseous water (H 2 O) inside the liquid, and those pockets of vapor rise as bubbles. It is a physical change. A would require breaking water molecules apart, a chemical change that boiling does not cause. B is a common mix-up: the tiny bubbles that appear early, as the water first warms, are dissolved air coming out, but the big bubbles of a rolling boil are water vapor. D is wrong because heat is energy, not matter; it cannot fill a bubble.
hint: Boiling is liquid water becoming gaseous water inside the liquid. Does boiling break water molecules apart?
new_hint: Boiling is a change of state, not a chemical change. Which substance is going from liquid to gas inside the pot?

title: Problem 1.58
question: Which pair contains two intensive properties? A. mass and density B. boiling point and color C. volume and melting point D. mass and volume
answer: B. Boiling point and color are the same for a drop or a drum of a substance, so neither depends on the amount. A: density is intensive, but mass is extensive (more sample, more mass). C: melting point is intensive, but volume is extensive. D: both are extensive.
hint: An intensive property is the same for a drop or a drum of the substance. Which pair has neither property depending on the amount?

title: Problem 1.68
question: A copper block is cut exactly in half. Which statement about one of the halves is correct? A. Its density is half the density of the original block. B. Its mass and volume are each half of the original, and its density is unchanged. C. Its density is twice the density of the original block. D. Its mass is half of the original, but its volume is unchanged.
answer: B. Mass and volume are extensive, so both are cut in half. Density is mass ÷ volume, and halving both leaves the ratio the same: density is intensive. A and C confuse density with an extensive property; the substance is still copper, so its density stays the same. D is wrong: a half block takes up half the space, so its volume also halves.
hint: Cutting in half halves both mass and volume. What happens to a ratio when its top and bottom are both cut in half?
new_hint: Which of these properties are extensive (depend on the amount) and which is a ratio of two of them? What happens to a ratio when its top and bottom change by the same factor?

title: Problem 1.70
question: Which object will float in water (1.00 g/mL)? A. mass 12.0 g, volume 10.0 mL B. mass 9.50 g, volume 10.0 mL C. mass 25.5 g, volume 25.0 mL D. mass 5.00 g, volume 4.00 mL
answer: B. Calculate each density and compare with 1.00 g/mL: A: 12.0 g ÷ 10.0 mL = 1.20 g/mL, denser than water, so it sinks. B: 9.50 g ÷ 10.0 mL = 0.950 g/mL, less dense than water, so it floats. C: 25.5 g ÷ 25.0 mL = 1.02 g/mL, slightly denser than water, so it sinks (slowly). D: 5.00 g ÷ 4.00 mL = 1.25 g/mL, denser than water, so it sinks. Notice that C has the largest mass and B is not the lightest object; floating depends on density, not on mass alone.
hint: Calculate each density (mass ÷ volume) and compare with water's 1.00 g/mL. An object floats only if it is less dense than water.

title: Problem 1.75
question: A science-night demonstrator drops a chunk of dry ice (solid CO 2 , density about 1.5 g/cm 3 ) into a bowl of warm water. It bubbles, and a thick white fog rolls over the rim of the bowl. First, the white fog is mostly: A. carbon dioxide gas B. tiny droplets of liquid water condensed from water vapor in the air that the very cold CO 2 gas chilled C. smoke from the dry ice burning D. hydrogen and oxygen gas from water breaking apart Then answer: (e) Does the dry ice sink or float? (f) Name the change of state the dry ice undergoes. (g) Classify CO 2 as an element, compound, or mixture. (h) Are the bubbles evidence of a chemical change?
answer: B. Carbon dioxide gas is colorless and invisible. The very cold CO 2 gas chills the moist air above the bowl, and the water vapor condenses into tiny droplets that you see as fog (the same physical change that makes tule fog). A is wrong: CO 2 gas is invisible, so it cannot be the white fog. C is wrong: nothing is burning; there is no flame and no new substance. D is wrong: breaking water into hydrogen and oxygen is a chemical change that warm water and dry ice do not cause. (e) Sinks: about 1.5 g/cm 3 is greater than water's 1.00 g/mL (1 cm 3 = 1 mL). (f) Sublimation (solid → gas), a physical change. (g) Compound: carbon and oxygen bonded in a fixed 1:2 ratio. (h) No. The bubbles are CO 2 gas from the dry ice subliming, and the CO 2 was already there as a solid. A gas forming is only a clue to a chemical change; here no new substance forms.
hint: Carbon dioxide gas is colorless. What visible thing forms when very cold gas chills moist air? For (e)–(h), compare densities, name the solid-to-gas change, and ask whether any new substance forms.

title: Problem 1.81
question: A 10 mL graduated cylinder is marked every 0.1 mL. The bottom of the meniscus is about three-tenths of the way from the 4.7 mL mark to the 4.8 mL mark. Which is the correct way to record the volume? A. 4.7 mL B. 4.73 mL C. 4.730 mL D. 5 mL
answer: B. The 0.1 mL marks make the tenths place certain (4.7), and you estimate one more digit, the hundredths (about 3). The reading has 3 significant figures. A: stops at the last tick mark and throws away the estimated digit the cylinder allows. C: claims a second estimated digit (the thousandths) that no one can read from 0.1 mL marks. D: rounds to the nearest whole milliliter, which is the precision of a much coarser tool, not this one.
hint: With 0.1 mL marks, the tenths are certain. Record one more estimated digit, and no more than one.

title: Problem 1.85
question: A toothpaste contains 0.243% sodium fluoride (NaF) by mass. How much sodium fluoride is in a 1.40 g strip of toothpaste on a brush? A. 3.40 mg NaF B. 340 mg NaF C. 576 g NaF D. 0.00340 mg NaF
answer: A. Write the percent as a conversion factor with both substances labeled, then convert to milligrams: \( 1.40\ \text{g toothpaste} \times \dfrac{0.243\ \text{g NaF}}{100\ \text{g toothpaste}} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{mg}}{1\ \text{g}} = 3.40\ \text{mg NaF} \) B: uses 0.243 as if it were already a decimal fraction (0.243 instead of 0.243/100), giving 0.340 g = 340 mg, a hundred times too much. A part cannot be a quarter of a strip that is mostly not NaF. C: flips the percent factor (toothpaste on top), so grams of toothpaste do not cancel; the "part" comes out hundreds of times larger than the whole. D: stops at grams (0.00340 g) and labels it mg, skipping the g → mg step; a smaller unit must give a larger number. (Context only; dental hygienists use these numbers to explain fluoride content, not to set doses.)
hint: Write the percent as a conversion factor: 0.243 g NaF / 100 g toothpaste. Then convert grams to milligrams. Size check: the part must be much smaller than 1.40 g.

title: Problem 1.86
question: A 50.0 mL sample of a clear, colorless liquid has a mass of 63.0 g. Using the density table in Section 1.9 (water 1.00, ethanol 0.789, methanol 0.792, glycerol 1.26 g/mL), what is the liquid most likely to be? A. water B. ethanol C. glycerol D. It cannot be identified, because 50.0 mL is too small a sample.
answer: C. d = 63.0 g ÷ 50.0 mL = 1.26 g/mL, which matches glycerol. A: water would have a mass of about 50.0 g for 50.0 mL (1.00 g/mL); this sample is heavier than that, so it is denser than water. B: ethanol (0.789 g/mL) would have a mass of about 39.5 g for 50.0 mL, far below 63.0 g; any liquid less dense than water is ruled out. D: density is intensive, so it does not depend on the size of the sample; a drop and a gallon of a liquid have the same density.
hint: Calculate the density (mass ÷ volume) and compare it with the table values. Does density depend on how big the sample is?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: Which is the correct scientific notation for 0.0007203 m? A. 7.203 × 10 −4 m B. 7.203 × 10 4 m C. 72.03 × 10 −5 m D. 7.2 × 10 −4 m
answer: A. Move the decimal point 4 places to the right to get 7.203; a number smaller than 1 gets a negative exponent. All 4 significant figures (7, 2, 0, 3) stay. B: the exponent has the wrong sign; 7.203 × 10 4 is 72,030, a large number. C: has the right value, but the first part (72.03) is not between 1 and 10, so it is not proper scientific notation. D: drops the significant figures 0 and 3. The sandwiched zero counts, so the number has 4 significant figures, not 2.
hint: The coefficient must be from 1 to 10, the exponent is negative for numbers less than 1, and all significant figures must stay.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{7}\)
question: Which mass is the largest? A. 0.025 kg B. 3.0 × 10 4 mg C. 2.5 × 10 7 µg D. 2.0 × 10 −5 Mg
answer: B. Convert each to grams: 3.0 × 10 4 mg × (1 g / 1000 mg) = 30. g, the largest. A: 0.025 kg × (1000 g / 1 kg) = 25 g. C: 2.5 × 10 7 µg × (1 g / 10 6 µg) = 25 g; a big exponent on a tiny unit does not mean a big mass. D: 2.0 × 10 −5 Mg × (10 6 g / 1 Mg) = 20. g; a megagram is huge, but the number in front is tiny.
hint: Convert every choice to grams before comparing. Remember the capital M in Mg means mega-, not milli-.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{10}\)
question: A clinic scale gives readings of 72.4 kg, 72.5 kg, and 72.4 kg for a patient. On a newly calibrated scale, the same patient weighs 70.1 kg. The clinic scale is: A. precise but not accurate B. accurate but not precise C. both accurate and precise D. neither accurate nor precise
answer: A. The three readings agree closely with each other (precise), but all are about 2.3 kg too high (not accurate). This is the pattern of a systematic error, such as a scale that is out of calibration; it can be fixed by recalibrating. B: accurate means close to the true value; 72.4 kg is not close to 70.1 kg. C: the readings are precise, but precision alone does not make them correct. D: the readings are within 0.1 kg of each other, so they are precise.
hint: Precision is how close the readings are to each other; accuracy is how close they are to the true value. Compare the clinic readings with the calibrated scale.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{14}\)
question: Round 6,451.7 to 2 significant figures. A. 6.5 × 10 3 B. 650 C. 6.4 × 10 3 D. 6,450
answer: A. Underline the second digit (6, 4 51.7); the digit to its right is 5, so round the 4 up to 5. Then keep the number's size with placeholder zeros or scientific notation: 6,500 or 6.5 × 10 3 . B: drops a placeholder zero; 650 is ten times too small. If someone owed you $6,500 and paid $650, you would notice. C: cuts off (truncates) instead of rounding; the 5 after the underlined digit means round up. D: keeps 3 significant figures, not 2.
hint: Underline the second digit and look at the digit to its right. Then keep the number's size: the answer must still be about six thousand.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{18}\)
question: A digital analytical balance displays 2.0500 g. What should you record? A. 2.0500 g B. 2.05 g C. 2.050 g D. 2 g
answer: A. Record every digit a digital balance shows, including trailing zeros; they are measured, so 2.0500 g has 5 significant figures. B: drops two measured zeros and makes the balance look 100 times less precise than it is. C: drops one measured zero. D: throws away almost all of the measurement.
hint: A digital balance measures every digit it shows, including trailing zeros. Do not drop any.
new_hint: Are the trailing zeros on a digital display measured digits or placeholders? Count the significant figures each choice keeps.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{20}\)
question: (Math practice only.) An order is written as 0.250 mg. How many micrograms (mcg) is this? A. 2.50 × 10 2 mcg B. 2.50 × 10 −4 mcg C. 25.0 mcg D. 2.50 × 10 5 mcg
answer: A. \( 0.250\ \text{mg} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{g}}{1000\ \text{mg}} \times \dfrac{10^{6}\ \text{mcg}}{1\ \text{g}} = 250.\ \text{mcg} = 2.50 \times 10^{2}\ \text{mcg} \). A smaller unit gives a bigger number. B: divides by 1000 instead of multiplying; the factor 1000 mcg = 1 mg was used upside down, and the number got smaller even though the unit got smaller. C: uses 100 mcg = 1 mg, a made-up factor. Go through the base unit and use factors from the sheet. D: multiplies by 10 6 as if the order were in grams; it skips the mg → g step and is 1000 times too large.
hint: Go through the base unit: mg → g → mcg. A smaller unit gives a bigger number.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{26}\)
question: (Math practice only.) An IV runs continuously at 125 mL/h. How many liters does it deliver per day? A. 3.00 L/day B. 3.00 × 10 3 L/day C. 5.21 × 10 −3 L/day D. 0.125 L/day
answer: A. \( \dfrac{125\ \text{mL}}{1\ \text{h}} \times \dfrac{24\ \text{h}}{1\ \text{day}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{L}}{1000\ \text{mL}} = 3.00\ \text{L/day} \) (3 significant figures; 24 h = 1 day is exact). B: 3000 is the number of milliliters per day; the mL → L step was skipped. C: divides by 24 instead of multiplying; "per hour" on the bottom needs 24 h on the top of the next factor to cancel. D: converts mL to L but never converts hours to days, so it is still the volume per hour.
hint: Use 24 h = 1 day to cancel hours, then 1000 mL = 1 L to cancel milliliters. Which choice is in a sensible range for a daily IV volume?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{27}\)
question: Convert 4.0 × 10 4 cm 2 to m 2 . A. 4.0 m 2 B. 4.0 × 10 2 m 2 C. 4.0 × 10 8 m 2 D. 0.040 m 2
answer: A. \( 4.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{cm}^{2} \times \left(\dfrac{1\ \text{m}}{100\ \text{cm}}\right)^{2} = 4.0 \times 10^{4} \div 10^{4} = 4.0\ \text{m}^{2} \). B: divides by 100, forgetting to square the factor. C: multiplies by 10 4 ; the factor is upside down, and a bigger unit must give a smaller number. D: divides by 10 6 , cubing a factor that should be squared (this is an area, not a volume).
hint: The unit is squared, so square the factor (1 m/100 cm). One square meter is 100 cm by 100 cm.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{32}\)
question: A nursing student drives from Fresno to a clinical site in Merced, 65 mi away, on a foggy morning at an average of 45 mi/h. How many minutes does the drive take? A. 87 min B. 1.4 min C. 42 min D. 2.9 × 10 3 min
answer: A. Start with the term that stands alone (65 mi): \( 65\ \text{mi} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{h}}{45\ \text{mi}} \times \dfrac{60\ \text{min}}{1\ \text{h}} = 86.7 \to 87\ \text{min} \) (2 significant figures). The city names and the fog are distractors. B: 1.4 is the time in hours ; the h → min step was skipped. C: uses the speed upside down (45 mi/h × 60 ÷ 65); miles do not cancel. D: multiplies 65 mi by 45 mi/h, which gives mi 2 /h, not a time.
hint: Start with the term that stands alone (the distance), use the speed with miles on the bottom, then convert hours to minutes. The fog is a distractor.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{36}\)
question: What volume of glycerol (d = 1.26 g/mL) has a mass of 75.6 g? A. 60.0 mL B. 95.3 mL C. 0.0600 mL D. 0.0167 mL
answer: A. \( 75.6\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mL}}{1.26\ \text{g}} = 60.0\ \text{mL} \) (3 significant figures). A liquid denser than water has fewer mL than g. B: multiplies by the density (75.6 × 1.26); grams do not cancel, and the volume came out larger than the mass, which is impossible for a liquid denser than water. C: 0.0600 is the volume in liters , labeled as mL. D: divides the density by the mass (1.26 ÷ 75.6); the units would be 1/mL, not mL.
hint: Start with the mass and flip the density so grams are on the bottom. A liquid denser than water has fewer mL than g.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: What volume of ethanol (d = 0.789 g/mL) has a mass of 150. g? A. 190. mL B. 118 mL C. 0.190 mL D. 5.26 × 10 −3 mL
answer: A. \( 150.\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mL}}{0.789\ \text{g}} = 190.1\ \text{mL} \to 190.\ \text{mL} \) (3 significant figures; the decimal point shows the zero is significant). B: multiplies the mass by the density (g × g/mL), so grams do not cancel; a liquid less dense than water must have more mL than g. C: is the right number of liters (0.190 L) but labeled mL. D: divides the density by the mass (0.789 ÷ 150); the units would be 1/mL, not mL, so the setup cannot be right.
hint: Start with the mass and flip the density so grams are on the bottom. A liquid less dense than water has more mL than g.

title: Problem 2.1
question: Which idea from Dalton's atomic theory was later shown to be incorrect ? A. Atoms combine in simple, whole-number ratios to form compounds. B. All atoms of a given element have the same mass. C. In a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed. D. Each element is made of tiny particles called atoms.
answer: B. Atoms of the same element always have the same number of protons, but they can have different numbers of neutrons, so they can have different masses. These versions of an element are isotopes (Section 2.5). A still holds: water is always 2 H atoms to 1 O atom. This idea explains the law of definite proportions. C still holds for chemical reactions, and it explains the law of conservation of mass. (Nuclear changes, in Chapter 14, are a different kind of change.) D is the heart of the theory and has held up for two centuries.
hint: Section 2.5 shows that atoms of one element can have different numbers of neutrons. Which statement does that discovery contradict?

title: Problem 2.4
question: In Thomson's cathode-ray tube, the glowing beam bent toward a positively charged plate. What did this show? A. The beam was made of negatively charged particles. B. The beam was made of positively charged particles. C. Atoms have a small, dense nucleus. D. The beam was made of neutral particles.
answer: A. Opposite charges attract (Section 1.7), so a beam pulled toward a positive plate must carry negative charge. Those particles are electrons. B is backward: positive particles would be pushed away from a positive plate. C is the conclusion of Rutherford's gold foil experiment, not Thomson's cathode-ray experiment. D cannot be right: neutral particles are not pulled by either plate, so the beam would go straight.
hint: Opposite charges attract (Section 1.7). What charge must the beam carry to be pulled toward a positive plate?

title: Problem 2.7
question: Which statement describes the nuclear model of the atom? A. Electrons sit inside the nucleus with the protons. B. The nucleus holds almost all of the atom's mass but takes up only a tiny fraction of its volume. C. Positive charge is spread evenly through the whole atom. D. The nucleus fills most of the atom, and electrons are packed tightly against it.
answer: B. Protons and neutrons, the heavy particles, are in the nucleus, and the nucleus is roughly 1/100,000 of the atom's diameter. The rest of the atom is mostly empty space where the electrons move. A is wrong: electrons are outside the nucleus, in the electron cloud. C describes Thomson's plum pudding model, which the gold foil experiment ruled out. D is wrong on size: if the nucleus filled most of the atom, most alpha particles would have been deflected, not 1 in 8000.
hint: Recall the nuclear model in three sentences: where is the mass, and how much of the volume does the nucleus fill? One choice is the plum pudding model.

title: Problem 2.10
question: What determines which element an atom is? A. its mass number B. its number of neutrons C. its number of protons D. its number of electrons
answer: C. The number of protons is the atomic number, and it defines the element. Every atom with 26 protons is iron, whatever else is true about it. A is wrong: atoms of different elements can share a mass number (argon-40 and calcium-40 both have A = 40). B is wrong: atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; those are isotopes. D is wrong: atoms gain and lose electrons to form ions, but a sodium ion is still sodium.
hint: Which count never changes when an atom becomes an ion or a different isotope? See "Key Idea: Never Change the Protons" in 2.2.

title: Problem 2.14
question: How is the atomic mass unit (amu) defined? A. as the mass of one hydrogen atom B. as exactly one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom C. as the mass of one proton D. as one gram divided by the number of atoms in a sample
answer: B. 1 amu is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, which works out to 1.6605 × 10 −24 g. A is close but not the definition: a hydrogen-1 atom is about 1.008 amu. C is also close but not exact: a proton is 1.0073 amu. D is not a definition at all; it depends on the size of the sample.
hint: Which reference atom is the amu scale built on? Two choices are close in value but are not the definition (see 2.2).

title: Problem 2.15
question: Which element and symbol are paired incorrectly ? A. mercury, Hg B. sodium, So C. gold, Au D. iron, Fe
answer: B. Sodium's symbol is Na , from its Latin name natrium . (There is no element with the symbol So.) A is correct: Hg comes from the Latin hydrargyrum , "liquid silver." C is correct: Au comes from aurum . D is correct: Fe comes from ferrum ; that is why an iron supplement is called ferrous sulfate.
hint: Check each symbol against the Latin-name table in 2.3. Which pair matches neither the English name nor the Latin name?

title: Problem 2.18
question: Which element is a halogen in period 4? A. Br B. Kr C. Se D. K
answer: A. Bromine is in group 17 (the halogens) and period 4. It is also the only nonmetal that is a liquid at room temperature. B, krypton, is in period 4 but in group 18: it is a noble gas. C, selenium, is in period 4 but in group 16, the chalcogens (oxygen family). D, potassium, is in period 4 but in group 1: it is an alkali metal. All four choices are in period 4; only the group decides the family.
hint: All four choices are in period 4, so only the group decides. Which group number belongs to the halogens?

title: Problem 2.22
question: Which set contains only metalloids? A. B, Si, As B. C, Si, Ge C. Al, Si, P D. Si, Ge, Sn
answer: A. Boron, silicon, and arsenic all sit along the staircase line. B includes carbon, a nonmetal. C includes aluminum, a metal, and phosphorus, a nonmetal. D includes tin, a metal. Silicon and germanium are metalloids, but group 14 changes from nonmetal (C) to metalloids (Si, Ge) to metals (Sn, Pb) as you go down.
hint: Metalloids sit along the staircase line between the metals and nonmetals. Check every element in each set on the periodic table; one element off the staircase rules a set out.

title: Problem 2.25
question: A cation forms when an atom A. gains one or more protons. B. loses one or more electrons. C. gains one or more electrons. D. loses one or more neutrons.
answer: B. Losing negative electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive. A is wrong: the number of protons never changes when an ion forms. Changing the protons would make a different element. C describes how an anion forms. D is wrong: neutrons have no charge, so losing them could not create a charge (and ions do not form that way).
hint: Which particle is gained or lost when an ion forms? Losing negative particles leaves more protons than electrons.
new_hint: A cation is a positive ion. Which particles can an atom gain or lose when it forms an ion, and which change leaves the charge positive?

title: Problem 2.28
question: Which of these is not the usual ion formed by the element? A. Cs + B. Sr 2+ C. Br 2− D. S 2−
answer: C. Bromine is in group 17, and group 17 elements form 1− ions. The usual ion is Br − , bromide. A is the usual ion: cesium is in group 1, which forms 1+ ions. B is the usual ion: strontium is in group 2, which forms 2+ ions. D is the usual ion: sulfur is in group 16, which forms 2− ions.
hint: Use the group pattern from 2.4: group 1 is 1+, group 2 is 2+, group 16 is 2−, group 17 is 1−. Check each choice's group.

title: Problem 2.31
question: Which pair of species has the same number of electrons? A. Na + and Mg 2+ B. Na and Na + C. F − and Cl − D. Mg 2+ and Ca 2+
answer: A. Na + has 11 − 1 = 10 electrons, and Mg 2+ has 12 − 2 = 10 electrons. B: the neutral Na atom has 11 electrons; Na + has 10. Losing that electron is what makes the ion. C: F − has 10 electrons and Cl − has 18. Same charge, different counts. D: Mg 2+ has 10 electrons and Ca 2+ has 18.
hint: Count the electrons for every species with electrons = Z − charge, then look for the pair whose counts match.

title: Problem 2.34
question: A nursing student is reviewing potassium results. Which statement about the potassium ion, K + , is correct? A. It has 19 protons and 18 electrons. B. It has 20 protons and 19 electrons. C. It is a potassium atom that has gained one proton. D. It is an anion.
answer: A. Potassium's atomic number is 19, so every potassium particle has 19 protons. The 1+ charge means 19 − 1 = 18 electrons. B is wrong: 20 protons would make the particle calcium, not potassium. C is wrong: ions form by losing or gaining electrons; the proton count never changes. D is wrong: K + is positive, so it is a cation. Metals such as potassium form cations.
hint: Find potassium's Z for the proton count, then electrons = protons − charge. Protons never change when an ion forms, and cats have paws.

title: Problem 2.41
question: Which pair are isotopes of the same element? A. \( ^{14}_{6}\text{C} \) and \( ^{14}_{7}\text{N} \) B. \( ^{12}_{6}\text{C} \) and \( ^{13}_{6}\text{C} \) C. O 2 and O 3 D. Na and Na +
answer: B. Both have Z = 6 (carbon), but carbon-12 has 6 neutrons and carbon-13 has 7. Same protons, different neutrons: isotopes. A: same mass number but different elements (6 versus 7 protons). Isotopes share Z, not A. C: these are two different molecules of the same element (oxygen gas and ozone). They differ in how many atoms are joined together, not in the number of neutrons in each atom. D: an atom and its ion differ in electrons, not neutrons.
hint: Isotopes share Z (same protons) but differ in neutrons. Check each pair: same element? Different mass number? Single atoms, not molecules or ions?

title: Problem 2.42
question: How many protons, neutrons, and electrons are in \( ^{80}_{34}\text{Se}^{2-} \)? A. 34 protons, 46 neutrons, 36 electrons B. 34 protons, 46 neutrons, 32 electrons C. 34 protons, 44 neutrons, 36 electrons D. 46 protons, 34 neutrons, 36 electrons
answer: A. Protons = Z = 34. Neutrons = 80 − 34 = 46. A 2− charge means two electrons were gained: 34 + 2 = 36. B subtracts the charge the wrong way: a negative ion has more electrons than protons. C subtracts the charge from the neutron count (80 − 34 − 2). Charge affects electrons only. D swaps protons and neutrons. The subscript, 34, is always the proton count.
hint: Protons = Z (the subscript), neutrons = A − Z, and a 2− charge means electrons were gained. The charge never changes the neutrons.

title: Problem 2.51
question: Iridium-192 is a radioactive isotope used in some cancer treatments in which a tiny radioactive source is placed inside or next to a tumor. Natural iridium is made of iridium-191 and iridium-193, and its average atomic mass is 192.22 amu. Which statement is correct? A. Iridium-193 is more abundant than iridium-191. B. The two natural isotopes are equally abundant. C. Iridium-191 is more abundant than iridium-193. D. Most natural iridium is iridium-192, because 192.22 is closest to 192.
answer: A. If the two isotopes were equally common, the average would be near 192, halfway between 191 and 193. The real average, 192.22, is above 192, so it is pulled toward the heavier isotope. (Natural iridium is about 63% iridium-193.) B would give an average very close to 192. C would pull the average below 192, toward 191. D confuses the average with an isotope. The problem says natural iridium contains only iridium-191 and iridium-193; iridium-192 is made artificially for medical use. An average atomic mass can be near a mass number that no natural atom has.
hint: Find the midpoint of the two mass numbers. Is the average above or below it? The average is pulled toward the more abundant isotope.

title: Problem 2.54
question: The periodic table lists 85.47 amu for rubidium, which has two natural isotopes, rubidium-85 and rubidium-87. Which statement is correct? A. Every rubidium atom has a mass of 85.47 amu. B. No single rubidium atom has a mass of 85.47 amu; the value is a weighted average of the masses of rubidium-85 and rubidium-87 atoms. C. 85.47 is the mass number of rubidium. D. Natural rubidium is half rubidium-85 and half rubidium-87.
answer: B. Each atom is either rubidium-85 (about 84.91 amu) or rubidium-87 (about 86.91 amu). 85.47 describes the natural mixture, not any one atom. A is the most common misunderstanding: the average describes the mixture. C is wrong: a mass number counts protons plus neutrons, so it is always a whole number and belongs to one isotope. D would give an average near 86. The real average, 85.47, is much closer to 85, so rubidium-85 is the large majority (about 72%).
hint: Is the periodic-table value the mass of one atom, or a weighted average of a mixture? A mass number is always a whole number.
new_hint: Each rubidium atom is either rubidium-85 or rubidium-87. Can one atom have a mass between them? Is a mass number ever a decimal?

title: Problem 2.60
question: When a sulfur atom gains two electrons, the particle that forms is A. a cation with a 2+ charge B. an anion with a 2− charge C. an anion with a 2+ charge D. sulfur-34, a heavier isotope of sulfur
answer: B. Gaining two negative electrons gives 16 protons and 18 electrons: charge = 16 − 18 = 2−. A negative ion is an anion (onions make you cry: anions are the negative ones). The ion is S 2− , sulfide. A gets the sign backward. Cations (cats have paws: "paws-itive") form when electrons are lost . C mixes the two: an anion is always negative. D confuses electrons with neutrons. Electrons have almost no mass and do not change the mass number; adding neutrons makes an isotope.
hint: Gaining negative electrons makes the charge negative: charge = protons − electrons. Onions make you cry: which ions are the negative ones?
new_hint: Use charge = protons − electrons for sulfur (Z = 16) after it gains two electrons. Does gaining electrons change the mass number?

title: Problem 2.61
question: Which set shows the correct fixed charges of aluminum, zinc, and silver? A. Al 3+ , Zn 2+ , Ag + B. Al 3+ , Zn + , Ag 2+ C. Al + , Zn 2+ , Ag 3+ D. Al 2+ , Zn 2+ , Ag +
answer: A. Walk down the steps: aluminum (top step) 3+, zinc 2+, silver 1+. B swaps zinc and silver. C walks the steps in the wrong direction: start at aluminum with 3+. D gives aluminum 2+; aluminum always forms Al 3+ .
hint: Use "the steps" from 2.4: start at aluminum on the top step and walk down the diagonal, one charge lower each step.

title: Problem 2.62
question: Potassium (Z = 19) comes right after argon (Z = 18), but on the periodic table it starts a new row, directly under sodium. Why? A. Potassium is heavier than argon, and heavier elements always start new rows. B. Potassium behaves like sodium (a soft metal that reacts violently with water), and the table stacks elements with similar properties in the same column. C. Mendeleev arranged the elements alphabetically by their Latin names (kalium, natrium). D. Every row of the periodic table has exactly eight elements.
answer: B. The table is ordered by atomic number, but a new row starts whenever properties repeat, so that each column holds a family of similar elements. Potassium is an alkali metal like lithium and sodium, so it lands in group 1. A: every element is heavier than the one before it (with a few exceptions), but that alone does not decide where rows break. C: the order is by atomic number, not by name; the Latin names only explain the symbols K and Na. D: rows have 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, and 32 elements; only periods 2 and 3 have eight.
hint: Mendeleev started a new row whenever properties repeated. How does potassium behave compared with sodium?

title: Problem 2.65
question: Silicon, the element in computer chips and in the quartz of Sierra granite, has three natural isotopes. Silicon-28 (27.977 amu) is 92.23% of silicon atoms and silicon-29 (28.976 amu) is 4.68%. The rest is silicon-30 (29.974 amu). (a) What is the percent abundance of silicon-30? A. 3.09% B. 7.77% C. 96.91% D. 33.3% Then (b) calculate silicon's average atomic mass.
answer: (a) A. The three percents must add to 100%: 100.00% − 92.23% − 4.68% = 3.09% . B subtracted only silicon-28 (100.00 − 92.23) and forgot silicon-29. C added the two given percents instead of subtracting them from 100%. D assumes the three isotopes are equally common; the problem says they are not. (b) Change each percent to a decimal and keep each product in parentheses on the calculator: \( (0.9223)(27.977) + (0.0468)(28.976) + (0.0309)(29.974) = 25.803 + 1.3561 + 0.92620 = 28.09\ \text{amu} \) The answer is 28.09 amu , rounded to the hundredths place (the last place known in the 1.36 and 25.80 terms). It is very close to 28 because silicon-28 is the large majority, and it matches the yellow-sheet value.
hint: (a) The three percents must add to 100%: subtract both given values. (b) Change each percent to a decimal, multiply by its mass, and add all three.

title: Problem 3.1
question: Moving through the electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves toward gamma rays, which statement is true? A. Wavelength increases and photon energy increases. B. Wavelength decreases and frequency increases. C. Frequency decreases and photon energy increases. D. The waves travel faster.
answer:
B. Radio waves are the longest waves and gamma rays the shortest. Because \( c = \lambda
u \) and \( c \) is fixed, a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency, and by \( E = h
u \) a higher photon energy. A is wrong: wavelength gets shorter toward gamma rays. Wavelength and energy never rise together. C is wrong: frequency and energy always change in the same direction, because \( E = h
u \). Both increase toward gamma rays. D is wrong: all electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed in a vacuum, \( 3.00 	imes 10^{8}\ 	ext{m s}^{-1} \).
hint: Use c = λν (c is fixed) and E = hν. Which way does the wavelength change from radio waves to gamma rays?

title: Problem 3.6
question: Compare a 254 nm photon from a germicidal UV-C lamp with a 940 nm photon from a pulse oximeter. Which statement is correct? A. The UV-C photon has a higher frequency and more energy. B. The infrared photon has more energy, because its wavelength is longer. C. The two photons have the same energy, because both travel at the speed of light. D. The UV-C photon has a lower frequency but more energy.
answer:
A. The UV-C photon has the shorter wavelength, so it has the higher frequency (\( 
u = c/\lambda \)) and the higher energy (\( E = h
u \)). By the ratio of wavelengths, 940 ÷ 254 = 3.7, it carries about 3.7 times the energy. (The zero in 940 has no decimal point, so 940 has two significant figures.) B has the relationship backward: longer wavelength means less energy. C is wrong: all light has the same speed, but energy depends on frequency, and these frequencies are different. D is impossible: a photon with more energy must have a higher frequency, since \( E = h
u \).
hint: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency (ν = c/λ) and higher energy (E = hν). Which photon has the shorter wavelength?
new_hint: Use ν = c/λ and E = hν to decide how frequency and energy change as wavelength changes. Then compare 254 nm with 940 nm.

title: Problem 3.7
question: A phototherapy lamp is switched to a higher intensity setting, so it is brighter, but its color stays at 458 nm. What changes? A. Each photon carries more energy. B. More photons reach the skin each second, but each photon has the same energy. C. The wavelength becomes shorter. D. The frequency increases.
answer: B. Brightness (intensity) is the number of photons. The energy of each photon depends only on its wavelength, and the wavelength has not changed. A is wrong: the photon energy is set by \( E = hc/\lambda \), and \( \lambda \) is still 458 nm. C is wrong: the color, and so the wavelength, stays the same. D is wrong: with the same wavelength, \( \nu = c/\lambda \) gives the same frequency.
hint: Brightness (intensity) is the number of photons. Does each photon's energy depend on brightness or on wavelength?
new_hint: Which property of light sets the energy of one photon (E = hν)? Did that property change when the lamp got brighter but kept its color?

title: Problem 3.10
question: Which light source, viewed through a prism or spectroscope, gives a line spectrum? A. sunlight B. the glowing filament of an old-style incandescent light bulb C. a sodium vapor street lamp D. a red-hot electric stove burner
answer: C. The lamp holds sodium atoms as a glowing gas. Their electrons can drop only between certain energy levels, so the lamp gives off only certain wavelengths: a few bright lines, the strongest near 589 nm. A is wrong: sunlight spreads into a continuous rainbow. B is wrong: a hot solid filament gives a continuous spectrum. D is wrong: the hot burner is also a hot solid. It glows with a continuous spread of wavelengths, mostly infrared plus some red.
hint: Hot solids give a continuous rainbow; a glowing gas of one element gives only certain lines. Which source is a glowing gas?
new_hint: Line spectra come from separate atoms whose electrons drop between fixed energy levels. For each source, is the glowing material a hot solid or a gas of one element?

title: Problem 3.12
question: A hydrogen electron absorbs a photon and jumps from n = 2 to n = 4. A moment later it drops straight back from n = 4 to n = 2. How does the photon it gives off compare with the photon it absorbed? A. It has the same energy and the same wavelength. B. It has more energy, because the electron is falling. C. It has a longer wavelength, because emitted light is always redder. D. No photon is given off when the electron drops.
answer: A. The energy gap between n = 4 and n = 2 is fixed. Going up takes exactly that much energy, and coming down gives back exactly that much, as one photon of the same wavelength (486 nm, blue-green). B is wrong: the electron cannot give off more energy than the gap between the two levels. C is wrong for a single atom dropping back between the same two levels. (A fluorescent molecule can give off a longer wavelength because it loses some energy first, as in the fluorescent stain problem later in this section, but that is not what happens here.) D is wrong: dropping to a lower level is exactly how the atom gives off a photon.
hint: The gap between two levels is fixed. Is the energy needed to go up the same as the energy released coming back down?
new_hint: Both jumps connect the same two levels. What sets the energy of a photon that is absorbed or given off?

title: Problem 3.16
question: Which statement about the Bohr model is correct? A. It explains hydrogen's line spectrum, and its idea of fixed energy levels is still used today. B. It correctly predicts the line spectra of all the elements. C. It says an electron can have any amount of energy. D. It describes electrons as clouds of probability called orbitals.
answer: A. Bohr's model matches hydrogen's lines very well, and the idea that electron energies are quantized carried over into the modern model. B is wrong: the model fails for atoms with more than one electron. C is the opposite of the model: energies are quantized, like steps on a staircase, with nothing in between. D describes the later quantum-mechanical model (Section 3.3). Bohr pictured electrons moving in fixed circular orbits.
hint: Bohr's model fit hydrogen but failed for atoms with more than one electron. Which of its ideas survived, and which choice describes the later orbital model instead?

title: Problem 3.18
question: Which of these can hold the most electrons? A. one 4p orbital B. the 2s subshell C. the 3p subshell D. the n = 2 shell
answer: D. The n = 2 shell contains the 2s subshell (2 electrons) and the 2p subshell (6 electrons), so it holds 2 + 6 = 8. A is wrong: any single orbital holds at most 2 electrons. B is wrong: an s subshell is one orbital, so it holds 2. C is wrong: a p subshell is three orbitals, so it holds 6, fewer than the 8 of the whole second shell.
hint: One orbital holds 2 electrons; s, p, and d subshells have 1, 3, and 5 orbitals. A shell includes all of its subshells.

title: Problem 3.21
question: Which drawing shows the 2p subshell of a ground-state nitrogen atom correctly? A. 2p [↑↓][↑][  ] B. 2p [↑][↑][↑] C. 2p [↑↓↑][  ][  ] D. 2p [↑][↓][↑]
answer: B. Nitrogen (7 electrons) is 1s 2 2s 2 2p 3 . By Hund's rule, the three 2p electrons go one per orbital, all with the same spin. A breaks Hund's rule: two electrons are paired while an orbital of the same energy is still empty. C breaks the Pauli exclusion principle: no orbital can hold three electrons. D breaks Hund's rule: the electrons are one per orbital, but they must all have the same spin before any pairing.
hint: Nitrogen has three 2p electrons. Apply Hund's rule (one per orbital, same spin) and the Pauli principle (at most 2 per box, opposite spins).

title: Problem 3.27
question: Which is the correct ground-state electron configuration of selenium (Se, Z = 34)? A. 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 6 4s 2 4d 10 4p 4 B. 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 6 4s 2 3d 10 4p 4 C. 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 6 4s 2 4p 4 D. 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 6 3d 10 4s 2 4p 6
answer: B. Reading across row 4, you pass the s block (4s 2 ), the whole d block (3d 10 ), and then four columns of the p block (4p 4 ). Check: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 10 + 4 = 34. A labels the d subshell 4d. The d block in row 4 is 3d (row number minus 1); 4d does not fill until row 5. C leaves out the 3d electrons entirely. Its superscripts add to only 24, not 34. D adds to 36 electrons: that is krypton, not selenium. (Listing 3d before 4s is not the problem; the electron count is.)
hint: Read across row 4: s block, then d block, then p block. The d block in row 4 is the row number minus 1. Check that the superscripts add to 34.

title: Problem 3.30
question: Which element's ground-state configuration ends in 4p 2 ? A. silicon B. germanium C. tin D. calcium
answer: B. A configuration ending in 4p 2 belongs to row 4, second column of the p block: group 14. That is germanium, Ge ([Ar] 4s 2 3d 10 4p 2 , 32 electrons). A is in group 14 but row 3, so silicon ends in 3p 2 . C is in group 14 but row 5, so tin ends in 5p 2 . D is in row 4 but in the s block (group 2), so calcium ends in 4s 2 .
hint: A configuration ending in 4p<sup>2</sup> is in row 4, second column of the p block. Which choice is in that row and that group?

title: Problem 3.32
question: Which ion is not isoelectronic with argon? A. K + B. S 2− C. Ca 2+ D. Al 3+
answer: D. Al 3+ has 13 − 3 = 10 electrons, 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 : it is isoelectronic with neon , not argon (18 electrons). A: K + has 19 − 1 = 18 electrons, like argon. B: S 2− has 16 + 2 = 18 electrons, like argon. C: Ca 2+ has 20 − 2 = 18 electrons, like argon.
hint: Find each ion's electron count (Z − charge for cations, Z + charge for anions). Argon has 18; which one does not match?

title: Problem 3.36
question: Sodium and potassium both react with water in the same way, and both form 1+ ions. Why do they have such similar chemistry? A. They have the same number of protons. B. They have the same number of valence electrons, in the same kind of subshell. C. They have the same number of shells. D. They have nearly the same atomic mass.
answer: B. Both are in group 1 and end in ns 1 (Na: [Ne] 3s 1 ; K: [Ar] 4s 1 ). Valence electrons decide how an element reacts, and each loses its single valence electron to form a 1+ ion. A is wrong: Na has 11 protons and K has 19. Different proton counts mean different elements. C is wrong: sodium's electrons are in 3 shells and potassium's are in 4. D is wrong: their average atomic masses are about 22.99 and 39.10 amu, not close. Mass does not decide chemistry.
hint: Valence electrons decide how an element reacts. What do group 1 elements share at the end of their configurations?

title: Problem 3.38
question: A main-group element X forms the ion X 2− , as the octet rule predicts. In which group is X? A. group 2 B. group 14 C. group 16 D. group 18
answer: C. A 2− ion has gained 2 electrons. An atom gains 2 to reach an octet when it starts with 6 valence electrons, and group 16 elements (O, S, Se) have 6. A is wrong: group 2 atoms have 2 valence electrons and lose them, forming 2+ ions, not 2−. B is wrong: group 14 atoms have 4 valence electrons, halfway to an octet, and usually share electrons instead of forming ions. D is wrong: group 18 atoms already have a full octet and do not form ions.
hint: A 2− ion gained 2 electrons. How many valence electrons must the atom start with to reach an octet by gaining 2?

title: Problem 3.42
question: Which pair of ions are both isoelectronic with krypton? A. Rb + and Br − B. K + and Cl − C. Sr 2+ and Na + D. Se 2− and Ca 2+
answer: A. Krypton has 36 electrons. Rb + : 37 − 1 = 36. Br − : 35 + 1 = 36. Both match. B: K + (18) and Cl − (18) are both isoelectronic with argon. C: Sr 2+ (38 − 2 = 36) matches krypton, but Na + (10) matches neon. D: Se 2− (34 + 2 = 36) matches krypton, but Ca 2+ (18) matches argon.
hint: Krypton has 36 electrons. Find each ion's electron count (Z − charge); both ions in the pair must match.

title: Problem 3.44
question: Which atom has the highest first ionization energy? A. Rb B. Sr C. Ca D. Mg
answer: D. Mg, Ca, and Sr are in group 2, and ionization energy decreases going down a group, so Mg (highest in the group) holds its valence electrons most tightly. Its valence electrons are in shell 3, closest to the nucleus of the four. A is wrong: Rb is in group 1 and period 5, the lowest and farthest left of the four, so it has the lowest ionization energy. B is wrong: Sr is below Ca and Mg in group 2, with valence electrons in shell 5, farther out and easier to remove. C is wrong: Ca is below Mg, with valence electrons in shell 4.
hint: Ionization energy increases up a group and to the right. Look for the extreme: which choice is highest up and farthest right?

title: Problem 3.46
question: Which size comparison is correct? A. Na + is smaller than a Na atom. B. Cl − is smaller than a Cl atom. C. Ca 2+ is larger than a Ca atom. D. O 2− is smaller than an O atom.
answer: A. Na + has lost its only 3s electron, so its outermost electrons are in shell 2, and 11 protons pull on just 10 electrons. Cations are smaller than their atoms. B is backward: Cl − has an extra electron, so the electrons repel each other more and the cloud spreads out. Anions are larger than their atoms. C is backward: Ca 2+ has lost its whole 4s shell, so it is smaller than Ca. D is backward: O 2− has gained two electrons and is larger than O.
hint: Cations lose electrons and are smaller than their atoms; anions gain electrons and are larger. Check each choice against that rule.
new_hint: When an atom loses electrons or gains electrons, how do the number of shells and the repulsion between electrons change? Use that to decide which way the size goes for each choice.

title: Problem 3.47
question: Which element has the most metallic character? A. Ba B. Mg C. Al D. S
answer: A. Metallic character increases toward the lower left of the table, where ionization energy is lowest. Barium is in group 2 and period 6, below magnesium, so it loses its valence electrons most easily. B is a metal, but it is above Ba in group 2, so it holds its valence electrons more tightly. C is a metal to the right of Mg in period 3, so it is less metallic than Mg, and less than Ba. D is a nonmetal at the right side of period 3.
hint: Metallic character increases toward the lower left, where ionization energy is lowest. Look for the extreme.

title: Problem 3.56
question: Which particle has 12 protons, 12 neutrons, and 10 electrons? A. \( ^{24}_{12}\text{Mg} \) B. \( ^{23}_{11}\text{Na}^{+} \) C. \( ^{24}_{12}\text{Mg}^{2+} \) D. \( ^{22}_{10}\text{Ne} \)
answer: C. Z = 12 gives 12 protons (magnesium); 24 − 12 = 12 neutrons; a 2+ charge means 12 − 2 = 10 electrons. A is the neutral atom: 12 protons, 12 neutrons, but 12 electrons. B has 10 electrons and 23 − 11 = 12 neutrons, but only 11 protons. D has 10 electrons and 22 − 10 = 12 neutrons, but only 10 protons. All four particles have 12 neutrons, and B, C, and D are isoelectronic (10 electrons), but only the proton count identifies the element.
hint: Use protons = Z, neutrons = A − Z, and electrons = Z − charge for each choice. Which one gives all three counts?

title: Problem 3.57
question: A dental assistant turns a curing light to a higher power setting. The light gets brighter but stays the same blue. Which property of the light wave increased? A. Amplitude B. Wavelength C. Frequency D. Energy of each photon
answer: A. Amplitude is the height of the wave, which we see as brightness (intensity): turning up the power is like turning up a dimmer switch. B: a change in wavelength would change the color. C: frequency is tied to wavelength by \( c = \lambda\nu \), so it also would change the color. D: each photon's energy depends only on its frequency (\( E = h\nu \)); a brighter beam has more photons, not more energetic ones.
hint: Which wave property do we see as brightness? A change in wavelength or frequency would change the color.

title: Problem 3.60
question: Which electron configuration is impossible? A. 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 6 4s 1 B. 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 3 C. 1s 2 2s 2 2p 5 3s 1 D. 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 4
answer: B. An s subshell holds at most 2 electrons, so 3s 3 cannot exist. Work it out yourself before reading the choices, then check every subshell against its capacity. A is the ground state of potassium (19 electrons). C is an excited state of neon (10 electrons): one 2p electron has moved up to 3s. Unusual, but possible. D is the ground state of sulfur (16 electrons).
hint: Check every subshell against its capacity: s holds 2, p holds 6. An excited state is possible; an overfilled subshell is not.

title: Problem 3.61
question: Which configuration describes a magnesium atom in an excited state? A. [Ne] 3s 2 B. [Ne] 3s 1 3p 1 C. [Ne] 3s 3 D. [Ne] 3s 2 3p 1
answer: B. It still has 10 + 2 = 12 electrons (magnesium), but one 3s electron has moved up to 3p. A is magnesium's ground state. C is impossible (an s subshell holds only 2). D has 13 electrons: that is the ground state of aluminum, not magnesium.
hint: An excited state keeps magnesium's 12 electrons but moves one up. Check each choice's electron count and each subshell's capacity.

title: Problem 3.63
question: Which description of the electron-dot (Lewis) symbol of the phosphide ion, P 3− , is correct? A. P with 5 dots and no brackets B. P with 8 dots, in brackets, with a 3− charge outside C. P in empty brackets with a 3− charge outside D. P with 3 dots, in brackets, with a 3− charge outside
answer: B. Phosphorus (group 15) has 5 valence electrons; the 3− ion gained 3 more, for 8 dots (an octet). Ions are written in brackets with the charge outside. A is the neutral phosphorus atom. C is how a cation is drawn (its valence electrons are gone); an anion keeps and adds dots. D shows only the 3 gained electrons and forgets the original 5.
hint: How many valence electrons does phosphorus have, and how many does the 3− ion gain? Ions are drawn in brackets with the charge outside.

title: Problem 3.64
question: Na + , Mg 2+ , Al 3+ , and F − all have 10 electrons. Which list puts them in order from smallest to largest? A. Al 3+ < Mg 2+ < Na + < F − B. F − < Na + < Mg 2+ < Al 3+ C. Na + < Mg 2+ < Al 3+ < F − D. They are all the same size, because they have the same number of electrons.
answer: A. The same 10 electrons are pulled by 13, 12, 11, and 9 protons. The more protons, the tighter the pull and the smaller the ion: a 3+ ion "hoards" its electrons most, and the anion, with more electrons than protons, spreads out most. B is the exact reverse: it treats more positive charge as bigger. C orders the cations backward; a larger positive charge makes a cation smaller, not larger. D ignores the nucleus. Equal electron counts do not mean equal sizes when the proton counts differ.
hint: All four have 10 electrons, so compare protons. More protons pull the same electrons in tighter, making the ion smaller.
new_hint: All four ions have the same 10 electrons. What is different about them, and how does that difference change how tightly the electrons are held?

title: Problem 3.65
question: Which atom has the lowest first ionization energy? A. Cs B. Ca C. Se D. F
answer: A. Look for the extreme: cesium is the farthest down and to the left (group 1, period 6). Its one valence electron is far from the nucleus, and giving it away reaches an octet, so it comes off easily. B, calcium, is higher up (period 4) and one group farther right, so it is smaller and holds its electrons more tightly. C, selenium, is a nonmetal on the right side; it tends to gain electrons, not lose them. D, fluorine, is near the upper right corner, with one of the highest ionization energies of all.
hint: Ionization energy is lowest toward the lower left. Look for the extreme: which choice is farthest down and to the left?

title: Problem 3.66
question: Which is the correct ground-state electron configuration of chromium (Cr, Z = 24)? A. [Ar] 4s 2 3d 4 B. [Ar] 4s 1 3d 5 C. [Ar] 3d 6 D. [Ar] 4s 2 4d 4
answer: B. Chromium is one of the two famous exceptions. The filling order would end in 4s 2 3d 4 , but a half-filled d subshell is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves to 3d, giving every one of the six outer electrons its own orbital. Check: 18 + 1 + 5 = 24. A follows the filling order but misses the exception. A configuration that ends in s 2 d 4 is the signal to move one s electron. C moves both 4s electrons. Only one moves; 3d 6 is neither half-filled nor filled, so it gains no extra stability. D uses 4d in row 4. The d block is n − 1, so row 4 fills 3d; it also misses the exception.
hint: Never end a configuration in s<sup>2</sup>d<sup>4</sup>. Which arrangement of the d subshell is extra stable for chromium?

title: Problem 4.1
question: How many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit of calcium phosphate, Ca 3 (PO 4 ) 2 , the main mineral in bone? A. 4 B. 8 C. 12 D. 13
answer: B. The subscript 2 after the parentheses multiplies everything inside them: 2 phosphate groups × 4 O each = 8 O atoms. A counts only one phosphate group; it forgets to multiply by the 2 outside the parentheses. C multiplies the 4 by the 3 that belongs to calcium. A subscript only counts the atom (or parentheses) just before it. D is the total number of atoms of all three elements: 3 Ca + 2 P + 8 O = 13. The question asks only for oxygen.
hint: The subscript after the parentheses multiplies everything inside. How many O are in one phosphate, and how many phosphates are there?

title: Problem 4.3
question: Which compound is molecular? A. NH 4 Cl B. N 2 O C. KNO 3 D. Fe(OH) 3
answer: B. N 2 O (nitrous oxide, the "laughing gas" used in dental offices) contains only nonmetals, nitrogen and oxygen, so its atoms share electrons in a molecule. A starts with the ammonium ion, NH 4 + , so it is ionic even though every element in it is a nonmetal. C starts with potassium, a metal: it is ionic (K + and NO 3 − ). D starts with iron, a metal: it is ionic (Fe 3+ and three OH − ions). Ending in OH does not make it an acid.
hint: Check the first part of each formula: a metal or NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> means ionic. Which compound is made only of nonmetals, with no ammonium ion?

title: Problem 4.5
question: Which list contains only elements that exist as diatomic molecules when they are uncombined? A. hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, chlorine B. hydrogen, helium, nitrogen, oxygen C. sodium, chlorine, bromine, iodine D. oxygen, sulfur, fluorine, chlorine
answer: A. H 2 , N 2 , O 2 , and Cl 2 are four of the seven diatomic elements (H 2 , N 2 , O 2 , F 2 , Cl 2 , Br 2 , I 2 ). B includes helium, a noble gas that exists as single atoms. C includes sodium, a metal. Chlorine, bromine, and iodine are diatomic, but sodium is not. D includes sulfur, which is not one of the seven. (It sits below oxygen, but the "7" shape on the periodic table goes N, O, F and then down the halogens.)
hint: Recall the seven diatomic elements: hydrogen plus the "7" shape (N, O, F, then down the halogens). Eliminate any list with a noble gas, a metal, or an element off that list.
new_hint: Recall the seven diatomic elements and where they sit on the periodic table (the “7” shape). Check every element in each list; one element off that list rules the list out.

title: Problem 4.8
question: Ammonium nitrate, NH 4 NO 3 , is a nitrogen fertilizer used on Central Valley farms. Which statement about it is true? A. It is molecular, because every element in it is a nonmetal. B. It is ionic, made of NH 4 + and NO 3 − ions. C. It is an acid, because its formula contains hydrogen. D. One formula unit contains 3 nitrogen atoms.
answer: B. The formula starts with the ammonium ion, NH 4 + , so the compound is ionic. Its anion is nitrate, NO 3 − . A falls into the ammonium trap: ammonium is the one cation in this course with no metal, but it is still an ion. C is wrong: acids start with H. Here the H atoms are inside the ammonium ion. D is wrong: there is one N in NH 4 + and one in NO 3 − , so 2 N atoms (with 4 H and 3 O, 9 atoms in all).
hint: Look at the first part of the formula: NH<sub>4</sub> is a cation. Also count the N atoms in both ions before you trust any atom count.
new_hint: Is the first part of the formula a metal, a nonmetal atom, or a polyatomic ion from the green sheet? Count the N atoms in the whole formula before you trust any atom count.

title: Problem 4.10
question: What is the formula of magnesium phosphate? A. MgPO 4 B. Mg 3 (PO 4 ) 2 C. Mg 2 (PO 4 ) 3 D. Mg 3 P 2
answer: B. Mg 2+ and PO 4 3− : swap-drop gives Mg 3 (PO 4 ) 2 . Check: 3(2+) + 2(3−) = 6+ + 6− = 0. A is not neutral: (2+) + (3−) = 1−. C puts each ion's own charge on itself instead of swapping: 2(2+) + 3(3−) = 4+ + 9− = 5−. D is magnesium phosphide , made with the P 3− ion, not phosphate. It has no oxygen.
hint: Write the ions first: Mg<sup>2+</sup> and phosphate from the green sheet. Swap-drop, then check which choice gives zero total charge and still contains phosphate.

title: Problem 4.14
question: Calcium nitrate is sold as a fertilizer that supplies both calcium and nitrogen. What is its formula? A. CaNO 3 B. Ca(NO 3 ) 2 C. Ca 2 NO 3 D. CaNO 32
answer: B. Ca 2+ needs two NO 3 − ions, and two of a polyatomic ion go in parentheses: Ca(NO 3 ) 2 . Check: (2+) + 2(1−) = 0. A is not neutral: (2+) + (1−) = 1+. C has the ratio backward: 2(2+) + (1−) = 3+. D has the right idea but no parentheses, so it reads as 32 oxygen atoms in one ion. Never change or add to the subscripts inside a polyatomic ion.
hint: Write Ca<sup>2+</sup> and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>. How many nitrates balance one calcium, and how do you show more than one polyatomic ion?

title: Problem 4.17
question: A metal M forms an oxide with the formula M 2 O 3 . Assuming the metal keeps the same charge, what is the formula of its chloride? A. MCl B. MCl 2 C. MCl 3 D. M 3 Cl
answer: C. In M 2 O 3 , three O 2− ions give 6−, shared by two M ions, so M is 3+. M 3+ needs three Cl − : MCl 3 . A would need M + . B would need M 2+ ; it reads the subscript 2 in M 2 O 3 as the charge. D has a total charge of 3(3+) + (1−) = 8+, so it is not neutral.
hint: Use the oxide to find the metal's charge: three O<sup>2−</sup> give how much negative charge, shared by two M? Then pair that cation with Cl<sup>−</sup>.

title: Problem 4.20
question: What is the name of Fe 2 (SO 4 ) 3 ? A. iron(II) sulfate B. iron(III) sulfate C. diiron trisulfate D. iron(III) sulfite
answer: B. Three sulfate ions give 3(2−) = 6−, shared by two iron ions, so each is Fe 3+ : iron(III) sulfate (ferric sulfate). A uses the subscript 2 as the charge. The Roman numeral is the charge of one iron ion. C uses Greek prefixes, which are for molecular compounds; this is ionic. D changes the anion. SO 4 2− is sulfate; sulfite is SO 3 2− .
hint: Start from sulfate's charge on the green sheet. Three sulfates carry how much negative charge, and how many iron ions share it?

title: Problem 4.21
question: Which compound needs a Roman numeral (or an -ous/-ic ending) in its name? A. ZnCl 2 B. AgBr C. SnF 2 D. Al 2 O 3
answer: C. Tin forms both Sn 2+ and Sn 4+ , so the name must say which: tin(II) fluoride, or stannous fluoride. A: zinc is always Zn 2+ , so ZnCl 2 is simply zinc chloride. B: silver is always Ag + in this course, so AgBr is silver bromide. D: aluminum is always Al 3+ , so Al 2 O 3 is aluminum oxide.
hint: Which metal is not on the fixed-charge list (group 1, group 2, Al, Zn, Ag)? That metal's name must state its charge.

title: Problem 4.25
question: Iron supplements are often sold as ferrous sulfate . What is its formula? A. FeSO 4 B. Fe 2 (SO 4 ) 3 C. FeSO 3 D. Fe 2 SO 4
answer: A. Ferrous is the lower charge of iron, Fe 2+ (iron(II)). Fe 2+ and SO 4 2− combine 1 : 1: FeSO 4 , iron(II) sulfate. B is ferric sulfate, iron(III) sulfate. The -ic ending is the higher charge, Fe 3+ . C is iron(II) sulfite. SO 3 2− is sulfite, not sulfate. D is not neutral with Fe 2+ : 2(2+) + (2−) = 2+. It would need Fe + , which is not an iron ion in this course.
hint: Ferrous means the lower charge of iron. Write that ion with sulfate (check -ate versus -ite on the green sheet) and balance the charges.

title: Problem 4.29
question: What is the name of P 4 O 6 ? A. phosphorus oxide B. tetraphosphorus hexoxide C. diphosphorus trioxide D. phosphorus(III) oxide
answer: B. Phosphorus and oxygen are both nonmetals, so the name uses prefixes: tetra- for 4 P and hexa- for 6 O, with the a dropped before "oxide." A leaves out the prefixes, so it does not say which phosphorus oxide this is (P 4 O 10 is also a phosphorus oxide). C is the name of P 2 O 3 . Molecular formulas are never reduced, so the name must match P 4 O 6 . D uses a Roman numeral, which is only for variable-charge metals in ionic compounds.
hint: Classify first: two nonmetals means Greek prefixes with the exact atom counts. Molecular formulas are never reduced, and Roman numerals are only for metals.

title: Problem 4.30
question: Which formula and name are correctly matched? A. CO, monocarbon monoxide B. SO 3 , sulfur trioxide C. PCl 5 , phosphorus chloride D. NF 3 , nitrogen(III) fluoride
answer: B. One S (no prefix on the first element) and three O (tri-), with the -ide ending. A uses mono- on the first element. CO is carbon monoxide. C is missing the prefix on chlorine: phosphorus pentachloride. (PCl 3 is also a phosphorus chloride.) D uses a Roman numeral on a nonmetal. NF 3 is nitrogen trifluoride.
hint: Check three rules for molecular names: no mono- on the first element, a prefix on the second element, and no Roman numerals.

title: Problem 4.32
question: Which compound is molecular and correctly named? A. AlCl 3 , aluminum trichloride B. PCl 3 , phosphorus trichloride C. MgCl 2 , magnesium dichloride D. NaCl, sodium monochloride
answer: B. Phosphorus and chlorine are both nonmetals, so prefixes are used. A is ionic (aluminum is a metal); its name is aluminum chloride, with no prefix. C is ionic; its name is magnesium chloride. D is ionic; its name is sodium chloride.
hint: First find which compounds are molecular (nonmetals only). Ionic compounds never take prefixes.

title: Problem 4.37
question: What is the name of H 2 SO 3 ? A. sulfuric acid B. sulfurous acid C. hydrosulfurous acid D. hydrosulfuric acid
answer: B. The anion is SO 3 2− , sulfite. An -ite ion becomes an -ous acid: sulfurous acid. A is H 2 SO 4 , from sulfate (-ate → -ic). C adds hydro- to an oxyacid. Hydro- is only for acids with no oxygen. D is H 2 S(aq), the binary acid from sulfide.
hint: Which anion is SO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>: sulfate or sulfite? Switch its ending, and remember that hydro- is only for acids with no oxygen.

title: Problem 4.38
question: When bleach dissolves in water, the main germ-killing species is an acid with the formula HClO. Some wound-care solutions also contain it. What is its name? A. chloric acid B. chlorous acid C. hypochlorous acid D. hydrochloric acid
answer: C. The anion ClO − is hypochlorite. The -ite ending becomes -ous, and the prefix hypo- stays: hypochlorous acid. A is HClO 3 , from chlorate. B is HClO 2 , from chlorite. D is HCl(aq), from chloride; it has no oxygen.
hint: Name the anion ClO<sup>−</sup> first (one less O than chlorite). Keep any prefix, and switch -ite to -ous or -ate to -ic.

title: Problem 4.42
question: An oxyacid has the formula H 3 XO 4 and a name that ends in "-ic acid." What are the charge and the name ending of its anion, XO 4 ? A. 3−; the anion name ends in -ate B. 3−; the anion name ends in -ite C. 3+; the anion name ends in -ate D. 4−; the anion name ends in -ide
answer: A. Three H + cancel the anion's charge, so it is 3−. An -ic acid comes from an -ate ion. (Phosphoric acid, H 3 PO 4 , from phosphate, PO 4 3− , fits this pattern.) B has the right charge but the wrong ending: an -ite ion gives an -ous acid. C has the wrong sign. The H + ions are positive, so the anion must be negative. D confuses the 4 oxygen atoms with the charge, and an -ide ion contains no oxygen and gives a hydro-...-ic acid.
hint: How many H<sup>+</sup> does the acid have, and what anion charge cancels them? Which anion ending gives an -ic acid?

title: Problem 4.45
question: Which compound is named with Greek prefixes? A. K 2 O B. Cl 2 O C. Cu 2 O D. Na 2 O 2
answer: B. Chlorine and oxygen are both nonmetals, so Cl 2 O is molecular: dichlorine monoxide. A is ionic (potassium is a metal): potassium oxide. C is ionic: one O 2− over two Cu gives Cu + , copper(I) oxide (cuprous oxide). It uses a Roman numeral, not a prefix. D is ionic: sodium peroxide.
hint: Greek prefixes are only for molecular compounds. Which choice has no metal in it?

title: Problem 4.47
question: Which formula and name are correctly matched? A. FeO, iron oxide B. NO, nitrogen monoxide C. Na 2 S, disodium sulfide D. HClO 4 , hydroperchloric acid
answer: B. NO is molecular (two nonmetals): one N, no prefix, and one O, mono-. Its common name is nitric oxide. A needs the iron charge: one O 2− means Fe 2+ , so iron(II) oxide (ferrous oxide). C is ionic, so no prefixes: sodium sulfide. D is an oxyacid, so no hydro-: perchloric acid.
hint: Check each against its type's rules: iron needs its charge in the name, ionic names never use prefixes, and oxyacids never get hydro-.

title: Problem 4.50
question: A student names Co 2 (CO 3 ) 3 "cobalt(II) carbonate." What is the correct name? A. cobalt(III) carbonate B. dicobalt tricarbonate C. cobaltous carbonate D. cobalt(III) carbide
answer: A. Three carbonate ions give 3(2−) = 6−, shared by two cobalt ions, so each is Co 3+ : cobalt(III) carbonate (cobaltic carbonate). The student used the subscript 2 as the charge. B uses prefixes, which are not used for ionic compounds. C means cobalt(II), the same mistake as the student's. D changes the anion. CO 3 2− is carbonate, a polyatomic ion that keeps its name.
hint: Find cobalt's charge from carbonate: three CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> carry how much charge, shared by how many cobalt ions? Also check that the anion name matches CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>.

title: Problem 4.53
question: An ion has 16 protons and 18 electrons. Which choice identifies the ion and correctly gives the formula of its compound with aluminum? A. S 2− ; Al 2 S 3 B. S 2− ; Al 3 S 2 C. Cl − ; AlCl 3 D. Ar; no compound forms
answer: A. 16 protons means sulfur, and 2 more electrons than protons gives a 2− charge: S 2− , sulfide. With Al 3+ , swap-drop gives Al 2 S 3 (aluminum sulfide). Check: 2(3+) + 3(2−) = 0. B identifies the ion correctly but does not swap the charges: 3(3+) + 2(2−) = 5+. C is wrong because chlorine has 17 protons, not 16. D is wrong because argon has 18 protons. A particle with 16 protons is sulfur, whatever its electron count; it only has as many electrons as argon.
hint: Protons identify the element; extra electrons give the negative charge. Then pair that ion with Al<sup>3+</sup> using swap-drop.

title: Problem 4.56
question: In which compound do both ions have the same electron configuration as neon? A. NaF B. KCl C. MgS D. CaO
answer: A. Na + (11 − 1 = 10 electrons) and F − (9 + 1 = 10 electrons) are both isoelectronic with neon, 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 . The compound is sodium fluoride. B: K + and Cl − both have 18 electrons, like argon (potassium chloride). C: Mg 2+ has 10 electrons (neon), but S 2− has 18 (argon) (magnesium sulfide). D: O 2− has 10 electrons (neon), but Ca 2+ has 18 (argon) (calcium oxide).
hint: Count each ion's electrons: subtract for a cation, add for an anion. Neon has 10. Which choice has both ions at that count?

title: Problem 4.58
question: What is the formula of cobalt(III) oxide? A. CoO 3 B. Co 3 O C. Co 2 O 3 D. CoO
answer: C. The Roman numeral is the charge: Co 3+ . Oxide is O 2− . Swap-drop gives Co 2 O 3 . Check: 2(3+) + 3(2−) = 0. A treats the numeral III as a subscript on oxygen; CoO 3 would need Co 6+ . B puts the numeral on cobalt as a subscript; three Co 3+ and one O 2− give 7+, not 0. D is cobalt(II) oxide, Co 2+ with O 2− .
hint: The Roman numeral is cobalt's charge, not a subscript. Write the cobalt ion and O<sup>2−</sup> with their charges, then swap-drop.

title: Problem 4.59
question: Which formula is written correctly? A. K 2 (CO 3 ), potassium carbonate B. Mg(NO 3 ) 2 , magnesium nitrate C. Ba(Cl) 2 , barium chloride D. Sn 2 (SO 4 ) 4 , tin(IV) sulfate
answer: B. Mg 2+ needs two NO 3 − ions, so the nitrate is in parentheses with a 2 outside. A has the right atoms, but parentheses are used only when the polyatomic ion's subscript is 2 or more. Write K 2 CO 3 . C puts parentheses around a single atom. Parentheses are only for polyatomic ions: BaCl 2 . D was not reduced. The outside subscripts 2 and 4 share a factor of 2: Sn(SO 4 ) 2 .
hint: Parentheses go only around a polyatomic ion that appears two or more times, and subscripts must be reduced. Test each choice against both rules.

title: Problem 4.60
question: A student names Sn(SO 4 ) 2 by moving each subscript back up as a charge ("reverse swap-drop"). What is the correct charge on tin, and the correct name? A. Sn 2+ ; tin(II) sulfate B. Sn 4+ ; tin(IV) sulfate C. Sn 2+ ; tin disulfate D. Sn 4+ ; tin(II) sulfate
answer: B. Start from the ion you know: sulfate is always SO 4 2− . Two sulfates carry 2(2−) = 4−, so the single tin ion is Sn 4+ , tin(IV) sulfate. The formula was reduced from Sn 2 (SO 4 ) 4 . A is what un-swapping gives. It would also make sulfate 1−, which it never is. C uses a prefix; ionic compounds never use di-, and the charge is wrong. D has the right charge but the wrong numeral; the numeral must match the charge, IV.
hint: Start from the ion you know: sulfate is always 2−. Two sulfates carry how much charge, all on one tin ion? The numeral must equal that charge.

title: Problem 4.63
question: A bottle in the stockroom is labeled MnSO 4 . What is its correct name? A. magnesium sulfate B. manganese sulfate C. manganese(II) sulfate D. magnesium(II) sulfate
answer: C. Mn is manganese, a transition metal that forms more than one ion, so it needs a Roman numeral. Sulfate is 2−, so the manganese is 2+: manganese(II) sulfate. A and D name the wrong metal. Magnesium is Mg (MgSO 4 , the electrolyte Mateo received by IV (intravenously)), and as a group 2 metal it never takes a numeral, so D is wrong twice.
