B is the right metal, but leaving off the numeral does not say which manganese ion is present.
hint: Mn or Mg? Check the symbol on the periodic table. Then ask whether that metal has a fixed charge or needs a Roman numeral.

title: Problem 5.1
question: One mole of sodium chloride, NaCl, contains A. 58.44 formula units of NaCl. B. 6.0221 × 10 23 formula units of NaCl. C. 6.0221 × 10 23 ions in total, half Na + and half Cl − . D. exactly 1 g of NaCl.
answer: B. A mole of anything is 6.0221 × 10 23 of that thing. NaCl is ionic, so its particles are formula units (Section 4.1), and one mole is 6.0221 × 10 23 of them. A mixes up the molar mass with the count: 58.44 is the mass of one mole in grams, not the number of formula units. C undercounts the ions. Each formula unit holds one Na + and one Cl − , so one mole of NaCl holds 6.0221 × 10 23 of each ion, 1.2044 × 10 24 ions in total. D treats the mole as a mass. One mole of NaCl has a mass of 58.44 g; a mole is a number, not a mass.
hint: A mole is a count of the particles named, and for an ionic compound the particle is a formula unit. Is 58.44 a count or a mass?
new_hint: A mole is a count of whatever particle the formula names. What is the basic particle of an ionic compound like NaCl? Is 58.44 a count or a mass?

title: Problem 5.4
question: A glass of water contains 1.20 × 10 24 water molecules. How many moles of water is that? A. 7.23 × 10 47 mol B. 1.99 mol C. 0.502 mol D. 35.9 mol
answer: B. \( 1.20 \times 10^{24}\ \text{molecules} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol}}{6.0221 \times 10^{23}\ \text{molecules}} = 1.99\ \text{mol H}_2\text{O} \) The count is about twice Avogadro's number, so about 2 mol makes sense. A multiplies by Avogadro's number instead of dividing. A number of moles near 10 47 is the sign of an upside-down factor. C divides the wrong way round, 6.0221 × 10 23 ÷ 1.20 × 10 24 . The units come out as “per mole,” not moles, and the answer is too small for a count about twice Avogadro's number. D goes one step too far: 1.99 mol × 18.015 g/mol = 35.9, which is the mass in grams , not the number of moles.
hint: Is the count larger or smaller than one mole's worth? Molecules are given, so divide by Avogadro's number; then check which choice is in moles, not grams.

title: Problem 5.6
question: Compare 1.00 mol of hydrogen gas, H 2 , with 1.00 mol of oxygen gas, O 2 . Which statement is true? A. They have the same number of molecules and the same mass. B. They have the same number of molecules, but the O 2 sample has the greater mass. C. The O 2 sample has more molecules, because oxygen molecules are heavier. D. The H 2 sample has more molecules, because hydrogen molecules are smaller.
answer: B. One mole is always 6.0221 × 10 23 particles, so both samples hold the same number of molecules. Each O 2 molecule is heavier, so the oxygen sample weighs more (31.998 g versus 2.016 g; Section 5.2). A is wrong: the same number of heavier particles has more mass, like a dozen bricks versus a dozen marbles. C and D are wrong for the same reason: a mole is a fixed count, like a dozen. The size or mass of the particles does not change how many are in a mole.
hint: A mole is a fixed count, like a dozen. With the same count of heavier molecules, what happens to the mass?
new_hint: What does one mole of any substance always contain? Then compare the molar masses of H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>.

title: Problem 5.9
question: Which sample contains the greatest number of sodium atoms? A. 0.10 mol of Na B. 5.0 × 10 22 Na atoms C. 9.0 × 10 21 Na atoms D. 0.050 mol of Na
answer: A. Put every choice in the same unit before comparing. 0.10 mol × 6.0221 × 10 23 = 6.0 × 10 22 atoms, which is more than any other choice. B looks biggest only because 5.0 × 10 22 is a large-looking number next to "0.10." In the same unit, 5.0 × 10 22 is less than 6.0 × 10 22 . C is 9.0 × 10 21 atoms, about one-seventh of choice A. D is half of choice A: 0.050 mol × 6.0221 × 10 23 = 3.0 × 10 22 atoms.
hint: Put every choice in the same unit before comparing: convert the mole amounts to atoms with Avogadro's number.

title: Problem 5.12
question: A balloon holds 0.20 mol of helium atoms. Which answer reports the number of helium atoms with the correct significant figures? A. 1.2044 × 10 23 atoms B. 1.20 × 10 23 atoms C. 1.2 × 10 23 atoms D. 1 × 10 23 atoms
answer: C. In multiplication, the answer keeps the fewest significant figures of the measured values. 0.20 has 2 significant figures (the trailing zero after the decimal point counts), and Avogadro's number as given has 5, so the answer has 2: 0.20 × 6.0221 × 10 23 = 1.2 × 10 23 . A copies every digit from the calculator (5 significant figures), more precision than 0.20 mol supports. B has 3 significant figures; it would be right for 0.200 mol. D has only 1 significant figure; it treats 0.20 as if it were 0.2.
hint: In multiplication, the answer keeps the fewest significant figures. How many does the mole value have? (A trailing zero after the decimal point counts.)

title: Problem 5.14
question: Calcium nitrate, Ca(NO 3 ) 2 , is sold to Valley growers as a fertilizer that supplies both calcium and nitrogen. What is its molar mass? (Ca 40.08, N 14.007, O 15.999) A. 82 g/mol B. 102.08 g/mol C. 116.09 g/mol D. 164.09 g/mol
answer: D. The 2 outside the parentheses multiplies everything inside, so one formula unit has 1 Ca, 2 N, and 6 O: \( 40.08 + 2(14.007) + 6(15.999) = 40.08 + 28.014 + 95.994 = 164.088 \rightarrow 164.09\ \text{g/mol} \) A adds atomic numbers (20 + 2 × 7 + 6 × 8 = 82) instead of atomic masses. B ignores the subscript 2 after the parentheses and calculates CaNO 3 (1 N, 3 O): 102.08. C applies the 2 to nitrogen only, giving 2 N but just 3 O: 116.09.
hint: Count atoms first: the 2 outside the parentheses multiplies both N and O. Use atomic masses, not atomic numbers.

title: Problem 5.15
question: A patient on supplemental oxygen breathes O 2 molecules. What is the mass of one mole of O 2 molecules? A. 15.999 g B. 31.998 g C. 16 g D. 5.3134 × 10 −23 g
answer: B. Each O 2 molecule has two oxygen atoms, so its molar mass is 2(15.999) = 31.998 g/mol, and one mole has a mass of 31.998 g. A is the mass of one mole of oxygen atoms , not O 2 molecules. C doubles oxygen's atomic number (8 × 2 = 16) instead of using its atomic mass. D is the mass of a single O 2 molecule (31.998 g ÷ 6.0221 × 10 23 ), not of a whole mole.
hint: One O<sub>2</sub> molecule contains two oxygen atoms. Is the question about atoms, molecules, or a single molecule?

title: Problem 5.19
question: Potassium sulfate, K 2 SO 4 , is used as a potassium fertilizer on Valley orchards. Using K 39.10, S 32.06, and O 15.999, which answer reports its molar mass correctly? A. 135.16 g/mol B. 174.256 g/mol C. 174.26 g/mol D. 174.3 g/mol
answer: C. 2(39.10) + 32.06 + 4(15.999) = 78.20 + 32.06 + 63.996 = 174.256. This is an addition, so the answer keeps the fewest decimal places : K and S have 2, so the answer has 2, 174.26 g/mol. A counts only one potassium: 39.10 + 32.06 + 63.996 = 135.16. The subscript 2 on K is missing. B keeps 3 decimal places, but 39.10 and 32.06 are known only to the hundredths place. D applies the multiplication rule (fewest significant figures, 4 from 39.10) to a sum. Sums follow the decimal-place rule, and subscripts are exact, so they never limit the answer.
hint: Count both K atoms, add the masses, then use the addition rule: keep the fewest decimal places, not the fewest significant figures.

title: Problem 5.21
question: Why is the molar mass of an element, in g/mol, the same number as its average atomic mass, in amu? A. Because Avogadro's number was chosen so that one mole of atoms has a mass in grams equal to the atomic mass in amu. B. Because 1 amu and 1 g are the same mass. C. Because every atom has a mass of 1 g. D. It is true only for carbon-12; for every other element the numbers are different.
answer: A. The mole is defined so that 6.0221 × 10 23 atoms of mass x amu have a total mass of x grams. That is why the number under each symbol on the yellow sheet serves both as the atomic mass (amu) and the molar mass (g/mol). B is far off: 1 g is 6.0221 × 10 23 amu. A single atom is unimaginably lighter than a gram. C is false: one atom has a mass of about 10 −23 g or less (for example, one iron atom is 9.274 × 10 −23 g). D is false: carbon-12 sets the scale, but the match holds for every element and compound (for example, Na 22.99 amu and 22.99 g/mol).
hint: Think about how Avogadro's number was chosen: it links amu for one particle to grams for one mole. Can 1 amu really equal 1 g?
new_hint: Compare the size of 1 amu with 1 g: are they the same mass? Then think about how Avogadro's number was chosen.

title: Problem 5.27
question: An ibuprofen tablet contains 200. mg of ibuprofen, C 13 H 18 O 2 (206.285 g/mol). How many millimoles of ibuprofen is that? A. 0.970 mmol B. 970. mmol C. 4.13 × 10 4 mmol D. 9.70 × 10 −4 mmol
answer: A. Because 1 mmol of ibuprofen has a mass of 206.285 mg (both units are scaled by 10 −3 ), the molar mass can be used as 206.285 mg/mmol: \( 200.\ \text{mg} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mmol}}{206.285\ \text{mg}} = 0.970\ \text{mmol} \) (The decimal point in "200." makes all three digits significant.) The same answer comes from 0.200 g ÷ 206.285 g/mol = 9.70 × 10 −4 mol = 0.970 mmol. B is a mg/g slip: it treats 200. mg as 200. g, which gives 0.970 mol , or 970. mmol, a thousand times too much. C multiplies by the molar mass instead of dividing; the units would be mg 2 /mmol, not mmol. D is the answer in moles (9.70 × 10 −4 mol) mislabeled as millimoles, or divided by 1000 one time too many.
hint: Molar mass in g/mol is the same number in mg/mmol, so divide the mg by it directly. Should the answer be more or less than 1 mmol?

title: Problem 5.33
question: You have 10.0 g of each of the four substances below. Which sample contains the greatest number of molecules? A. water, H 2 O (18.015 g/mol) B. carbon dioxide, CO 2 (44.009 g/mol) C. methane, CH 4 (16.043 g/mol) D. All four contain the same number of molecules.
answer: C. For the same mass, the substance with the smallest molar mass has the most moles, and so the most molecules: 10.0 g ÷ 16.043 g/mol = 0.623 mol CH 4 , or 3.75 × 10 23 molecules. (Water: 0.555 mol, 3.34 × 10 23 ; CO 2 : 0.227 mol, 1.37 × 10 23 .) A is close but second: water's molar mass (18.015) is a little larger than methane's (16.043), so 10.0 g of water is slightly fewer moles. B has it backward. Heavier molecules mean fewer of them fit into 10.0 g, so CO 2 has the fewest. D confuses equal masses with equal moles. Equal moles would have equal numbers of molecules; equal masses do not.
hint: Same mass for each: does a smaller or a larger molar mass give more moles, and so more molecules?

title: Problem 5.37
question: What is the mass of 0.150 mol of carbon dioxide, CO 2 (44.009 g/mol)? A. 3.41 × 10 −3 g B. 6.60 g C. 293 g D. 9.03 × 10 22 g
answer: B. Moles to grams: multiply by the molar mass. \( 0.150\ \text{mol CO}_2 \times \dfrac{44.009\ \text{g CO}_2}{1\ \text{mol CO}_2} = 6.60\ \text{g CO}_2 \) A divides moles by molar mass (0.150 ÷ 44.009); the units come out mol 2 /g, not g. C divides molar mass by moles (44.009 ÷ 0.150). Less than one mole must weigh less than 44 g, not more. D multiplies by Avogadro's number. That gives the number of molecules (9.03 × 10 22 ), not a mass in grams.
hint: Moles to grams: which way does the molar mass factor go so moles cancel? Less than a mole should weigh less than the molar mass.

title: Problem 5.38
question: How many moles of oxygen atoms are in 0.50 mol of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO 3 ) 2 ? A. 0.50 mol B. 1.5 mol C. 3.0 mol D. 1.0 mol
answer: C. One formula unit of Ca(NO 3 ) 2 contains 2 × 3 = 6 O atoms, so \( 0.50\ \text{mol Ca(NO}_3)_2 \times \dfrac{6\ \text{mol O}}{1\ \text{mol Ca(NO}_3)_2} = 3.0\ \text{mol O} \) A skips the subscript step: 0.50 mol is the amount of the compound, not of oxygen atoms. B uses 3 O per formula unit and ignores the 2 outside the parentheses. D is the moles of nitrogen atoms (2 N per formula unit), not oxygen.
hint: Count the O in one formula unit: the 2 outside the parentheses multiplies the 3 O. Use that count as the mole ratio.

title: Problem 5.41
question: A calcium supplement tablet contains 1.25 g of calcium carbonate, CaCO 3 (100.09 g/mol). What mass of calcium does it contain? (Ca 40.08) A. 1.25 g B. 0.501 g C. 3.12 g D. 0.250 g
answer: B. Grams of compound → moles of compound → moles of Ca (1 : 1) → grams of Ca: \( 1.25\ \text{g CaCO}_3 \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol CaCO}_3}{100.09\ \text{g CaCO}_3} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol Ca}}{1\ \text{mol CaCO}_3} \times \dfrac{40.08\ \text{g Ca}}{1\ \text{mol Ca}} = 0.501\ \text{g Ca} \) That is about 501 mg, which is why a 1250 mg calcium carbonate tablet is labeled as providing about 500 mg of calcium. A treats the mass of the salt as the mass of calcium. The carbonate is most of the tablet's mass. C flips the last factors (1.25 × 100.09 ÷ 40.08). The calcium in a tablet can never weigh more than the whole compound. D uses calcium's atomic number (20) in place of its molar mass (40.08 g/mol).
hint: Grams of compound to moles of compound to moles of Ca (1 : 1) to grams of Ca. Can the calcium weigh more than the whole compound?

title: Problem 5.45
question: What mass of oxygen is contained in 0.250 mol of CO 2 ? (C 12.011, O 15.999) A. 4.00 g B. 8.00 g C. 16.0 g D. 11.0 g
answer: B. Moles of CO 2 → moles of O atoms → grams of O, using the molar mass of O atoms : \( 0.250\ \text{mol CO}_2 \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol O}}{1\ \text{mol CO}_2} \times \dfrac{15.999\ \text{g O}}{1\ \text{mol O}} = 8.00\ \text{g O} \) A forgets the subscript 2: 0.250 mol × 15.999 g/mol = 4.00 g. C uses the molar mass of O 2 (31.998 g/mol) for oxygen atoms , after already doubling the moles: 0.500 mol × 31.998 = 16.0 g. That counts every oxygen twice. D is the mass of the whole CO 2 sample (0.250 × 44.009 = 11.0 g), carbon included.
hint: Moles of CO<sub>2</sub> to moles of O atoms (subscript ratio), then grams with the molar mass of O atoms, not O<sub>2</sub>.

title: Problem 5.48
question: How many atoms in total (C, H, and O combined) are in 0.100 mol of glucose, C 6 H 12 O 6 ? A. 6.02 × 10 22 atoms B. 3.61 × 10 23 atoms C. 7.23 × 10 23 atoms D. 1.45 × 10 24 atoms
answer: D. Each glucose molecule has 6 + 12 + 6 = 24 atoms, so \( 0.100\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \times \dfrac{24\ \text{mol atoms}}{1\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6} \times \dfrac{6.0221 \times 10^{23}\ \text{atoms}}{1\ \text{mol atoms}} = 1.45 \times 10^{24}\ \text{atoms} \) A is the number of glucose molecules , not atoms; it skips the subscripts. B counts only the 6 carbon atoms per molecule (0.600 mol C). C counts only the 12 hydrogen atoms per molecule (1.20 mol H).
hint: Add the subscripts to get atoms per molecule, use that as the mole ratio, then multiply by Avogadro's number.

title: Problem 5.53
question: A student is asked for the molar mass of ammonium phosphate. Which value is correct? (H 1.008, N 14.007, O 15.999, P 30.97) A. 113.01 g/mol B. 131.04 g/mol C. 133.08 g/mol D. 149.08 g/mol
answer: D. Ammonium is NH 4 + and phosphate is PO 4 3− , so it takes three ammonium ions to balance one phosphate: (NH 4 ) 3 PO 4 , with 3 N, 12 H, 1 P, and 4 O. \( 3(14.007) + 12(1.008) + 30.97 + 4(15.999) = 42.021 + 12.096 + 30.97 + 63.996 = 149.083 \rightarrow 149.08\ \text{g/mol} \) A is the molar mass of "NH 4 PO 4 ," which ignores the charges: one 1+ ion cannot balance a 3− ion. B is "(NH 4 ) 2 PO 4 ," which treats phosphate as 2− (like sulfate). C is "(NH 4 ) 3 PO 3 ," which uses phosphite (PO 3 3− ) in place of phosphate. Check the ending: -ate is PO 4 3− on the green sheet.
hint: Write the formula first: how many NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> balance one PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>? Then count every N and H before adding masses.

title: Problem 5.57
question: A 0.0800 mol sample of a pure metal has a mass of 4.40 g. Which metal is it? A. Iron, Fe B. Manganese, Mn C. Chromium, Cr D. Cobalt, Co
answer: B. Molar mass = grams ÷ moles = 4.40 g ÷ 0.0800 mol = 55.0 g/mol , which matches manganese (54.94). A, iron (55.85), is the neighbor most students pick, but it is 0.85 g/mol away; manganese is 0.06 away. C, chromium (52.00), would need 4.16 g for 0.0800 mol. D, cobalt (58.93), would need 4.71 g.
hint: Molar mass = grams ÷ moles. Compare your result with each metal's atomic mass and pick the closest.

title: Problem 5.58
question: Bromine is a dark red liquid made of Br 2 molecules. How many bromine atoms are in 4.00 g of Br 2 ? (Br 79.90) A. 1.51 × 10 22 B. 3.01 × 10 22 C. 6.03 × 10 22 D. 7.70 × 10 26
answer: B. Br 2 is 2(79.90) = 159.80 g/mol, and each molecule holds 2 atoms: \( 4.00\ \text{g Br}_2 \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol Br}_2}{159.80\ \text{g Br}_2} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol Br}}{1\ \text{mol Br}_2} \times \dfrac{6.0221 \times 10^{23}\ \text{Br atoms}}{1\ \text{mol Br}} = 3.01 \times 10^{22}\ \text{Br atoms} \) You get the same answer by using the atom's molar mass (79.90 g/mol) and no ×2 step, because 4.00 g of bromine is the same atoms either way. A is the number of Br 2 molecules : the ×2 step was skipped. C used 79.90 g/mol and multiplied by 2, counting every atom twice. D multiplied by the molar mass instead of dividing.
hint: Bromine is diatomic: grams to moles of Br<sub>2</sub> (molar mass 2 × 79.90), then moles of Br atoms (2 per molecule), then atoms.

title: Problem 6.1
question: A fluoride treatment at the dentist can leave a thin layer of calcium fluoride on tooth enamel. Which statement correctly describes how calcium and fluorine atoms form this compound? A. Each Ca atom gives one electron to one F atom, forming CaF. B. Each Ca atom gives one electron to each of two F atoms, forming Ca 2+ and two F − ions: CaF 2 . C. Each F atom gives one electron to a Ca atom, forming Ca − and F + ions. D. Ca and F share a pair of electrons in a covalent bond.
answer: B. Calcium (group 2) has 2 valence electrons and loses both to reach the configuration of argon; each fluorine (group 17) has 7 and needs 1. One Ca atom therefore gives one electron to each of two F atoms. Electrons lost (2) = electrons gained (2 × 1), and the charges cancel: (2+) + 2(1−) = 0, so the formula is CaF 2 . A leaves calcium with one valence electron, which is not a noble-gas configuration, and Ca + with F − is not the ion pair that forms. Calcium always forms Ca 2+ . C moves electrons the wrong way. Metals lose electrons and nonmetals gain them; fluorine, the most electronegative element, never gives up an electron to a metal. D describes a covalent bond, which forms between two nonmetals. Calcium is a metal and fluorine is a nonmetal, so electrons transfer (the electronegativity difference, 4.0 − 1.0 = 3.0, is far above 2.0; Section 6.5).
hint: Calcium is in group 2 and fluorine in group 17. How many electrons must Ca lose, and how many can one F accept? Metals lose, nonmetals gain.

title: Problem 6.4
question: Electrolytes are substances whose dissolved ions conduct electricity. Which of these conducts electricity well? A. A crystal of solid sodium chloride B. Potassium chloride dissolved in water, as in an IV electrolyte solution C. Glucose dissolved in water, as in a 5% dextrose IV solution D. Pure, distilled water
answer: B. KCl is ionic. When it dissolves, the K + and Cl − ions separate and are free to move, so they carry an electric current. A contains ions, but in a solid crystal lattice they are locked in place and cannot move, so solid NaCl does not conduct. C: glucose, C 6 H 12 O 6 , is a molecular compound of nonmetals. It dissolves as whole, neutral molecules, not ions, so the solution does not conduct (glucose is a nonelectrolyte). D: pure water is made of neutral molecules and contains almost no ions, so it conducts very poorly. Tap water conducts a little only because of dissolved salts.
hint: A current needs charged particles that can move. Which choice has ions, and are they free to move?

title: Problem 6.6
question: In Experiment 5a, magnesium burns in air to form magnesium oxide, MgO. Which statement about the ions in MgO is true? A. Mg 2+ and O 2− both have the electron configuration of neon. B. Mg 2+ has the configuration of argon, and O 2− has the configuration of neon. C. Mg 2+ has the configuration of neon, and O 2− has the configuration of helium. D. Neither ion has a noble-gas configuration, because the electrons are shared.
answer: A. Mg (12 electrons) loses 2 to become Mg 2+ with 10 electrons. O (8 electrons) gains 2 to become O 2− with 10 electrons. Both have 10 electrons, 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 , the configuration of neon. (Ions with the same configuration are called isoelectronic.) B: losing electrons cannot move magnesium up to argon (18 electrons). Mg 2+ drops back to the noble gas before it, neon. C: helium has 2 electrons. Oxygen gains electrons, so O 2− has more electrons (10) than an O atom, not fewer. D: in an ionic compound electrons are transferred, not shared, and the whole point of the transfer is that each ion reaches a noble-gas configuration.
hint: Count electrons: Mg has 12 and O has 8. How many does each ion have after losing or gaining 2? Which noble gas has that many?

title: Problem 6.7
question: Nitrogen gas, N 2 , makes up most of the air you breathe. Which description of its Lewis structure is correct? A. N–N single bond with three lone pairs on each N B. N=N double bond with two lone pairs on each N C. N≡N triple bond with one lone pair on each N D. N≡N triple bond with no lone pairs
answer: C. N 2 has 2 × 5 = 10 valence electrons. A triple bond (6 electrons) plus one lone pair on each N (4 electrons) uses exactly 10, and each N has 6 + 2 = 8 electrons. Each N forms 3 bonds, as HONC predicts. A uses 2 + 12 = 14 electrons, 4 more than N 2 has. Never add electrons to complete octets. B uses 4 + 8 = 12 electrons, still 2 too many, and each N would have only 2 bonds instead of 3. D uses only 6 electrons, and each N would have just 6 electrons around it, not an octet.
hint: Count N<sub>2</sub>'s valence electrons, then count the electrons each choice uses. Never add electrons to complete octets; HONC says N forms 3 bonds.

title: Problem 6.9
question: Which carbon–carbon bond is the longest? A. C≡C (triple) B. C=C (double) C. C–C (single) D. All three are the same length, because they join the same two kinds of atoms.
answer: C. The more pairs two atoms share, the more tightly they are pulled together. A single bond (one shared pair) is the longest and weakest of the three; a triple bond is the shortest and strongest. A is backward: the triple bond is the shortest , because three shared pairs hold the atoms closest together. B is in the middle: shorter than a single bond, longer than a triple bond. D ignores bond order. Bond length depends on the number of shared pairs as well as on which atoms are bonded.
hint: Bond length depends on how many pairs are shared. More shared pairs pull the atoms closer together.
new_hint: Count the shared electron pairs in each bond. Does sharing more pairs hold the two carbons closer together or farther apart?

title: Problem 6.11
question: Ethylene gas is the plant hormone that ripens fruit; packers use it in ripening rooms for bananas and tomatoes. Which molecule contains a double bond? A. Methanol, CH 3 OH B. Ethylene, C 2 H 4 C. Ethane, C 2 H 6 D. Ammonia, NH 3
answer: B. In C 2 H 4 , each carbon is bonded to two H atoms. That is only 3 bonds per carbon if the C–C bond is single, but carbon forms 4 bonds (HONC), so the two carbons share two pairs: H 2 C=CH 2 . A: in methanol, C already has 4 single bonds (three H and the O), and O has 2 (C and H). Every atom is satisfied with single bonds. C: in ethane, each carbon is bonded to three H atoms and the other carbon, 4 single bonds each, so no double bond is needed. D: N forms 3 single bonds to H and keeps one lone pair; no double bond.
hint: Use HONC (carbon forms 4 bonds). In which molecule can't every atom reach its usual bond count with single bonds alone?

title: Problem 6.14
question: Chloromethane, CH 3 Cl, has 14 valence electrons. Which description of its Lewis structure is correct? A. C in the center, single-bonded to three H atoms and to Cl; three lone pairs on Cl; no lone pairs on C B. Cl in the center, single-bonded to C and to the three H atoms; no lone pairs on Cl C. C in the center, single-bonded to three H atoms and to Cl; three lone pairs on Cl and one lone pair on C D. C in the center, single-bonded to three H atoms and double-bonded to Cl; two lone pairs on Cl
answer: A. Carbon is central (H is never central, and halogens are usually on the outside). Four single bonds use 8 electrons; the other 6 go on Cl as three lone pairs. Check: C has 4 bonds (8 electrons), Cl has 1 bond + 3 lone pairs (8), each H has 2, and 8 + 6 = 14 electrons are used. B gives chlorine 4 bonds and carbon only 1. Chlorine usually forms 1 bond and carbon 4 (HONC), and carbon would have only 2 electrons. C uses 16 electrons, 2 more than the molecule has, and gives carbon 10 electrons, more than an octet. D uses 14 electrons, but carbon now has 5 bonds (10 electrons). Carbon never exceeds an octet, and chlorine usually forms only 1 bond.
hint: Check each choice: total electrons used must be 14, carbon makes 4 bonds (HONC), Cl usually 1, and no atom other than H has more or less than 8.

title: Problem 6.18
question: Ethylene, C 2 H 4 , has 12 valence electrons. Which description of its Lewis structure is correct? A. The two carbons are joined by a double bond, each carbon is single-bonded to two H atoms, and there are no lone pairs. B. The two carbons are joined by a single bond, each carbon is single-bonded to two H atoms, and each carbon has one lone pair. C. The two carbons are joined by a single bond, each carbon is single-bonded to two H atoms, and there are no lone pairs. D. The two carbons are joined by a triple bond, and each carbon is single-bonded to two H atoms.
answer: A. H 2 C=CH 2 : four C–H bonds (8 electrons) + one C=C double bond (4 electrons) = 12. Each carbon has 2 + 2 + 4 = 8 electrons and 4 bonds. B gives each carbon an octet, but it uses 10 + 4 = 14 electrons, 2 more than ethylene has. When you run out of electrons before the octets are full, make a multiple bond instead of adding electrons. C uses only 10 electrons, leaving 2 unused, and each carbon has only 6 electrons around it. D gives each carbon 5 bonds (10 electrons, more than an octet) and uses 14 electrons. A C≡C triple bond appears in acetylene, C 2 H 2 , where each carbon has only one H.
hint: Count the electrons each description uses (it must be 12) and check that every carbon has 4 bonds and 8 electrons.

title: Problem 6.21
question: Water's shape is why it dissolves the salts and sugars carried in blood. What is the molecular shape of H 2 O? A. Linear, 180° B. Bent, about 109.5° C. Trigonal planar, 120° D. Tetrahedral, 109.5°
answer: B. O has 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs: 4 electron groups, so the electron geometry is tetrahedral. Only the 3 atoms are named in the shape, so the molecule is bent , with an angle of about 109.5° (measured: 104.5°, squeezed by the lone pairs). A comes from reading the flat Lewis drawing H–O–H as the real shape and ignoring the two lone pairs on O. C would need 3 electron groups; O in water has 4. D is the electron-group geometry, which counts the lone pairs. The molecular shape names only where the atoms are.
hint: Count electron groups on O, including lone pairs. Then name the shape from the atoms only, not from the flat Lewis drawing.

title: Problem 6.22
question: Every breath you exhale carries carbon dioxide, O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O. How many electron groups surround the carbon, and what is the shape of CO 2 ? A. 4 groups; tetrahedral B. 2 groups; linear C. 2 groups; bent D. 4 groups; bent
answer: B. Each double bond counts as one electron group, and carbon has no lone pairs, so C has 2 groups. Two groups point in opposite directions: linear, 180° . A counts each double bond as two groups. A double bond is one region of electrons between the same two atoms, so it is one group. C counts the lone pairs on the oxygen atoms. Only lone pairs on the central atom change the shape, and carbon has none. D makes both mistakes: double bonds counted twice and outer lone pairs treated as if they were on carbon.
hint: A double bond counts as one electron group, and only lone pairs on the central atom count. How many groups does carbon have?

title: Problem 6.25
question: Which pair of molecules or ions has the same molecular shape? A. H 2 O and CO 2 B. NH 3 and CH 2 O C. CH 4 and NH 4 + D. H 2 S and HCN
answer: C. In both CH 4 and NH 4 + , the central atom has four single bonds and no lone pairs (8 electrons each): 4 groups, 0 lone pairs, tetrahedral , 109.5°. The charge on NH 4 + does not change the shape. A: H 2 O is bent (4 groups, 2 lone pairs on O); CO 2 is linear (2 groups, 0 lone pairs on C). B: NH 3 is trigonal pyramidal (4 groups, 1 lone pair); CH 2 O is trigonal planar (3 groups, 0 lone pairs). D: H 2 S is bent (like water); HCN is linear (2 groups on C: a single bond and a triple bond).
hint: For each molecule or ion, count electron groups and lone pairs on the central atom. The same counts give the same shape, whatever the charge.

title: Problem 6.28
question: Which bond is the most polar? A. C–H B. N–H C. O–H D. C–Cl
answer: C. The larger the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond. O–H: 3.5 − 2.1 = 1.4 , the largest of the four. This strongly polar bond is why water and alcohols attract each other so strongly. A: C–H is 2.5 − 2.1 = 0.4, which counts as nonpolar covalent in this course. B: N–H is 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9, polar but less polar than O–H. D: C–Cl is 3.0 − 2.5 = 0.5, only slightly polar. Chlorine's large size does not make the bond more polar; only the electronegativity difference matters.
hint: Compute ΔEN for each bond (larger minus smaller). The largest difference is the most polar bond.

title: Problem 6.29
question: Using only the \( \Delta \text{EN} \) cutoffs from Section 6.5, which bond is classified as ionic? (Mg 1.2, Al 1.5, Ca 1.0, H 2.1, N 3.0, O 3.5, F 4.0, Cl 3.0, I 2.5) A. Mg–O B. Al–Cl C. H–F D. N–H
answer: A. Mg–O: 3.5 − 1.2 = 2.3, which is above 2.0, so it is ionic, as in the MgO made in Experiment 5a. B: Al–Cl is 3.0 − 1.5 = 1.5, in the polar-covalent range. It is a metal–nonmetal pair, so you still name AlCl 3 as an ionic compound (Chapter 4), but by the \( \Delta \text{EN} \) cutoffs alone it is polar covalent. The cutoffs are guidelines on a continuum. C: H–F is 4.0 − 2.1 = 1.9, very polar but still below 2.0, so it is polar covalent. HF is a molecule of two nonmetals. D: N–H is 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9, polar covalent.
hint: Compute ΔEN for each pair and compare with the cutoff: above 2.0 is ionic. Use only the numbers, not the metal–nonmetal rule.

title: Problem 6.30
question: Chloroform, CHCl 3 , was one of the first inhaled anesthetics (it is no longer used, because it damages the liver and heart). Carbon tetrachloride, CCl 4 , and methane, CH 4 , have the same tetrahedral shape. Which of these molecules is polar? A. CCl 4 B. CO 2 C. CH 4 D. CHCl 3
answer: D. In CHCl 3 , carbon has four single bonds and no lone pairs (26 electrons in all): tetrahedral. But the four outer atoms are not identical (one H, three Cl). The three polar C–Cl bonds (\( \Delta \text{EN} \) = 0.5) are not balanced by a matching bond on the fourth corner, so the dipoles do not cancel: the molecule is asymmetrical and polar (SNAP). A: CCl 4 has four identical polar C–Cl bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. They cancel, so it is nonpolar. B: CO 2 has two polar C=O bonds, but it is linear and they point in opposite directions, so they cancel. Nonpolar. C: CH 4 has only C–H bonds (\( \Delta \text{EN} \) = 0.4, nonpolar) in a symmetrical tetrahedron. Nonpolar.
hint: Each has a basic shape with no lone pairs on carbon, so check the outer atoms (SNAP). Which molecule has outer atoms that are not all the same?

title: Problem 6.31
question: Which statement correctly describes the bond in hydrogen chloride, H–Cl? (H 2.1, Cl 3.0) A. The bond is polar covalent; H is δ+, Cl is δ−, and the dipole arrow points toward Cl. B. The bond is polar covalent; H is δ−, Cl is δ+, and the dipole arrow points toward H. C. The bond is nonpolar, because both atoms are nonmetals. D. The bond is ionic, made of H + and Cl − ions.
answer: A. \( \Delta \text{EN} \) = 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9, polar covalent. Chlorine, the more electronegative atom, pulls the shared pair closer, so it carries the partial negative charge, and the dipole arrow points toward it (with the cross on the H end). B reverses the charges. The more electronegative atom is always the δ− end. C: two nonmetals form a covalent bond, but it is nonpolar only if their electronegativities are about equal (\( \Delta \text{EN} \) of 0.4 or less). Here the difference is 0.9. D: 0.9 is far below 2.0, so the electron is shared unequally, not transferred. (HCl does form ions when it dissolves in water, but that is a reaction with water, Chapter 12, not the bond itself.)
hint: Find ΔEN, then ask which atom is more electronegative. That atom pulls the shared pair closer and carries δ−; the dipole arrow points toward it.
new_hint: Find ΔEN to classify the bond. Then decide which atom pulls the shared pair closer, which end gets δ−, and which way the dipole arrow points.

title: Problem 6.35
question: Which compound has the greatest percent oxygen by mass? (H 1.008, C 12.011, N 14.007, O 15.999) A. Carbon dioxide, CO 2 B. Water, H 2 O C. Hydrogen peroxide, H 2 O 2 D. Dinitrogen monoxide, N 2 O
answer: C. H 2 O 2 : 2(15.999) ÷ 34.014 × 100% = 94.07% O . Its only other atoms are two very light H atoms. A: CO 2 is 2(15.999) ÷ 44.009 × 100% = 72.71% O. Having two O atoms does not guarantee the highest percent; the carbon atom adds 12 g/mol. B: H 2 O is 15.999 ÷ 18.015 × 100% = 88.81% O, high, but H 2 O 2 adds a second O with no extra H. D: N 2 O is 15.999 ÷ 44.013 × 100% = 36.35% O; the two N atoms make up most of the mass.
hint: For each, find the mass of O in one mole and the molar mass, then part ÷ whole. More O atoms alone does not guarantee the highest percent.

title: Problem 6.39
question: A student analyzes a 5.00 g sample of pure sodium chloride from a grocery store and a 50.0 g sample of pure sodium chloride harvested from seawater. Which statement is true? (Na 22.99, Cl 35.45) A. Both samples are 39.34% sodium by mass. B. The 50.0 g sample has the greater percent sodium, because it is larger. C. The two samples have different percents, because they came from different sources. D. The 5.00 g sample is 39.34% sodium and the 50.0 g sample is 393.4% sodium.
answer: A. By the law of constant composition, every sample of a pure compound has the same percent composition: 22.99 ÷ 58.44 × 100% = 39.34% Na , whatever the sample size or source. B confuses mass with percent. The larger sample contains more grams of sodium (19.7 g versus 1.97 g), but the same fraction of its mass is sodium. C: a pure compound has a fixed composition. Different sources can bring different impurities , but both samples here are pure NaCl. D multiplies the percent by the mass ratio. A percent can never exceed 100% for one part of a whole.
hint: Think about the law of constant composition. Does the percent of an element in a pure compound depend on sample size or source?

title: Problem 6.40
question: Which pair of compounds has the same empirical formula? A. Acetylene, C 2 H 2 , and benzene, C 6 H 6 B. Carbon monoxide, CO, and carbon dioxide, CO 2 C. Ethylene, C 2 H 4 , and ethane, C 2 H 6 D. Water, H 2 O, and hydrogen peroxide, H 2 O 2
answer: A. Divide each set of subscripts by the largest number that divides all of them: C 2 H 2 ÷ 2 = CH, and C 6 H 6 ÷ 6 = CH. Both have the empirical formula CH , even though they are different molecules. B: CO (1 : 1) and CO 2 (1 : 2) are already in lowest terms and have different ratios. C: C 2 H 4 reduces to CH 2 , but C 2 H 6 reduces to CH 3 . D: H 2 O cannot be reduced (it is H 2 O), while H 2 O 2 reduces to HO.
hint: Divide each set of subscripts by the largest number that divides all of them, then compare the reduced formulas in each pair.

title: Problem 6.45
question: Lactic acid builds up in muscles during intense exercise. Its empirical formula is CH 2 O and its molar mass is 90.08 g/mol. What is its molecular formula? (H 1.008, C 12.011, O 15.999) A. CH 2 O B. C 2 H 4 O 2 C. C 3 H 6 O 3 D. C 6 H 12 O 6
answer: C. The empirical formula mass is 12.011 + 2(1.008) + 15.999 = 30.026 g/mol, so \( n = \dfrac{90.08}{30.026} = 3.000 \) and the molecular formula is (CH 2 O) 3 = C 3 H 6 O 3 . A is the empirical formula. Its mass (30.03 g/mol) is only one-third of the given molar mass, so it cannot be the molecular formula. B uses n = 2 (60.05 g/mol, the molar mass of acetic acid, not lactic acid). D uses n = 6 (180.16 g/mol), the formula of glucose. Lactic acid is made from glucose in muscles, but each glucose gives two lactic acid molecules.
hint: Find the empirical formula mass of CH<sub>2</sub>O, then n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass. Which choice is (CH<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>n</sub>?

title: Problem 6.47
question: Many Valley growers spread gypsum, a hydrate of calcium sulfate, CaSO 4 ·xH 2 O, on their fields to help water soak into the soil. Heating 1.722 g of gypsum leaves 1.362 g of anhydrous CaSO 4 (136.14 g/mol). What is x? (H 2 O 18.015 g/mol) A. 0.5 B. 2 C. 4 D. 21
answer: B. Water lost: 1.722 − 1.362 = 0.360 g; 0.360 ÷ 18.015 = 0.01998 mol H 2 O. CaSO 4 : 1.362 ÷ 136.14 = 0.01000 mol. Ratio: 0.01998 ÷ 0.01000 = 2.00, so gypsum is CaSO 4 ·2H 2 O . A inverts the ratio: moles of CaSO 4 ÷ moles of water = 0.500. The formula needs water per CaSO 4 . C compares grams instead of moles: 1.362 g ÷ 0.360 g = 3.78, about 4. Masses must be converted to moles first. D mistakes the percent water by mass (0.360 ÷ 1.722 × 100% = 20.9%, about 21) for a count of water molecules.
hint: Find the water lost, then convert both the water and the CaSO<sub>4</sub> to moles. Compare moles, not grams, with water on top.

title: Problem 6.53
question: Nitrosyl chloride, NOCl, is a toxic gas formed when nitric acid and hydrochloric acid are mixed. Which atom is central, and what is the shape around it? A. O is central; bent B. N is central; bent C. Cl is central; linear D. There is no central atom; linear
answer: B. Usual bond counts: N 3, O 2, Cl 1, so N makes the most bonds and is central. Electrons: 5 + 6 + 7 = 18. Single bonds N–O and N–Cl use 4; Cl and O get three lone pairs each (12), and the last 2 go on N as a lone pair. N then has only 6 electrons and O only 1 bond, so one O lone pair becomes an N=O double bond. N has 3 groups (double bond, single bond, lone pair): bent , about 120°. A puts the most electronegative atom in the middle; O makes only 2 bonds, fewer than N. C puts a one-bond atom in the center; Cl, like H, belongs on the outside. D is true only for two-atom molecules. Here N bonds to two atoms, so it is a central atom.
hint: Use the usual bond counts: which atom forms the most bonds? Draw the structure, then count electron groups (including lone pairs) on that atom.

title: Problem 6.54
question: Which molecule is polar? (EN: H 2.1, C 2.5, F 4.0, Si 1.8, Cl 3.0, O 3.5) A. CO 2 B. CF 4 C. CH 3 F D. SiCl 4
answer: C. CH 3 F is tetrahedral, but only one bond is polar (C–F, 1.5); the three C–H bonds (0.4) are nonpolar. Following the bond arrows like driving directions, there is just one arrow, toward F, so you end up somewhere new: a net dipole. A: two equal C=O arrows (1.0 each) point opposite ways on a linear molecule and cancel. B: four equal C–F arrows point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel. D: Si–Cl bonds are polar (1.2), but four identical bonds in a tetrahedron cancel, just like CF 4 .
hint: A molecule is polar if its bond arrows do not cancel. For each, check which bonds are polar (ΔEN above 0.4) and whether the outer atoms are all the same.

title: Problem 6.58
question: An elemental analysis of a compound made by working muscles finds 0.400 mol C, 0.800 mol H, and 0.400 mol O. Its molar mass is 90.08 g/mol. What is its molecular formula? (C 12.011, H 1.008, O 15.999) A. CH 2 O B. C 3 H 6 O 3 C. C 2 H 4 O 2 D. C 6 H 12 O 6
answer: B. Divide each mole value by the smallest (0.400): C 1, H 2, O 1, so the empirical formula is CH 2 O (30.026 g/mol). n = 90.08 ÷ 30.026 = 3.000, so the molecular formula is C 3 H 6 O 3 (lactic acid). Check: 3(12.011) + 6(1.008) + 3(15.999) = 90.078 g/mol. A is only the empirical formula. The analysis alone cannot give more, but the molar mass shows the molecule is 3 times bigger. C would have a molar mass of 60.05 g/mol (n = 2), not 90.08. D would have a molar mass of 180.16 g/mol (n = 6). It is glucose, which shares the empirical formula CH 2 O.
hint: The data are already in moles: divide by the smallest to get the empirical formula, then n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass.

title: Problem 7.1
question: Which observation is the best evidence that a chemical reaction has happened? A. Rubbing alcohol evaporates from a patient's arm, and the skin feels cool. B. The inner pouch of an instant cold pack breaks, the ammonium nitrate inside dissolves in the water, and the pack gets cold. C. An effervescent antacid tablet containing sodium bicarbonate and citric acid is dropped into water and fizzes as a new gas forms. D. Water in a kettle bubbles as it boils.
answer: C. When the tablet dissolves, the bicarbonate and the citric acid react with each other and form carbon dioxide, a substance that was not in the tablet. A gas that forms from a new substance (not boiling, not a dissolved gas escaping) is evidence of a chemical change. A is evaporation, a change of state. The alcohol molecules are the same in the air as on the skin; the cooling is the energy needed to vaporize them. B shows an energy change, but dissolving is a physical change: the NH 4 + and NO 3 − ions just spread out in the water and no new substance forms. An energy change is a clue, not proof. D: the bubbles in boiling water are water vapor, the same substance as the liquid, so this is a physical change.
hint: Ask of each choice: did a new substance form? A gas, a temperature change, or bubbles can also come from a change of state or dissolving.

title: Problem 7.3
question: Ammonia for the nitrogen fertilizers used on Valley crops is made by the reaction below, run at high temperature and pressure with an iron catalyst (Fe written over the arrow). N 2 (g) + 3 H 2 (g) → 2 NH 3 (g)    (Fe catalyst) Which statement about this equation is correct? A. "3 H 2 " means three hydrogen molecules, which contain 6 hydrogen atoms in all. B. The 2 in "2 NH 3 " means each ammonia molecule contains two nitrogen atoms. C. The iron written over the arrow is a reactant that is used up in the reaction. D. The (g) labels mean that each substance is dissolved in water.
answer: A. A coefficient counts molecules, and the subscript counts atoms in each molecule: 3 molecules × 2 H atoms = 6 H atoms. The right side also has 6 H atoms (2 × 3), as conservation of mass requires. B confuses a coefficient with a subscript. "2 NH 3 " is two molecules, each with one N and three H atoms. C: a substance written over the arrow is a catalyst. It speeds up the reaction but is not used up, so it is not counted as a reactant or a product. D: (g) means gas. Dissolved in water is (aq), aqueous.
hint: Separate the three kinds of numbers: a coefficient counts molecules, a subscript counts atoms in one molecule, and anything over the arrow is a catalyst. Check what (g) means.

title: Problem 7.6
question: A 2.0 g effervescent antacid tablet is dropped into a cup holding 150.0 g of water. The cup is open to the air. After the fizzing stops, the cup and its contents (not counting the cup itself) have a mass of 151.4 g. Which statement best explains the result? A. About 0.6 g of mass was destroyed in the reaction. B. About 0.6 g of carbon dioxide gas escaped into the air; the total mass of all the products still equals the total mass of the reactants. C. The water evaporated, so the 0.6 g that was lost is water vapor. D. The atoms in the tablet changed into lighter elements.
answer: B. Before: 2.0 g + 150.0 g = 152.0 g. After: 151.4 g. The difference, 152.0 g − 151.4 g = 0.6 g, is the mass of the CO 2 that bubbled out of the open cup. In a sealed container, the mass would not change. A breaks the law of conservation of mass. Matter is not destroyed in a chemical reaction; it left the cup as a gas. C: a little water does evaporate from any open cup, but the fizzing is the gas formed by the reaction, CO 2 . Evaporation during a few minutes is far too slow to explain the loss. D: chemical reactions rearrange atoms; they never change one element into another (that happens only in nuclear reactions, Chapter 14).
hint: Add the masses before and after. Mass is conserved, so where could the missing mass have gone from an open cup that fizzes?

title: Problem 7.7
question: In a blast furnace, iron ore is reduced to iron metal with carbon. When the equation below is balanced with the smallest whole numbers, what is the coefficient of C? __ Fe 2 O 3 (s) + __ C(s) → __ Fe(s) + __ CO 2 (g) A. 1 B. 2 C. 3 D. 6
answer: C. O: Fe 2 O 3 has 3 O and CO 2 has 2, so the smallest equal number is 6: 2 Fe 2 O 3 and 3 CO 2 . Then C: 3 CO 2 needs 3 C. Fe: 2 × 2 = 4 Fe. 2 Fe 2 O 3 (s) + 3 C(s) → 4 Fe(s) + 3 CO 2 (g) Check: Fe 4 = 4; O 6 = 6; C 3 = 3. A: with 1 C, there would be 1 CO 2 (2 O), but O comes from Fe 2 O 3 in groups of 3; 2 and 3 cannot match unless both are adjusted. B: 2 C gives 2 CO 2 with 4 O, which no whole number of Fe 2 O 3 (3, 6, 9 … O) can supply. D: 6 C works only with 4 Fe 2 O 3 , 8 Fe, and 6 CO 2 , which is the right answer doubled. The coefficients must be the smallest whole numbers.
hint: Start with O: Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> has 3 and CO<sub>2</sub> has 2, so find the smallest number both divide into. Then balance C and Fe, and use the smallest whole numbers.

title: Problem 7.9
question: Which equation is balanced and uses correct formulas? A. 2 KI(aq) + Cl 2 (g) → 2 KCl(aq) + I 2 (aq) B. H 2 O 2 (aq) → H 2 O(l) + O 2 (g) C. N 2 (g) + H 2 (g) → 2 NH 3 (g) D. Na(s) + Cl 2 (g) → NaCl 2 (s)
answer: A. K 2 = 2; I 2 = 2; Cl 2 = 2, and every formula is correct (K + with I − or Cl − ; iodine is the diatomic element I 2 ). B is not balanced: 2 O on the left and 1 + 2 = 3 O on the right. The balanced form is 2 H 2 O 2 → 2 H 2 O + O 2 . C balances N (2 = 2) but not H: 2 on the left and 6 on the right. It needs 3 H 2 . D has the same atoms on both sides, but NaCl 2 is not a real compound. Na + and Cl − combine 1:1 as NaCl; the subscript was changed to force a balance. Correct: 2 Na + Cl 2 → 2 NaCl.
hint: Check two things for each choice: are the formulas real (diatomic elements, correct ion ratios), and does every atom count match on both sides?

title: Problem 7.11
question: When the equation below is balanced with the smallest whole numbers, what is the coefficient of NaNO 3 ? __ Ba(NO 3 ) 2 (aq) + __ Na 3 PO 4 (aq) → __ Ba 3 (PO 4 ) 2 (s) + __ NaNO 3 (aq) A. 2 B. 3 C. 5 D. 6
answer: D. Treat the ions as units. Ba 3 (PO 4 ) 2 needs 3 Ba(NO 3 ) 2 and 2 Na 3 PO 4 . That brings in 3 × 2 = 6 NO 3 and 2 × 3 = 6 Na, so 6 NaNO 3 . 3 Ba(NO 3 ) 2 (aq) + 2 Na 3 PO 4 (aq) → Ba 3 (PO 4 ) 2 (s) + 6 NaNO 3 (aq) A (2) balances neither Na (6 from 2 Na 3 PO 4 ) nor NO 3 (6 from 3 Ba(NO 3 ) 2 ). B (3) matches the number of Na in one Na 3 PO 4 , but two are needed to supply the 2 PO 4 in the product. C (5) is the sum 3 + 2 of the reactant coefficients, which has no meaning for counting atoms.
hint: Treat nitrate and phosphate as units. Start with the precipitate's 3 Ba and 2 PO<sub>4</sub>, then count how many Na and NO<sub>3</sub> that brings in.

title: Problem 7.13
question: In the catalase test, a microbiology student mixes a bit of a bacterial colony with a drop of 3% hydrogen peroxide. The mixture bubbles right away. Which gas makes the bubbles, and what type of reaction is it? 2 H 2 O 2 (aq) → 2 H 2 O(l) + O 2 (g)    (catalase) A. CO 2 ; combustion B. O 2 ; decomposition C. H 2 ; single displacement D. O 2 ; combination
answer: B. One reactant breaks down into two simpler products, so it is a decomposition, and the gas is oxygen, O 2 . The enzyme catalase is a catalyst, written over the arrow; bubbles mean the bacteria are catalase-positive. A: there is no carbon in the equation, so CO 2 cannot form, and combustion needs a fuel reacting with O 2 . Here O 2 is a product. C: no hydrogen gas forms, and a single displacement needs an element reacting with a compound. The only reactant is one compound. D has the right gas but the wrong pattern. A combination joins two or more reactants into one product; this is the reverse, one reactant into two products.
hint: Read the equation: how many reactants and products are there, and which product is a gas? Match that to a pattern.

title: Problem 7.16
question: A family uses a charcoal grill inside a closed garage during a power outage, and two of them come to the emergency department with headaches and confusion. Which balanced equation shows the incomplete combustion of charcoal (carbon) that produces carbon monoxide? A. C(s) + O 2 (g) → CO 2 (g) B. 2 C(s) + O 2 (g) → 2 CO(g) C. 2 CO(g) + O 2 (g) → 2 CO 2 (g) D. C(s) + O 2 (g) → CO(g)
answer: B. With too little O 2 , each carbon atom picks up only one oxygen atom and forms CO. The equation is balanced: C 2 = 2; O 2 = 2. In a closed space, the O 2 runs low and CO builds up. CO binds to hemoglobin much more tightly than O 2 does, which is why carbon monoxide poisoning causes these symptoms; respiratory therapists use a CO-oximeter, not a standard pulse oximeter, to measure it. (Context only; this is not treatment advice.) A is complete combustion (plenty of O 2 ), which makes CO 2 , not CO. C is carbon monoxide burning further to CO 2 . It removes CO rather than producing it. D shows the right product but is not balanced: 2 O on the left and 1 O on the right.
hint: Incomplete combustion means too little O<sub>2</sub>, so the product is CO. Which choice makes CO and is also balanced?

title: Problem 7.18
question: Which reaction is a double displacement? A. Zn(s) + 2 AgNO 3 (aq) → Zn(NO 3 ) 2 (aq) + 2 Ag(s) B. 2 KNO 3 (s) → 2 KNO 2 (s) + O 2 (g) C. K 2 CrO 4 (aq) + BaCl 2 (aq) → BaCrO 4 (s) + 2 KCl(aq) D. 2 SO 2 (g) + O 2 (g) → 2 SO 3 (g)
answer: C. Two ionic compounds exchange partners: K + ends up with Cl − , and Ba 2+ with CrO 4 2− . Barium chromate is insoluble (chromate row of the green sheet), so it precipitates as a yellow solid. A is a single displacement: an element (Zn) replaces the silver ion in a compound. B is a decomposition: one compound breaks into two simpler substances when heated. D is a combination: two reactants form one product.
hint: Look for two ionic compounds swapping partners (AB + CD). Classify each of the other choices by its pattern too.

title: Problem 7.19
question: Household ammonia cleaner is a solution of NH 3 in water. Which of the following is a weak electrolyte? A. HNO 3 B. NH 3 C. KCl D. C 12 H 22 O 11 (sucrose)
answer: B. Ammonia is a weak base: only a small fraction of the NH 3 molecules react with water to form NH 4 + and OH − ions, so its solution conducts weakly. A: nitric acid is on the green sheet's list of strong acids, so it ionizes completely. It is a strong electrolyte. C: potassium chloride is a soluble ionic compound (Group 1), which separates completely into K + and Cl − . Strong electrolyte. D: sucrose dissolves as whole molecules and forms no ions, so it is a nonelectrolyte.
hint: Use the step-by-step classification: is it ionic? Is it an acid or a base on the green-sheet strong list? If not on the list, it is weak.

title: Problem 7.22
question: All four compounds below matter in health care. According to the green-sheet solubility rules, which one is soluble in water? A. Ca 3 (PO 4 ) 2 , the mineral in bone B. CaC 2 O 4 , the main compound in most kidney stones C. BaSO 4 , the contrast agent swallowed before GI X-rays D. KCl, added to IV fluids to replace potassium
answer: D. K + is a Group 1 ion, and every Group 1 compound is soluble. KCl dissolves completely into K + and Cl − , which is why it can be given in solution. A: phosphates are insoluble except with Group 1 and NH 4 + . Its insolubility is what lets calcium phosphate form hard, lasting bone. B: oxalate (C 2 O 4 2− ) is in the insoluble row, and Ca 2+ is not an exception, so calcium oxalate precipitates as stones. C: sulfate is usually soluble, but Ba 2+ is one of the exceptions. Because BaSO 4 barely dissolves, almost no toxic Ba 2+ is absorbed.
hint: Check each against the green sheet. Which cation makes every compound soluble, and which anions have exceptions that include these cations?

title: Problem 7.24
question: The number of dissolved particles matters for osmosis in the body (Chapter 11). Which compound gives the most ions per formula unit when it dissolves? A. NaNO 3 B. MgCl 2 C. (NH 4 ) 3 PO 4 D. C 6 H 12 O 6
answer: C. (NH 4 ) 3 PO 4 (s) → 3 NH 4 + (aq) + PO 4 3− (aq): 4 ions . Each polyatomic ion counts as one ion. A gives 2 ions: Na + and NO 3 − . Nitrate stays together; it does not split into N and O. B gives 3 ions: Mg 2+ and 2 Cl − . D gives 0 ions. Glucose is a nonelectrolyte; it dissolves as 1 molecule per formula.
hint: Write each dissolving equation. Keep each polyatomic ion whole and count ions from the subscripts. A molecular compound gives no ions.

title: Problem 7.25
question: Milk of magnesia, Mg(OH) 2 , is made by precipitating it from magnesium salt solutions with a base. Which is the net ionic equation for mixing MgCl 2 (aq) and KOH(aq)? A. Mg 2+ (aq) + OH − (aq) → MgOH(s) B. Mg 2+ (aq) + 2 OH − (aq) → Mg(OH) 2 (s) C. 2 K + (aq) + 2 Cl − (aq) → 2 KCl(s) D. MgCl 2 (aq) + 2 OH − (aq) → Mg(OH) 2 (s) + 2 Cl − (aq)
answer: B. Molecular equation: MgCl 2 (aq) + 2 KOH(aq) → Mg(OH) 2 (s) + 2 KCl(aq) Mg(OH) 2 is insoluble (hydroxide, and Mg 2+ is not an exception); KCl is soluble (Group 1). K + and Cl − are spectators, leaving Mg 2+ + 2 OH − → Mg(OH) 2 (s). Check charge: +2 + 2(−1) = 0 on the left, 0 on the right. A uses a wrong formula. Mg 2+ needs two OH − ions to be neutral, so the solid is Mg(OH) 2 , not MgOH. C: KCl is soluble, so K + and Cl − stay dissolved; they are the spectators, not the precipitate. D leaves MgCl 2 (aq) unsplit. An aqueous strong electrolyte must be written as ions, and then the Cl − cancels as a spectator.
hint: Write the molecular equation, decide which product is insoluble, and cancel the spectators. Check that the solid's formula is neutral.

title: Problem 7.28
question: Strontium salts give road flares their red color. When Sr(NO 3 ) 2 (aq) and Li 2 SO 4 (aq) are mixed, a white precipitate forms. Which ions are the spectator ions? A. Sr 2+ and SO 4 2− B. Li + and NO 3 − C. Li + only D. There are no spectator ions, because a precipitate forms.
answer: B. Sr(NO 3 ) 2 (aq) + Li 2 SO 4 (aq) → SrSO 4 (s) + 2 LiNO 3 (aq). Strontium sulfate is insoluble (Sr 2+ is a sulfate exception); lithium nitrate is soluble. Li + and NO 3 − are dissolved on both sides, unchanged, so they are spectators. Net ionic: Sr 2+ (aq) + SO 4 2− (aq) → SrSO 4 (s). A names the ions that actually react to form the solid, the opposite of spectators. C forgets the nitrate. NO 3 − is also dissolved before and after mixing. D: a precipitation reaction almost always has spectators; only the ions that form the solid leave the solution.
hint: Write the swapped products and find the insoluble one. Spectators are the ions that stay dissolved and unchanged on both sides.

title: Problem 7.32
question: Which is the net ionic equation for the reaction of perchloric acid, HClO 4 (aq), with lithium hydroxide, LiOH(aq)? A. H + (aq) + OH − (aq) → H 2 O(l) B. HClO 4 (aq) + OH − (aq) → ClO 4 − (aq) + H 2 O(l) C. Li + (aq) + ClO 4 − (aq) → LiClO 4 (s) D. There is no net ionic equation, because both the acid and the base are soluble.
answer: A. Molecular: HClO 4 (aq) + LiOH(aq) → H 2 O(l) + LiClO 4 (aq). HClO 4 is on the green sheet's strong-acid list, LiOH is a strong base (Group 1 hydroxide), and LiClO 4 is soluble, so Li + and ClO 4 − are spectators. Only H + and OH − react. B treats HClO 4 as a weak acid. A strong acid is completely ionized, so it is written as H + and ClO 4 − , and the ClO 4 − then cancels. C: perchlorates and Group 1 compounds are always soluble, so LiClO 4 does not precipitate. D: a reaction happens because water forms. Something "leaving" the dissolved ions can be water, not only a solid or a gas.
hint: Is HClO<sub>4</sub> on the strong-acid list? Is LiClO<sub>4</sub> soluble? Split the strong electrolytes into ions and cancel the spectators.

title: Problem 7.34
question: Hard water leaves calcium carbonate scale inside coffee makers, and vinegar (acetic acid, HC 2 H 3 O 2 ) is a common descaler. What gas bubbles off as the scale dissolves? CaCO 3 (s) + 2 HC 2 H 3 O 2 (aq) → Ca(C 2 H 3 O 2 ) 2 (aq) + H 2 O(l) + ? (g) A. H 2 B. CO 2 C. O 2 D. No gas forms, because acetic acid is a weak acid.
answer: B. Swapping partners gives calcium acetate (soluble) and H 2 CO 3 , carbonic acid, which is unstable and becomes CO 2 (g) + H 2 O(l). Check: Ca 1 = 1; C 1 + 4 = 5 = 4 + 1; H 8 = 6 + 2; O 3 + 4 = 7 = 4 + 1 + 2. A: H 2 forms when an active metal reacts with an acid (single displacement). Calcium carbonate is a compound, and its carbonate ion is what reacts. C: O 2 is not formed in a double displacement; nothing in this reaction is decomposing into oxygen. D: weak acids still react with carbonates. Being weak means acetic acid is only partly ionized, not that it cannot react; as H + is used up, more acid ionizes.
hint: Swapping partners gives calcium acetate and H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>. Use the unstable-products table: what does carbonic acid become?

title: Problem 7.36
question: Which pair of solutions produces a gas when mixed? A. KCl(aq) + NaNO 3 (aq) B. HNO 3 (aq) + Ca(OH) 2 (aq) C. K 2 SO 3 (aq) + HI(aq) D. Mg(NO 3 ) 2 (aq) + Na 2 SO 4 (aq)
answer: C. A sulfite plus a strong acid gives H 2 SO 3 , which breaks down into sulfur dioxide gas and water: K 2 SO 3 (aq) + 2 HI(aq) → 2 KI(aq) + H 2 O(l) + SO 2 (g) A: the swapped products, KNO 3 and NaCl, are both soluble. No reaction. B is a neutralization: 2 HNO 3 + Ca(OH) 2 → 2 H 2 O + Ca(NO 3 ) 2 . Water forms, but no gas. D: the swapped products, MgSO 4 (Mg 2+ is not a sulfate exception) and NaNO 3 , are both soluble. No reaction.
hint: Swap partners for each pair and look for an unstable product (H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>, NH<sub>4</sub>OH, H<sub>2</sub>S) that gives off a gas.

title: Problem 7.38
question: Oxygen difluoride, OF 2 , is a toxic, very reactive gas. What is the oxidation number of oxygen in OF 2 ? A. −2 B. +2 C. −1 D. 0
answer: B. The rules are applied in order, and fluorine (rule 4) comes before oxygen (rule 6). Each F is −1, so O + 2(−1) = 0 and O = +2 . A uses the oxygen rule, but that rule loses when it conflicts with the earlier fluorine rule. With O = −2 and F = −1, the sum would be −4, not 0. C is the value for oxygen in peroxides such as H 2 O 2 , not in OF 2 ; it would give a sum of −3. D is the oxidation number of oxygen only as a free element (O 2 ). In a compound with fluorine, oxygen is not 0.
hint: Check the rule order: which comes first, the fluorine rule or the oxygen rule? Then make the oxidation numbers add to zero.

title: Problem 7.40
question: Silverware and silver jewelry tarnish in air that contains traces of hydrogen sulfide: 4 Ag(s) + 2 H 2 S(g) + O 2 (g) → 2 Ag 2 S(s) + 2 H 2 O(l) Which substance is the oxidizing agent? A. Ag B. H 2 S C. O 2 D. Ag 2 S
answer: C. Oxidation numbers: Ag 0 → +1 (in Ag 2 S, with S 2− ), so silver is oxidized. O 0 → −2 (in H 2 O), so oxygen is reduced. H stays +1 and S stays −2. The oxidizing agent is the reactant that contains the element reduced: O 2 . Check: 4 Ag each lose 1 electron (4 lost); 2 O atoms each gain 2 (4 gained). A: silver is oxidized, so Ag is the reducing agent. B: neither H (+1) nor S (−2) changes oxidation number, so H 2 S is neither oxidized nor reduced. D is a product. The oxidizing and reducing agents are reactants.
hint: Assign oxidation numbers and find the element whose number decreases. The oxidizing agent is the reactant that contains it.

title: Problem 7.42
question: Which reaction is not an oxidation–reduction reaction? A. 4 Li(s) + O 2 (g) → 2 Li 2 O(s) B. CaO(s) + CO 2 (g) → CaCO 3 (s) C. N 2 (g) + 3 H 2 (g) → 2 NH 3 (g) D. 2 CO(g) + O 2 (g) → 2 CO 2 (g)
answer: B. Ca is +2 in CaO and in CaCO 3 ; C is +4 in CO 2 and in CaCO 3 ; O is −2 throughout. No oxidation number changes, so no electrons are transferred. It is a combination of two compounds, not of elements, which is why it is not redox. A: Li goes from 0 to +1 (oxidized) and O from 0 to −2 (reduced). A metal combining with an element is redox. C: N goes from 0 to −3 (reduced) and H from 0 to +1 (oxidized). D: C goes from +2 in CO to +4 in CO 2 (oxidized), and O in O 2 goes from 0 to −2 (reduced).
hint: Assign oxidation numbers on both sides of each equation. A reaction where no oxidation number changes is not redox.

title: Problem 7.44
question: Use the activity series from Section 7.8, listed from most active to least active: Li, K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Ni, Sn, Pb, H 2 , Cu, Ag, Au Gold crowns and many dental alloys do not corrode in the mouth, even with acidic foods. Which of these metals will react with hydrochloric acid to release hydrogen gas? A. Cu B. Ag C. Ni D. Au
answer: C. Nickel is above H 2 in the series, so it displaces hydrogen from the acid: Ni(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → NiCl 2 (aq) + H 2 (g). A: copper is below H 2 , so it does not react with HCl. B: silver is below H 2 ; no reaction. D: gold is at the very bottom, the least active metal on the list. That resistance is why it is used for crowns.
hint: A metal reacts with acid to release H<sub>2</sub> only if it is above H<sub>2</sub> in the activity series. Find each metal's position.

title: Problem 7.46
question: Use the activity series, listed from most active to least active: Li, K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Ni, Sn, Pb, H 2 , Cu, Ag, Au Steel water heaters and the steel tanks used to store irrigation water are protected from rust by a "sacrificial anode," a rod of a more active metal that corrodes in place of the iron. Which metal could serve as a sacrificial anode for iron? A. Cu B. Sn C. Mg D. Pb
answer: C. Magnesium is above iron, so it gives up electrons more easily. As long as the Mg rod lasts, Mg is oxidized instead of Fe, and the electrons it releases flow into the steel, so the iron is not oxidized. (The activity series shows why: Mg(s) + Fe 2+ (aq) → Mg 2+ (aq) + Fe(s) goes, so Mg gives up electrons more easily than Fe.) A: copper is below iron, so the iron would corrode first; joining copper to steel can even speed up rusting. B: tin is below iron. Tin can coat steel as a barrier (as in "tin cans"), but it does not protect iron sacrificially. D: lead is below iron, so it would not be oxidized in place of the iron.
hint: A sacrificial anode must be oxidized more easily than iron. Where must that metal sit in the series compared with Fe?

title: Problem 7.48
question: Use the activity series, listed from most active to least active: Li, K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Ni, Sn, Pb, H 2 , Cu, Ag, Au Which reaction occurs? A. Cu(s) + ZnSO 4 (aq) → B. Pb(s) + MgCl 2 (aq) → C. Ni(s) + 2 AgNO 3 (aq) → D. Au(s) + HCl(aq) →
answer: C. Nickel is above silver, so it displaces Ag + : Ni(s) + 2 AgNO 3 (aq) → Ni(NO 3 ) 2 (aq) + 2 Ag(s) A: copper is below zinc, so Cu cannot displace Zn 2+ . No reaction. B: lead is far below magnesium. No reaction. D: gold is below H 2 and does not react with acids such as HCl.
hint: A free metal displaces only the ions of a metal below it (or H<sub>2</sub> from acid if it is above H<sub>2</sub>). Compare each pair.

title: Problem 7.53
question: Potassium hydrogen carbonate (potassium bicarbonate) is the active ingredient in some antacids. Which is the correct balanced equation for its reaction with hydrochloric acid? A. KHCO 3 (aq) + HCl(aq) → KCl(aq) + H 2 CO 3 (aq) B. KHCO 3 (aq) + HCl(aq) → KCl(aq) + H 2 O(l) + CO 2 (g) C. KHCO 3 (aq) + HCl(aq) → KCl(aq) + H 2 (g) + CO 3 (g) D. KHCO 3 (aq) + 2 HCl(aq) → KCl 2 (aq) + H 2 O(l) + CO 2 (g)
answer: B. From the names: potassium is K + and hydrogen carbonate is HCO 3 − , so KHCO 3 ; hydrochloric acid is HCl. Swapping partners gives KCl and H 2 CO 3 , and carbonic acid becomes H 2 O(l) + CO 2 (g). Check: K 1 = 1; H 2 = 2; C 1 = 1; O 3 = 1 + 2; Cl 1 = 1. A is balanced but stops too early. H 2 CO 3 is unstable and should never be a final product. C invents products. The carbonic acid breaks down into water and CO 2 , not H 2 gas, and "CO 3 (g)" is not a real substance. D uses a wrong formula: K + and Cl − combine 1:1, so the salt is KCl, not KCl 2 . (D is not balanced in H either.)
hint: Write the correct salt formula from the ion charges, then check the unstable-products table: what does H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> become?

title: Problem 7.56
question: (Going Further, not on CHEM 3A exams unless assigned) Many pacemakers run for years on a lithium–iodine battery, whose overall reaction is 2 Li(s) + I 2 (s) → 2 LiI(s) Which electrode is the anode, and what happens there? A. The lithium electrode; lithium is oxidized: Li → Li + + e − . B. The iodine electrode; iodine is oxidized: I 2 → 2 I − + 2 e − . C. The lithium electrode; lithium is reduced: Li + e − → Li − . D. The iodine electrode; iodine is reduced: I 2 + 2 e − → 2 I − .
answer: A. The anode is where oxidation happens. Lithium goes from 0 to +1 in LiI, so it loses electrons, which flow out through the wire to the pacemaker circuit. B: iodine gains electrons (0 → −1). The half-reaction as written is not even balanced in charge: 0 on the left, −4 on the right. C: lithium, a Group 1 metal, loses electrons to form Li + ; it does not gain them. Reduction happens at the cathode, not the anode. D correctly describes the cathode , where iodine is reduced. The question asks for the anode.
hint: The anode is where oxidation happens. Which element loses electrons as it goes from the element to LiI?
new_hint: Which process, oxidation or reduction, happens at the anode? Track each element's oxidation number from the reactants to LiI.

title: Problem 7.57
question: Balance with the smallest whole numbers. What is the coefficient of H 2 O? __ Sr(OH) 2 (aq) + __ H 3 PO 4 (aq) → __ Sr 3 (PO 4 ) 2 (s) + __ H 2 O(l) A. 2 B. 3 C. 6 D. 12
answer: C. Write water as HOH and zig-zag. Phosphate: 2 on the right, so 2 H 3 PO 4 . Zig to H: 6 H, so 6 HOH. Zag to OH: 6 OH, so 3 Sr(OH) 2 . Zig to Sr: 3 = 3. 3 Sr(OH) 2 (aq) + 2 H 3 PO 4 (aq) → Sr 3 (PO 4 ) 2 (s) + 6 H 2 O(l) Check: Sr 3 = 3; P 2 = 2; H 6 + 6 = 12 = 12; O 6 + 8 = 14 = 8 + 6. A is the coefficient of H 3 PO 4 , not of water. B is the coefficient of Sr(OH) 2 . With only 3 H 2 O, the 12 H atoms on the left would not all be accounted for. D is the total number of H atoms on each side (12), not the number of water molecules; each H 2 O holds 2 H.
hint: Write water as HOH and zig-zag: start with phosphate, zig to its partner H, zag to OH, then zig to Sr.

title: Problem 7.59
question: Which substance is a weak electrolyte? A. KNO 3 B. H 3 PO 4 C. HClO 4 D. C 6 H 12 O 6
answer: B. H in front marks an acid. Phosphoric acid is not on the green sheet's list of strong acids, so it is a weak acid and a weak electrolyte: only a small fraction of its molecules form ions. A is ionic (K + and NO 3 − ) and soluble (AANA), so it is a strong electrolyte. C, perchloric acid, is on the strong-acid list, so it is a strong electrolyte. D, glucose, is a carbon-based molecule with no H in front and no hydroxide ion: a nonelectrolyte. It dissolves, but as whole molecules.
hint: Use the step-by-step classification: H in front marks an acid. Is that acid on the green-sheet strong-acid list?

title: Problem 7.63
question: Which equation is correctly balanced? A. Zn(s) + Ag + (aq) → Zn 2+ (aq) + Ag(s) B. Zn(s) + 2 Ag + (aq) → Zn 2+ (aq) + 2 Ag(s) C. 2 Zn(s) + Ag + (aq) → 2 Zn 2+ (aq) + Ag(s) D. Zn(s) + Ag 2+ (aq) → Zn 2+ (aq) + Ag(s)
answer: B. Zinc loses 2 electrons (Zn → Zn 2+ + 2 e − ) and each silver ion gains 1 (Ag + + e − → Ag), so two silver ions are needed. Atoms balance (Zn 1, Ag 2), and charge balances: +2 on each side. A balances the atoms but not the charge: +1 on the left, +2 on the right. Electrons cannot just appear or vanish. C puts the coefficient on the wrong species. The atoms balance, but the charge gets worse: +1 on the left, +4 on the right. D changes the silver ion into Ag 2+ to force the charges to match. Like changing a subscript, changing an ion's charge changes the substance; silver ions are Ag + .
hint: Check both atoms and charge for each choice. How many electrons does Zn lose, and how many does each Ag<sup>+</sup> gain?

title: Problem 8.1
question: Natural gas contains a little ethane, C 2 H 6 , which burns by the reaction below. 2 C 2 H 6 (g) + 7 O 2 (g) → 4 CO 2 (g) + 6 H 2 O(g) Which conversion factor turns moles of ethane into moles of O 2 needed? A. \( \dfrac{7\ \text{mol O}_2}{2\ \text{mol C}_2\text{H}_6} \) B. \( \dfrac{2\ \text{mol C}_2\text{H}_6}{7\ \text{mol O}_2} \) C. \( \dfrac{1\ \text{mol O}_2}{1\ \text{mol C}_2\text{H}_6} \) D. \( \dfrac{7\ \text{g O}_2}{2\ \text{g C}_2\text{H}_6} \)
answer: A. The coefficients say 2 mol C 2 H 6 react with 7 mol O 2 . To cancel mol C 2 H 6 and leave mol O 2 , put O 2 (the unit you want) on top. B is the same ratio flipped. It is a true ratio, but multiplying moles of ethane by it leaves mol C 2 H 6 2 /mol O 2 , not mol O 2 . C ignores the coefficients. A 1 : 1 ratio is only correct when both coefficients are equal. D treats the coefficients as grams. Coefficients count molecules and moles, not masses; an O 2 molecule and a C 2 H 6 molecule have different masses.
hint: Put the unit you want (mol O<sub>2</sub>) on top so that mol C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> cancels. Do coefficients count grams or moles?

title: Problem 8.4
question: Yeast ferment glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide: C 6 H 12 O 6 (aq) → 2 C 2 H 5 OH(aq) + 2 CO 2 (g) How many moles of glucose must be fermented to make 3.40 mol of ethanol? A. 1.70 mol B. 6.80 mol C. 3.40 mol D. 0.567 mol
answer: A. \( 3.40\ \text{mol C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6}{2\ \text{mol C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}} = 1.70\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \) Each glucose makes two ethanol molecules, so you need half as many moles of glucose as the ethanol you want. B uses the flipped ratio (2 mol glucose / 1 mol ethanol), which would need more glucose than ethanol made. C skips the mole ratio, as if 1 glucose made 1 ethanol. D divides by the subscript 6 in C 6 H 12 O 6 . Mole ratios between substances come from the coefficients, not from the subscripts inside a formula.
hint: Work backward from the product: how many ethanol molecules does one glucose make? Should you need more or fewer moles of glucose than of ethanol?

title: Problem 8.7
question: Sulfur dioxide from burning fuels is turned into sulfur trioxide in the air: 2 SO 2 (g) + O 2 (g) → 2 SO 3 (g) Which statement is correct? A. 2 g of SO 2 react with 1 g of O 2 to make 2 g of SO 3 . B. 2 mol of SO 2 react with 1 mol of O 2 to make 2 mol of SO 3 . C. Moles are conserved, so 3 mol of reactants make 3 mol of products. D. 1 mol of SO 2 makes 2 mol of SO 3 .
answer: B. Coefficients give mole ratios: 2 mol SO 2 : 1 mol O 2 : 2 mol SO 3 . A reads the coefficients as grams. Also, 2 g + 1 g = 3 g of reactants could not make only 2 g of product; mass is conserved. C: atoms and mass are conserved, but moles of molecules are not. Here 3 mol of reactant molecules make only 2 mol of product molecules. D misreads the ratio. SO 2 and SO 3 have the same coefficient, so 1 mol of SO 2 makes 1 mol of SO 3 .
hint: Coefficients count molecules and moles, not grams. Which statement reads them as moles? Is the number of moles conserved in a reaction?
new_hint: What do the coefficients in a balanced equation count? In a reaction, which quantities are always conserved: atoms, mass, or moles?

title: Problem 8.10
question: Alcohol-based hand sanitizer is flammable because ethanol burns: C 2 H 5 OH(l) + 3 O 2 (g) → 2 CO 2 (g) + 3 H 2 O(g) What mass of O 2 is needed to burn 5.00 g of ethanol? (C 2 H 5 OH 46.069 g/mol; O 2 31.998 g/mol) A. 10.4 g B. 3.47 g C. 1.16 g D. 31.3 g
answer: A. \( 5.00\ \text{g C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}}{46.069\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{3\ \text{mol O}_2}{1\ \text{mol C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}} \times \dfrac{31.998\ \text{g O}_2}{1\ \text{mol O}_2} = 10.4\ \text{g O}_2 \) B leaves out the mole ratio (0.1085 mol × 31.998 g/mol), as if 1 mol of ethanol used 1 mol of O 2 . C uses the flipped ratio, 1 mol ethanol / 3 mol O 2 . D multiplies the molar mass of O 2 by the coefficient (3 × 31.998 = 95.994 g/mol) and uses the 3 : 1 mole ratio, counting the 3 twice. The molar mass of O 2 is always 31.998 g/mol.
hint: Set up grams → mol → mol → grams with the 3 : 1 mole ratio. Watch for choices that skip the ratio, flip it, or put a coefficient into a molar mass.

title: Problem 8.14
question: Railroad crews weld steel rails with the thermite reaction, which makes molten iron: Fe 2 O 3 (s) + 2 Al(s) → Al 2 O 3 (s) + 2 Fe(l) What mass of aluminum reacts completely with 20.0 g of Fe 2 O 3 ? (Fe 2 O 3 159.70 g/mol; Al 26.98 g/mol) A. 6.76 g B. 1.69 g C. 3.38 g D. 40.0 g
answer: A. \( 20.0\ \text{g Fe}_2\text{O}_3 \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol Fe}_2\text{O}_3}{159.70\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol Al}}{1\ \text{mol Fe}_2\text{O}_3} \times \dfrac{26.98\ \text{g Al}}{1\ \text{mol Al}} = 6.76\ \text{g Al} \) B uses the flipped ratio, 1 mol Fe 2 O 3 / 2 mol Al. C leaves out the mole ratio (0.1252 mol × 26.98 g/mol). D skips moles entirely and treats the coefficients as grams: 20.0 g × 2 = 40.0 g. Grams of A never go straight to grams of B.
hint: Grams Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> → mol, then 2 mol Al per 1 mol Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, then the molar mass of Al. Grams of A never go straight to grams of B.

title: Problem 8.18
question: In Experiment 8a (Determination of the Gas Constant R), a 0.0365 g piece of magnesium ribbon reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid. What volume of H 2 forms, corrected to STP? (Mg 24.31 g/mol) Mg(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → MgCl 2 (aq) + H 2 (g) A. 33.6 mL B. 67.3 mL C. 818 mL D. 33.6 L
answer: A. \( 0.0365\ \text{g Mg} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol Mg}}{24.31\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol H}_2}{1\ \text{mol Mg}} \times \dfrac{22.4\ \text{L H}_2}{1\ \text{mol H}_2} = 0.0336\ \text{L} = 33.6\ \text{mL} \) A few tens of milliliters is the right size for the gas-measuring tube used in the lab. B uses the 2 in front of HCl as the Mg-to-H 2 ratio. Mg and H 2 each have a coefficient of 1. C multiplies grams by 22.4 L/mol without converting to moles first (0.0365 × 22.4 = 0.818 L). The molar volume applies to moles of gas, not grams of metal. D is the right digits with the wrong unit: the calculation gives 0.0336 L , which is 33.6 mL, not 33.6 L.
hint: Grams Mg → mol Mg → mol H<sub>2</sub> (compare those two coefficients) → liters with 22.4 L/mol. Would a small strip of ribbon make liters or milliliters of gas?

title: Problem 8.20
question: In which case can a student correctly use 22.4 L/mol to convert between volume and moles? A. 2.00 L of N 2 gas at 0 °C and 1.00 atm B. 2.00 L of CO 2 gas in a room at 25 °C and 1.00 atm C. 2.00 L of 0.100 M HCl solution D. 2.00 L of liquid water at 0 °C and 1.00 atm
answer: A. 22.4 L/mol is the molar volume of an ideal gas at STP, 0 °C (273 K) and 1 atm. Any gas works, but only at those conditions: 2.00 L ÷ 22.4 L/mol = 0.0893 mol N 2 . B is a gas, but not at STP. At 25 °C a mole of gas takes up more room (about 24.5 L), so 22.4 L/mol would overcount the moles. Gases at other conditions need the gas laws of Chapter 10. C is a solution, not a gas. Use molarity: 2.00 L × 0.100 mol/L = 0.200 mol HCl. D is a liquid. Molar volume applies only to gases; 2.00 L of water is about 2.00 × 10 3 g, or 111 mol.
hint: 22.4 L/mol applies only to a gas at STP (0 °C and 1 atm). Check each choice for both: is it a gas, and is it at STP?

title: Problem 8.23
question: A water-quality lab tests for chloride by adding silver nitrate. What mass of silver chloride precipitates from 20.0 mL of 0.150 M CaCl 2 with excess AgNO 3 ? (AgCl 143.32 g/mol) CaCl 2 (aq) + 2 AgNO 3 (aq) → 2 AgCl(s) + Ca(NO 3 ) 2 (aq) A. 0.860 g B. 0.430 g C. 860. g D. 0.215 g
answer: A. \( 0.0200\ \text{L} \times \dfrac{0.150\ \text{mol CaCl}_2}{1\ \text{L}} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol AgCl}}{1\ \text{mol CaCl}_2} \times \dfrac{143.32\ \text{g AgCl}}{1\ \text{mol AgCl}} = 0.860\ \text{g AgCl} \) B leaves out the 2 : 1 mole ratio. Each CaCl 2 carries two Cl − ions, so it makes two AgCl. C multiplies the molarity by 20.0 mL instead of 0.0200 L, a thousand times too much. Molarity is moles per liter . D uses the flipped ratio, 1 mol AgCl / 2 mol CaCl 2 .
hint: CaCl<sub>2</sub> has the green light: convert 20.0 mL to liters first, find mol CaCl<sub>2</sub>, then use 2 AgCl per CaCl<sub>2</sub> and the molar mass of AgCl.

title: Problem 8.25
question: A mixture of 10.0 g of H 2 and 10.0 g of O 2 is ignited: 2 H 2 (g) + O 2 (g) → 2 H 2 O(l). Which is the limiting reactant? (H 2 2.016 g/mol; O 2 31.998 g/mol) A. H 2 , because each H 2 molecule is much lighter than an O 2 molecule. B. O 2 , because it can make only 0.625 mol of H 2 O, while the H 2 could make 4.96 mol. C. Neither, because equal masses of the two reactants are present. D. H 2 , because the equation needs twice as much H 2 as O 2 .
answer: B. Run each reactant to the same product: From H 2 : 10.0 g ÷ 2.016 g/mol = 4.960 mol H 2 × (2 mol H 2 O / 2 mol H 2 ) = 4.96 mol H 2 O. From O 2 : 10.0 g ÷ 31.998 g/mol = 0.3125 mol O 2 × (2 mol H 2 O / 1 mol O 2 ) = 0.625 mol H 2 O. O 2 makes less water, so it runs out first. Only 0.625 mol (11.3 g) of water forms, and 10.0 − 1.26 = 8.74 g of H 2 is left over. A gets the logic backward: because H 2 molecules are so light, 10.0 g of H 2 is a huge number of moles, far more than the O 2 can use. C: equal masses are not equal moles, and even equal moles would not match a 2 : 1 recipe. D looks only at the coefficients. The recipe needs twice the moles of H 2 , but here there are almost 16 times as many moles of H 2 as O 2 .
hint: Run each reactant to the same product: the moles of H<sub>2</sub>O each could make. The smaller amount marks the limiting reactant; mass alone does not decide.

title: Problem 8.27
question: A car's catalytic converter turns carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide: 2 CO(g) + O 2 (g) → 2 CO 2 (g). A particle diagram shows 8 CO molecules and 3 O 2 molecules before the reaction. Which describes the box after the reaction is over? A. 6 CO 2 molecules and 2 CO molecules B. 8 CO 2 molecules and no leftover molecules C. 3 CO 2 molecules and 5 CO molecules D. 6 CO 2 molecules and no leftover molecules
answer: A. The 8 CO molecules would need 4 O 2 , but there are only 3, so O 2 is limiting. The 3 O 2 react with 6 CO and make 6 CO 2 ; 8 − 6 = 2 CO molecules are left over. Count the atoms to check: before, 8 C and 8 + 6 = 14 O; after, 6 + 2 = 8 C and 12 + 2 = 14 O. B assumes all of the CO reacts. That would take 4 O 2 molecules, and only 3 are present.
