C uses a 1 : 1 ratio (each O 2 makes one CO 2 ). Each O 2 actually makes two CO 2 . D finds the right amount of product but forgets the excess reactant. Two CO molecules have nothing left to react with, and they are still in the box (atoms are not destroyed).
hint: Count recipes: each O<sub>2</sub> uses 2 CO and makes 2 CO<sub>2</sub>. How many O<sub>2</sub> would 8 CO need? Remember to show any leftover molecules.

title: Problem 8.30
question: Iron filings are heated with powdered sulfur: Fe(s) + S(s) → FeS(s). A student uses 5.00 g of Fe and 3.50 g of S. Which reactant is limiting, and what mass of FeS can form? (Fe 55.85 g/mol; S 32.06 g/mol; FeS 87.91 g/mol) A. Fe is limiting; 7.87 g of FeS B. S is limiting; 9.60 g of FeS C. Fe is limiting; 9.60 g of FeS D. Neither is limiting; 8.50 g of FeS
answer: A. FeS from each reactant (1 : 1 ratios): From Fe: 5.00 g ÷ 55.85 g/mol = 0.08953 mol Fe → 0.08953 mol FeS × 87.91 g/mol = 7.87 g From S: 3.50 g ÷ 32.06 g/mol = 0.1092 mol S → 0.1092 mol FeS × 87.91 g/mol = 9.60 g Fe makes less, so Fe is limiting and 7.87 g of FeS forms. Sulfur left: 3.50 − (0.08953 mol × 32.06 g/mol) = 3.50 − 2.87 = 0.63 g. B picks sulfur because it has the smaller mass. Mass is not moles: sulfur atoms are lighter, so 3.50 g of S is actually more moles than 5.00 g of Fe. C names the right limiting reactant but then calculates the product from the excess reactant. The product amount must come from the limiting reactant. D simply adds the two masses, assuming everything reacts. That is only true when the amounts match the recipe; here 0.63 g of sulfur is left over.
hint: Convert both masses to moles (1 : 1 ratios), then to grams of FeS. The reactant that makes less FeS limits; a smaller mass does not mean fewer moles.

title: Problem 8.33
question: Biogas from a dairy digester contains some hydrogen sulfide, which burns to sulfur dioxide: 2 H 2 S(g) + 3 O 2 (g) → 2 SO 2 (g) + 2 H 2 O(g) If 2.0 mol of H 2 S and 2.4 mol of O 2 react, which reactant is limiting, and how many moles of SO 2 form? A. O 2 ; 1.6 mol SO 2 B. H 2 S; 2.0 mol SO 2 C. O 2 ; 3.6 mol SO 2 D. H 2 S; 1.6 mol SO 2
answer: A. From H 2 S: 2.0 mol × (2 mol SO 2 / 2 mol H 2 S) = 2.0 mol SO 2 . From O 2 : 2.4 mol × (2 mol SO 2 / 3 mol O 2 ) = 1.6 mol SO 2 . O 2 makes less, so it is limiting; 1.6 mol SO 2 forms, and 2.0 − 1.6 = 0.4 mol H 2 S is left. B compares the moles of reactants directly: 2.0 < 2.4, so "H 2 S runs out first." That shortcut ignores the 2 : 3 recipe, which needs 3.0 mol O 2 for 2.0 mol H 2 S. C finds the right limiting reactant but uses the flipped ratio, 2.4 × 3/2. D has the right amount of product but names the wrong limiting reactant. The reactant that gives the smaller amount of product is the limiting one, and here that is O 2 .
hint: Find the moles of SO<sub>2</sub> each reactant could make, using the 2 : 2 and 2 : 3 ratios. Comparing 2.0 with 2.4 directly ignores the recipe.

title: Problem 8.35
question: Acetaminophen, the pain reliever in Tylenol, can be made in a teaching lab from 4-aminophenol and excess acetic anhydride: C 6 H 7 NO(s) + C 4 H 6 O 3 (l) → C 8 H 9 NO 2 (s) + C 2 H 4 O 2 (l) Starting with 2.75 g of 4-aminophenol, a student collects 3.02 g of dry acetaminophen. What is the percent yield? (C 6 H 7 NO 109.128 g/mol; C 8 H 9 NO 2 151.165 g/mol) A. 79.3% B. 126% C. 110.% D. 3.81%
answer: A. Theoretical yield, from the limiting reactant (4-aminophenol): \( 2.75\ \text{g C}_6\text{H}_7\text{NO} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_7\text{NO}}{109.128\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol C}_8\text{H}_9\text{NO}_2}{1\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_7\text{NO}} \times \dfrac{151.165\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mol C}_8\text{H}_9\text{NO}_2} = 3.81\ \text{g} \) Percent yield: 3.02 g ÷ 3.81 g × 100% = 79.3% . B divides theoretical by actual (3.81 ÷ 3.02). The ratio is always actual ÷ theoretical, and a result above 100% should make you check. C compares the product mass with the starting mass (3.02 ÷ 2.75). The product molecule is heavier than the starting molecule, so grams of product and grams of reactant cannot be compared without going through moles. D reports the theoretical yield, 3.81 g, as if it were the percent. The theoretical yield is only the first step.
hint: Find the theoretical yield of acetaminophen from 4-aminophenol first (grams → mol → mol → grams). Then actual on top, theoretical on the bottom.

title: Problem 8.38
question: A student reports a 108% yield of a solid product. Which explanation fits a yield above 100%? A. The product was weighed before it was completely dry. B. Some crystals were left on the filter paper. C. A side reaction made a different product from some of the reactant. D. The theoretical yield was calculated from the limiting reactant.
answer: A. Water still in the product adds mass that is not product, so the "actual yield" is too high and can push the percent above 100%. B loses product, which lowers the yield. C turns some reactant into something else, which also lowers the yield of the product you want. D is the correct way to find the theoretical yield, so it cannot explain an error. (Using the excess reactant would make the theoretical yield too big and the percent yield too small.)
hint: A yield above 100% needs extra mass in the weighed product. Which choice adds mass instead of losing product?

title: Problem 8.41
question: A drug is made in two steps. Step 1 has an 80.0% yield, and step 2 has a 90.0% yield. What is the overall percent yield from the starting material to the drug? A. 72.0% B. 85.0% C. 90.0% D. 170.%
answer: A. Step 2 can only work on the 80.0% that step 1 made, so multiply the fractions: 0.800 × 0.900 = 0.720, or 72.0% . B averages the two yields. Losses build on each other, so the overall yield is lower than either step. C uses only the last step and ignores the product lost in step 1. D adds the yields. No yield can be above 100%.
hint: Step 2 can only work on the product step 1 made. Try it with 100 g: how much is left after step 1, and then after step 2?

title: Problem 8.42
question: A sports-medicine hot pack contains calcium chloride and a pouch of water. When the pouch breaks, the CaCl 2 dissolves and the pack warms up. Which statement is correct? A. The process is exothermic: ΔH is negative, and heat flows from the pack into the skin. B. The process is endothermic: ΔH is positive, and heat flows from the pack into the skin. C. The process is exothermic: ΔH is positive, because heat is produced. D. The process is endothermic: ΔH is negative, and heat flows from the skin into the pack.
answer: A. The pack gets warm, so the process releases heat to its surroundings (the pack's contents, then your skin). Heat released means exothermic and a negative ΔH. B pairs "endothermic" with warming. An endothermic process absorbs heat and feels cold, like an instant cold pack. C gets the sign backward. ΔH is the change in the system's enthalpy; when the system gives heat away, its enthalpy goes down, so ΔH is negative. D describes a cold pack (heat flowing from the skin into the pack), which would be endothermic with a positive ΔH, so both halves are wrong for a hot pack.
hint: The pack warms your skin, so which way does heat flow? Heat leaving the system goes with which sign of ΔH?

title: Problem 8.44
question: Hydrogen fuel-cell buses burn hydrogen without a flame, but the overall reaction and its heat are the same as for burning: 2 H 2 (g) + O 2 (g) → 2 H 2 O(l)    ΔH = −571.6 kJ How much energy is released by 5.00 g of H 2 ? (H 2 2.016 g/mol) A. 709 kJ released B. 1.42 × 10 3 kJ released C. 709 kJ absorbed D. 2.86 × 10 3 kJ released
answer: A. The ΔH goes with 2 mol of H 2 , the coefficient in the equation as written: \( 5.00\ \text{g H}_2 \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol H}_2}{2.016\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{571.6\ \text{kJ released}}{2\ \text{mol H}_2} = 709\ \text{kJ released} \) B ignores the coefficient and uses 571.6 kJ per 1 mol of H 2 , doubling the answer. C has the right size but the wrong direction. A negative ΔH means heat is released, not absorbed. D skips moles and multiplies grams by ΔH (5.00 × 571.6). ΔH is per mole, so convert grams to moles first.
hint: ΔH goes with the equation as written: 571.6 kJ per 2 mol H<sub>2</sub>. Convert grams to moles first, and check the sign: released or absorbed?

title: Problem 8.47
question: The thermochemical equation for making ammonia is N 2 (g) + 3 H 2 (g) → 2 NH 3 (g)    ΔH = −92.2 kJ What is ΔH for 4 NH 3 (g) → 2 N 2 (g) + 6 H 2 (g)? A. +184.4 kJ B. −184.4 kJ C. +92.2 kJ D. −46.1 kJ
answer: A. The new equation is the original reversed (change the sign: +92.2 kJ) and doubled (double the size: 2 × 92.2 = 184.4 kJ). ΔH = +184.4 kJ ; breaking ammonia apart is endothermic. B doubles the equation but forgets that reversing it changes the sign. C reverses the equation but forgets to double ΔH for twice the moles. D is ΔH per mole of NH 3 formed (−92.2 ÷ 2), which answers a different question.
hint: Two changes: reversing an equation changes the sign of ΔH, and doubling it doubles ΔH. Apply both.

title: Problem 8.56
question: Ethane burns: 2 C 2 H 6 (g) + 7 O 2 (g) → 4 CO 2 (g) + 6 H 2 O(g). A burner produced 3.0 mol of H 2 O. How many moles of O 2 were used? A. 2.6 mol B. 3.5 mol C. 21 mol D. 1.0 mol
answer: B. Work backward from the product, using only the ratio that links H 2 O and O 2 : \( 3.0\ \text{mol H}_2\text{O} \times \dfrac{7\ \text{mol O}_2}{6\ \text{mol H}_2\text{O}} = 3.5\ \text{mol O}_2 \) A uses the ratio upside down (3.0 × 6/7 = 2.6). Put the substance you want, O 2 , on top. C multiplies by 7 but forgets to divide by 6, as if 1 mol H 2 O went with 7 mol O 2 . D uses the ethane ratio (2 C 2 H 6 : 6 H 2 O), which gives moles of C 2 H 6 , not O 2 .
hint: Use only the ratio that links H<sub>2</sub>O and O<sub>2</sub>, with the unit you want, mol O<sub>2</sub>, on top.

title: Problem 8.60
question: 10.0 g of zinc reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: Zn(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → ZnCl 2 (aq) + H 2 (g). After evaporating the water, a student collects 18.0 g of ZnCl 2 . What is the percent yield? (Zn 65.39 g/mol; ZnCl 2 136.29 g/mol) A. 55.6% B. 86.4% C. 116% D. 180%
answer: B. Find the theoretical yield of ZnCl 2 first: 10.0 g ÷ 65.39 g/mol × (1 mol ZnCl 2 / 1 mol Zn) × 136.29 g/mol = 20.84 g. Then 18.0 g ÷ 20.84 g × 100% = 86.4%. A divides the zinc's mass by the product's mass (10.0 ÷ 18.0). Those are different substances; this is the most common percent-yield mistake. C divides theoretical by actual (20.84 ÷ 18.0). The actual yield goes on top, and a result above 100% should make you stop and check. D divides the product's mass by the zinc's mass (18.0 ÷ 10.0), again comparing two different substances.
hint: Find the theoretical yield of ZnCl<sub>2</sub> from the zinc first. Then actual ÷ theoretical × 100%; never divide grams of a reactant by grams of product.

title: Problem 8.63
question: Lightning makes nitrogen monoxide in air: N 2 (g) + O 2 (g) + 181 kJ → 2 NO(g). What is ΔH for this reaction as written? A. −181 kJ B. +181 kJ C. +90.5 kJ D. −90.5 kJ
answer: B. Heat is written on the reactant side, so it is absorbed: the reaction is endothermic and ΔH is positive. ΔH belongs to the equation as written (1 mol N 2 , 1 mol O 2 , 2 mol NO), so it is the full 181 kJ. A has the wrong sign: a negative ΔH would mean heat is released, which would put the 181 kJ on the product side. C is the heat per mole of NO (181 ÷ 2). That is a correct conversion factor, but it is not ΔH for the equation as written. D is wrong in both ways: the sign and the per-mole scaling.
hint: Heat written on the reactant side is absorbed. Which sign goes with absorbed heat? Does ΔH belong to the equation as written or to one mole of NO?

title: Problem 9.1
question: Which of these is mainly potential energy? A. Red blood cells moving through an artery B. Glucose dissolved in a sports drink C. The fast-moving water molecules in the steam inside an autoclave D. A spinning centrifuge rotor in a clinical lab
answer: B. Glucose stores chemical potential energy in the arrangement of its atoms. Nothing is happening to that energy yet; your cells release it later in cellular respiration. A is kinetic energy: the cells are moving with the blood. C is kinetic energy too. The random motion of particles is thermal energy, a kind of kinetic energy; the hotter the steam, the faster its molecules move. D is kinetic energy: the rotor is moving. It took electrical energy to get it spinning, but right now its energy is energy of motion.
hint: Which choices describe something moving? Potential energy is stored energy, such as the energy in the arrangement of a molecule's atoms.

title: Problem 9.3
question: A car brakes from highway speed to a stop. What happens to its kinetic energy? A. It is destroyed, because the car is no longer moving. B. It is turned back into chemical potential energy in the gasoline. C. It becomes temperature, which is a form of energy. D. It becomes heat in the brakes, tires, and air, so the total energy is unchanged.
answer: D. By the law of conservation of energy, energy changes form but is never created or destroyed. Friction in the brakes turns the car's kinetic energy into heat, which is why brakes get hot after a hard stop. A breaks the law of conservation of energy. The car's kinetic energy is gone, but the energy itself has moved into the brakes and surroundings. B is backward. Burning gasoline is a one-way chemical change; ordinary brakes cannot rebuild fuel molecules. C confuses temperature with energy. The brakes' temperature rises because their particles gain kinetic energy, but temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy, not a form of energy itself.
hint: Energy changes form but is never created or destroyed. What gets hot when a car brakes hard? Temperature is a measurement, not a form of energy.
new_hint: Apply the law of conservation of energy to each choice. Can energy be destroyed? Is temperature a form of energy or a measurement?

title: Problem 9.7
question: A patient's temperature is 38.6 °C. What is it in °F? A. 3.7 °F B. 53.4 °F C. 101.5 °F D. 127.1 °F
answer: C. \( {}^\circ\text{F} = 1.8(38.6) + 32 = 69.5 + 32 = 101.5\ {}^\circ\text{F} \) Multiplying by the exact 1.8 keeps three significant figures (69.5), and adding the exact 32 keeps one decimal place. The answer makes sense: 38.6 °C is above the 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) commonly used as the fever threshold. A uses the °F-to-°C formula in the wrong direction: (38.6 − 32)/1.8. A temperature of 3.7 °F would be well below freezing. B divides by 1.8 instead of multiplying (38.6/1.8 + 32). A Fahrenheit degree is smaller than a Celsius degree, so the Fahrenheit number grows by a factor of 1.8. D adds 32 before multiplying, 1.8(38.6 + 32). The formula multiplies first, then adds 32.
hint: Use °F = 1.8(°C) + 32. A fever in °F should be a little above 98.6 °F.

title: Problem 9.9
question: Hospitals store oxygen for patients as a liquid in large insulated tanks. Liquid oxygen boils at −183 °C. What is this temperature in kelvins? A. 90. K B. 456 K C. −90. K D. −183 K
answer: A. \( \text{K} = -183 + 273.15 = 90.\ \text{K} \) The sum 90.15 is rounded to the ones place, like −183, and the decimal point in "90." shows that the zero is significant. B adds 183 to 273.15, dropping the negative sign. A temperature below 0 °C must be below 273.15 K. C subtracts in the wrong order (−183 + 273.15 is positive, not negative). Kelvin temperatures are never negative, since 0 K is absolute zero. D assumes the scales are the same. A kelvin and a Celsius degree are the same size , but the zero points differ by 273.15.
hint: K = °C + 273.15; keep the negative sign of the Celsius value. Can a Kelvin temperature ever be negative?

title: Problem 9.12
question: A medium banana provides about 105 Cal of food energy. How many kilojoules is that? A. 0.439 kJ B. 25.1 kJ C. 439 kJ D. 4.39 × 10 5 kJ
answer: C. \( 105\ \text{Cal} \times \dfrac{4184\ \text{J}}{1\ \text{Cal}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{kJ}}{1000\ \text{J}} = 439\ \text{kJ} \) Since 1 Cal = 4.184 kJ, the number of kilojoules is a little more than 4 times the number of Calories. A treats the food Calorie as a small calorie: 105 cal × 4.184 J/cal = 439 J = 0.439 kJ. A food Calorie is 1000 cal. B divides by 4.184 instead of multiplying. A kilojoule is smaller than a Calorie, so there must be more kilojoules than Calories. D is the answer in joules (4.39 × 10 5 J) labeled as kilojoules; the last step, dividing by 1000 J/kJ, was skipped.
hint: A food Calorie is 1000 cal, and 1 Cal = 4.184 kJ. Should the number of kilojoules be bigger or smaller than the number of Calories?

title: Problem 9.14
question: Which is the largest amount of energy? A. 2.50 kJ B. 500. cal C. 0.750 Cal D. 2.80 × 10 3 J
answer: C. Convert each to joules: 0.750 Cal × 4184 J/Cal = 3138 J, or 3.14 × 10 3 J, the largest. A is 2.50 kJ = 2500 J (2.50 × 10 3 J). B has the biggest number, but calories are larger than joules by only a factor of 4.184: 500. cal × 4.184 J/cal = 2092 J (2.09 × 10 3 J), the smallest of the four. D is 2.80 × 10 3 J, more than A and B but less than C.
hint: Convert every choice to joules (1 cal = 4.184 J; 1 Cal = 4184 J), then compare. The biggest number is not always the most energy.

title: Problem 9.15
question: Which process releases heat to its surroundings? A. Sweat evaporating from the skin B. An instant cold pack being activated C. Water from sprinklers freezing on almond blossoms on a frosty night D. Dry ice subliming in a box used to ship vaccines
answer: C. Freezing is exothermic (q < 0 for the water): as the molecules lock into the ice structure, they release heat to the blossoms and the air around them. Some growers use this on purpose to protect blossoms on frosty nights. A is endothermic: evaporating sweat absorbs heat from the skin, which is why it cools you. B is endothermic: the dissolving solid absorbs heat from its surroundings, so the pack feels cold. D is endothermic: sublimation (solid to gas) separates the CO 2 molecules completely, which takes energy. Dry ice keeps the box cold by absorbing heat from its contents.
hint: Changes that pull particles apart absorb heat; changes that bring them together release heat. Which choice brings molecules together?
new_hint: Name the process in each choice. Does it pull particles apart or bring them together, and which of those releases heat to the surroundings?

title: Problem 9.18
question: A 455 g length of copper pipe cools from 65.0 °C to 22.5 °C. What is q for the pipe? A. +7.44 × 10 3 J B. −7.44 × 10 3 J C. −3.94 × 10 3 J D. −8.09 × 10 4 J
answer: B. ΔT = T final − T initial = 22.5 − 65.0 = −42.5 °C. \( q = (455\ \text{g})\left(0.385\ \dfrac{\text{J}}{\text{g}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C}}\right)(-42.5\ {}^\circ\text{C}) = -7.44 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J} \) The negative sign means the pipe releases 7.44 kJ of heat as it cools. A has the right size but the wrong sign; it comes from subtracting initial minus final. A cooling object releases heat, so q is negative. C uses the final temperature, 22.5 °C, as if it were ΔT. D uses the specific heat of water (4.184) instead of copper's (0.385). Use the specific heat of the substance whose temperature is changing.
hint: Use q = mcΔT with c for copper, 0.385 J/(g·°C), and ΔT = final − initial. A cooling object releases heat, so what sign should q have?

title: Problem 9.20
question: A beaker holds 1.50 × 10 2 g of water at 18.5 °C. It absorbs 8.20 kJ of heat. What is the final temperature of the water? A. 13.1 °C B. 18.5 °C C. 31.6 °C D. 5.4 °C
answer: C. \( \Delta T = \dfrac{8200\ \text{J}}{(150.\ \text{g})(4.184\ \text{J/(g}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C)})} = 13.1\ {}^\circ\text{C} \qquad T_\text{final} = 18.5 + 13.1 = 31.6\ {}^\circ\text{C} \) A is ΔT, not the final temperature. The question asks where the temperature ends up, so add ΔT to the starting temperature. B leaves the heat in kJ: 8.20/(150. × 4.184) = 0.0131 °C, a change too small to see. The specific heat is in joules, so 8.20 kJ must become 8200 J. D subtracts ΔT from the starting temperature. The water absorbed heat, so its temperature went up.
hint: Convert kJ to J, solve ΔT = q/(mc), then add ΔT to the starting temperature. The question asks for the final temperature, not the change.

title: Problem 9.25
question: On the heating curve for water, heat is still being added while ice melts at 0 °C, but the temperature does not change. Where does that heat go? A. It breaks the O–H covalent bonds inside the water molecules. B. Nowhere; since ΔT = 0, q = mcΔT shows that no heat is absorbed. C. It makes the molecules move faster, raising their kinetic energy. D. It overcomes the attractions holding the molecules in the ice, raising their potential energy.
answer: D. During a phase change, the added heat goes into separating the molecules against their intermolecular attractions (hydrogen bonds in ice). Their potential energy rises while their average kinetic energy, and so the temperature, stays the same. The heat is q = nΔH fus . A confuses intermolecular forces with bonds. Melting separates whole H 2 O molecules from each other; each molecule keeps its O–H bonds. B uses q = mcΔT on a plateau. That equation only describes temperature changes; a phase change absorbs heat even though ΔT = 0. C would make the temperature rise, since temperature measures average kinetic energy. On a plateau it does not.
hint: On a plateau the temperature, and so the average kinetic energy, stays the same. Does melting break bonds inside H<sub>2</sub>O molecules, or separate the molecules from each other?

title: Problem 9.27
question: In an autoclave, steam condenses on the surgical instruments being sterilized and heats them. What is q for 42.0 g of steam condensing to liquid water at 100 °C? A. −94.9 kJ B. +94.9 kJ C. −1.71 × 10 3 kJ D. −14.0 kJ
answer: A. \( 42.0\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol}}{18.015\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{40.7\ \text{kJ}}{1\ \text{mol}} = 94.9\ \text{kJ} \qquad q = -94.9\ \text{kJ} \) Condensation is the reverse of vaporization, so it releases the same amount of heat: the steam's q is negative, and the instruments absorb +94.9 kJ. That large release is why condensing steam heats a load so quickly. B has the right size but the sign for vaporizing . Condensing releases heat, so q for the steam is negative. C skips the gram-to-mole step: 42.0 × 40.7 = 1709. The ΔH vap is per mole , so grams must be converted to moles first. D uses ΔH fus (6.02 kJ/mol), the value for melting and freezing. Steam ↔ liquid uses ΔH vap .
hint: Grams → moles, then q = nΔH<sub>vap</sub>. Condensing is the reverse of vaporizing: same size, opposite sign.

title: Problem 9.31
question: How much heat is needed to turn 30.0 g of liquid water at 60.0 °C into steam at 100.0 °C? A. 5.02 kJ B. 67.8 kJ C. 72.8 kJ D. 5.09 × 10 3 kJ
answer: C. Two steps: warm the liquid to 100.0 °C (a slope), then boil it (a plateau). \( q_1 = (30.0\ \text{g})(4.184)(100.0 - 60.0\ {}^\circ\text{C}) = 5.02 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J} = 5.02\ \text{kJ} \) \( q_2 = 30.0\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol}}{18.015\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{40.7\ \text{kJ}}{1\ \text{mol}} = 67.8\ \text{kJ} \qquad q_\text{total} = 5.02 + 67.8 = 72.8\ \text{kJ} \) A stops at 100.0 °C: it warms the water but never boils it. Reaching 100 °C is not the same as becoming steam. B boils the water but skips warming it from 60.0 °C to 100.0 °C. D adds 5020 J to 67.8 kJ as if both were in the same unit. Convert every step to kJ (or every step to J) before adding.
hint: Two steps: warm the liquid to 100.0 °C (q = mcΔT), then boil it (q = nΔH<sub>vap</sub>). Put both heats in the same unit before adding.

title: Problem 9.32
question: How much heat is needed to warm 40.0 g of ice from −25.0 °C to −5.0 °C? A. 2.09 × 10 3 J B. 3.35 × 10 3 J C. 1.50 × 10 4 J D. 1.67 × 10 3 J
answer: D. The sample stays solid the whole time (it never reaches 0 °C), so this is one sloped segment with the specific heat of ice . ΔT = −5.0 − (−25.0) = 20.0 °C. \( q = (40.0\ \text{g})\left(2.09\ \dfrac{\text{J}}{\text{g}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C}}\right)(20.0\ {}^\circ\text{C}) = 1.67 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J} \) A uses 25.0 °C as ΔT, the size of the starting temperature instead of the change. B uses the specific heat of liquid water (4.184). Ice has its own, smaller specific heat, 2.09 J/(g·°C). C adds a melting step (40.0 g ÷ 18.015 g/mol × 6020 J/mol). No ice melts, because the final temperature is still below 0 °C; sketch the heating curve to see which segments the change really crosses.
hint: Does the ice ever reach 0 °C? If not, it is one sloped segment: q = mcΔT with c for ice, 2.09 J/(g·°C), and ΔT = final − initial.

title: Problem 9.33
question: Which substance can hydrogen bond with itself? A. Formaldehyde, H 2 CO B. Difluoromethane, CH 2 F 2 C. Ethylamine, CH 3 CH 2 NH 2 D. Hydrogen chloride, HCl
answer: C. Ethylamine has two H atoms bonded directly to N, and the N has a lone pair, so an N–H on one molecule can hydrogen bond to the N of a neighbor. A has an O, but both H atoms are bonded to C. A C–H hydrogen is not positive enough to hydrogen bond; formaldehyde is polar, so its strongest force is dipole–dipole. B has F atoms and H atoms, but again every H is on carbon. Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O, or F. D is polar, with H bonded to Cl, but Cl is not N, O, or F. HCl has dipole–dipole forces, not hydrogen bonds.
hint: Hydrogen bonding needs an H bonded directly to N, O, or F (the donor) and a lone pair on N, O, or F (the acceptor). Check where each H is attached.

title: Problem 9.35
question: Dichloromethane, CH 2 Cl 2 , is a solvent used to remove caffeine from coffee beans. What is the strongest intermolecular force between CH 2 Cl 2 molecules? A. Dipole–dipole forces B. Hydrogen bonding C. Dispersion forces only, because a tetrahedral molecule is symmetric D. Ion–dipole forces
answer: A. The C–Cl bonds are polar (ΔEN = 0.5) and the C–H bonds count as nonpolar, so the two Cl atoms pull electron density toward one side of the molecule. The bond dipoles do not cancel, so CH 2 Cl 2 is polar: dipole–dipole forces (plus dispersion). B: CH 2 Cl 2 contains H, but every H is bonded to C, and there is no N, O, or F. No hydrogen bonding. C: the shape is tetrahedral, but a tetrahedron is only symmetric when all four atoms around the center are the same, as in CH 4 or CCl 4 . Two H and two Cl make it asymmetric. D needs ions. CH 2 Cl 2 is a molecular compound made only of nonmetals.
hint: Is CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> polar? A tetrahedron is symmetric only when all four atoms around carbon are the same. Is any H bonded to N, O, or F?

title: Problem 9.36
question: Which statement correctly describes water boiling at 100 °C? A. The bubbles are H 2 and O 2 gas, formed as water molecules break apart. B. Hydrogen bonds between neighboring molecules are overcome, and each H 2 O molecule stays intact. C. The O–H covalent bonds inside each molecule break. D. Hydrogen bonds are covalent bonds between the H atoms of neighboring molecules, and boiling breaks them.
answer: B. Boiling is a physical change. The molecules move apart from each other, so the intermolecular forces (mainly hydrogen bonds) are overcome, but the molecules themselves do not change; the bubbles are water vapor, H 2 O(g). A describes a chemical change (decomposition, as in electrolysis). Boiling water does not make hydrogen or oxygen gas. C: covalent O–H bonds are far stronger than intermolecular forces; breaking them takes far more energy than boiling provides. D: a hydrogen bond is not covalent. It is an attraction between an H on one molecule and a lone pair on the O of a different molecule, a few percent as strong as a covalent bond.
hint: Is boiling a physical or a chemical change? Ask whether the H<sub>2</sub>O molecules themselves come apart, or only separate from each other.
new_hint: Is boiling a physical or a chemical change? Decide whether a hydrogen bond is an attraction inside one molecule or between neighboring molecules.

title: Problem 9.38
question: Which substance has the strongest dispersion forces? A. HF B. HCl C. HBr D. HI
answer: D. Dispersion forces grow with the number of electrons. HI has 54 electrons (1 + 53), the largest, most polarizable electron cloud of the four. A, HF, has the fewest electrons (10) and the weakest dispersion forces. HF does hydrogen bond, but hydrogen bonding is a different force; the question asks only about dispersion. B, HCl, has 18 electrons. C, HBr, has 36 electrons: stronger dispersion than HCl, but weaker than HI.
hint: Dispersion forces grow with the number of electrons. Count the electrons in each molecule: 1 for H plus the halogen's atomic number.

title: Problem 9.40
question: Quartz (SiO 2 ) melts at about 1700 °C, while dry ice (solid CO 2 ) sublimes at −78 °C. What is the best explanation? A. Quartz is a covalent network: melting it breaks Si–O covalent bonds. Dry ice is a molecular solid held only by dispersion forces. B. Both are molecular solids, and SiO 2 has the larger molar mass, so its dispersion forces are stronger. C. Quartz is an ionic solid, because Si and O have very different electronegativities. D. SiO 2 molecules hydrogen bond with each other; CO 2 molecules do not.
answer: A. Quartz has no separate SiO 2 molecules: every Si is covalently bonded to four O atoms, and every O to two Si atoms, in an endless network. To melt it, covalent bonds must break. Dry ice is made of separate, nonpolar O=C=O molecules held together only by weak dispersion forces. B treats SiO 2 as a molecule. The formula SiO 2 only gives the ratio of atoms in the network. A difference of 16 g/mol in molar mass could never explain a difference of nearly 1800 °C. C: silicon is a metalloid and oxygen a nonmetal, and the Si–O bond is polar covalent, not ionic. Quartz does not conduct even when melted. D: quartz has no H atoms at all, so it cannot hydrogen bond.
hint: Classify each solid first. Does quartz have separate SiO<sub>2</sub> molecules, or covalent bonds running through the whole crystal?
new_hint: Classify each solid first: molecular, ionic, covalent network, or metallic. What must break when quartz melts, compared with dry ice subliming?

title: Problem 9.43
question: Which liquid has the highest surface tension at room temperature? A. Hexane, C 6 H 14 B. Diethyl ether, CH 3 CH 2 OCH 2 CH 3 C. Ethanol, CH 3 CH 2 OH D. Water, H 2 O
answer: D. Surface tension rises with the strength of the attractions pulling surface molecules inward. Water forms an extensive network of hydrogen bonds (two O–H hydrogens and two lone pairs per molecule), the strongest attractions of the four. A, hexane, is nonpolar, with dispersion forces only. Its larger size does not make up for the lack of stronger forces. B, diethyl ether, is polar but has no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself; its strongest force is dipole–dipole. C, ethanol, does hydrogen bond, but with only one O–H per molecule it forms fewer hydrogen bonds than water does, so its surface tension is much lower.
hint: Surface tension rises with the strength of the intermolecular forces. Find the strongest force in each liquid, then compare how many hydrogen bonds each molecule can make.

title: Problem 9.45
question: Inside a running autoclave, the pressure is roughly twice normal atmospheric pressure, and water boils at about 121 °C instead of 100 °C. Why? A. The higher pressure makes the hydrogen bonds between water molecules stronger. B. Water's vapor pressure is lower inside an autoclave, so it must be heated more. C. Boiling happens when the vapor pressure equals the pressure above the liquid, and water's vapor pressure reaches the higher pressure only at a higher temperature. D. The steam has extra heat added to it, and the boiling point rises with the amount of heat added.
answer: C. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the outside pressure. Water's vapor pressure rises with temperature and reaches 1 atm at 100 °C; to match a pressure about twice as high, the water must be hotter, about 121 °C. Steam at that temperature kills heat-resistant bacterial spores that survive boiling at 100 °C. A: the intermolecular forces are the same; the molecules are still water. What changed is the pressure the vapor must push against. B: vapor pressure depends on the liquid and its temperature, not on the container. At any given temperature, water's vapor pressure is the same inside or outside the autoclave. D: adding heat at the boiling point turns more liquid into steam, but it does not change the boiling temperature. Only the outside pressure does that.
hint: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the pressure above it. If the outside pressure is higher, what must happen to the temperature?
new_hint: What condition must be met for a liquid to boil? Then think about how water's vapor pressure changes as its temperature rises.

title: Problem 9.47
question: Ethane (C 2 H 6 ), fluoromethane (CH 3 F), and methanol (CH 3 OH) each have 18 electrons. Rank them from lowest to highest boiling point. A. C 2 H 6 < CH 3 OH < CH 3 F B. C 2 H 6 < CH 3 F < CH 3 OH C. CH 3 OH < CH 3 F < C 2 H 6 D. All three about the same, because they have the same number of electrons
answer: B. With the size (electron count) the same, the strongest force decides. Ethane is nonpolar (dispersion only). Fluoromethane is polar because of its C–F bond (ΔEN = 1.5), but all its H atoms are on carbon, so its strongest force is dipole–dipole. Methanol has an O–H and hydrogen bonds. The real boiling points are about −89 °C, −78 °C, and 65 °C. A ranks by molar mass (30.070 < 32.042 < 34.033 g/mol). Hydrogen bonding in methanol outweighs fluoromethane's slightly larger mass; compare the strongest force first and use size only to break ties. C is the order of vapor pressure (lowest to highest), which is the reverse of the boiling-point order. D: equal electron counts make the dispersion forces similar, but methanol and fluoromethane have additional, stronger forces on top of dispersion.
hint: The electron counts are equal, so dispersion is similar. Find each molecule's strongest force (nonpolar? polar? H on O?) and rank by it.

title: Problem 9.48
question: Which liquid has the highest vapor pressure at 20 °C? A. Acetone B. Ethanol C. Water D. Glycerol, C 3 H 5 (OH) 3
answer: A. Acetone is polar but cannot hydrogen bond with itself, so it has the weakest intermolecular forces of the four. Its molecules escape most easily: it is the most volatile, with the highest vapor pressure and the lowest boiling point (56 °C). B, ethanol, hydrogen bonds through its one O–H group, so it holds its molecules more tightly than acetone does. C, water, hydrogen bonds even more extensively than ethanol; its vapor pressure is lower still. D, glycerol, has three O–H groups per molecule and the highest boiling point of the four. Picking it uses the boiling-point order; vapor pressure runs the opposite way, so glycerol has the lowest vapor pressure.
hint: The highest vapor pressure goes with the weakest intermolecular forces. Which liquid cannot hydrogen bond with itself? Among the rest, count O–H groups.

title: Problem 9.56
question: In a foam-cup calorimeter, 25.0 mL of hydrochloric acid (density 1.02 g/mL) is mixed with 25.0 mL of sodium hydroxide solution (density 1.04 g/mL). The temperature rises from 22.3 °C to 28.9 °C. Using c = 4.184 J/(g·°C) for the mixture and the total mass of the solution, what is q reaction ? A. −1.4 kJ B. +1.4 kJ C. −0.70 kJ D. −6.2 kJ
answer: A. Total mass: 25.0 × 1.02 = 25.5 g and 25.0 × 1.04 = 26.0 g, so m = 51.5 g. ΔT = 28.9 − 22.3 = 6.6 °C (two significant figures after the subtraction). \( q_\text{solution} = (51.5\ \text{g})(4.184)(6.6\ {}^\circ\text{C}) = 1.4 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J} \qquad q_\text{reaction} = -q_\text{solution} = -1.4\ \text{kJ} \) The solution warmed, so the reaction released heat: it is exothermic. B is q solution , not q reaction . The signs are opposite: heat gained by the solution was lost by the reaction. C uses the mass of only one of the two solutions (25.5 g). The thermometer reads the whole mixture, so m is the total mass. D uses the final temperature, 28.9 °C, as ΔT. ΔT is final minus initial.
hint: Mass = each volume × its density, added. ΔT = final − initial; q<sub>solution</sub> = mcΔT and q<sub>reaction</sub> = −q<sub>solution</sub>. Watch the significant figures in ΔT.

title: Problem 9.58
question: A steam pipe leaks 40.0 g of steam at 100.0 °C. The steam condenses, the water cools, and the water freezes at 0.0 °C on a cold surface. How much heat is released in all? (ΔH vap = 40.7 kJ/mol; ΔH fus = 6.02 kJ/mol; c water = 4.184 J/(g·°C); H 2 O 18.015 g/mol) A. 120.5 kJ B. 103.7 kJ C. 90.4 kJ D. 107.1 kJ
answer: A. n = 40.0 ÷ 18.015 = 2.220 mol. Condense: 2.220 × 40.7 = 90.37 kJ. Cool from 100.0 to 0.0 °C: (40.0)(4.184)(100.0) = 16,736 J = 16.74 kJ. Freeze: 2.220 × 6.02 = 13.37 kJ. Total released: 90.37 + 16.74 + 13.37 = 120.5 kJ (q = −120.5 kJ for the water). B leaves out the cooling step: the water must cool from 100 °C to 0 °C between the two plateaus. C counts only the condensing step. D leaves out the freezing step at 0.0 °C.
hint: Three steps, all releasing heat: condense at 100 °C, cool the water to 0 °C, then freeze. Do not skip the cooling slope between the two plateaus.

title: Problem 9.61
question: Which molecule can hydrogen bond with itself? A. dimethyl ether, CH 3 OCH 3 B. methylamine, CH 3 NH 2 C. phosphine, PH 3 D. trimethylamine, N(CH 3 ) 3
answer: B. Methylamine has H atoms bonded directly to N (donors) and a lone pair on that N (an acceptor), so one molecule can donate to the next. A has a lone pair on O, so it can accept a hydrogen bond (from water, for example), but every H is on carbon: no donor. Its strongest force with itself is dipole–dipole. C: P is not F, N, or O, and P–H bonds count as nonpolar (2.1 and 2.1). PH 3 has dispersion forces only. D has a lone pair on N (an acceptor) but no H on N: no donor.
hint: A molecule hydrogen bonds with itself only if it has an H on N, O, or F (a donor) and a lone pair on N, O, or F (an acceptor). Check where each H sits.

title: Problem 9.62
question: Which solid conducts electricity? A. NaCl(s) B. Ag(s) C. I 2 (s) D. Ar(s)
answer: B. Silver is a metallic solid: its cations sit in a sea of electrons that are free to move, so it conducts as a solid. A is ionic. Its ions are locked in the lattice, so it conducts only when melted or dissolved. C is a molecular solid held by dispersion forces; it has no free charges. D is an atomic nonbonding solid (argon atoms held by dispersion forces only); it does not conduct, and it melts at −189 °C.
hint: To conduct, charges must be free to move inside the solid. Which type of solid has mobile electrons?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
question: A pat of margarine provides 145 kJ of energy when it is metabolized. How many food Calories is that? A. 34.7 Cal B. 607 Cal C. 0.0347 Cal
answer: A. 1 Cal = 4.184 kJ, so 145 kJ ÷ 4.184 kJ/Cal = 34.7 Cal. B multiplies by 4.184 instead of dividing (a Calorie is bigger than a kilojoule, so the number of Calories must be smaller). C divides 145 by 4184 J/Cal without first changing kJ to J (145 kJ = 145,000 J); a kilojoule-to-Calorie conversion uses 4.184 kJ/Cal.
hint: Use 4.184 kJ per Cal. A Calorie is bigger than a kilojoule, so should the number of Calories be smaller or larger than the number of kilojoules?

title: Problem 10.1
question: Which statement is not part of kinetic molecular theory for an ideal gas? A. The particles are in constant, random, straight-line motion. B. The particles attract one another, which holds the gas together. C. Collisions between particles and with the walls are elastic. D. The average kinetic energy of the particles is proportional to the Kelvin temperature.
answer: B. Kinetic molecular theory assumes the particles neither attract nor repel each other. Nothing holds a gas together, which is why it spreads out to fill any container. (Attractions do matter for real gases near condensation, which is why the ideal model fails there.) A is part of the theory: constant random motion explains diffusion and why a gas fills its container. C is part of the theory: in elastic collisions no kinetic energy is lost overall, so a gas left alone at constant temperature never "runs down" and its pressure stays steady. D is part of the theory, and it is the reason every gas law needs temperatures in kelvins.
hint: Compare each choice with the KMT list in Section 10.1. A gas spreads out to fill any container: what does that say about forces between its particles?

title: Problem 10.2
question: What causes the pressure of the oxygen inside a sealed cylinder? A. The O 2 molecules are attracted to the steel walls and pull on them. B. The O 2 molecules swell when they are warm and press against the walls. C. The O 2 molecules constantly collide with the walls, and each collision pushes on them. D. The weight of the gas presses down on the bottom of the cylinder.
answer: C. Pressure is force per area. Each molecule that hits a wall gives it a tiny push, and billions upon billions of hits every second add up to a steady pressure on every wall, not just the bottom. A is wrong: kinetic molecular theory assumes no attractions, and a pull would not explain why the gas pushes outward on the walls. B is a common misconception. Heating makes molecules move faster , not grow larger; faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often. D is wrong: a gas pushes equally on the top, sides, and bottom of its container. The weight of a gas this small is negligible compared with its collisions.
hint: Pressure is force per area. In KMT, what are gas particles constantly doing to the walls? Heating changes their speed, not their size.

title: Problem 10.4
question: A sample of helium is at 310. K (about body temperature). To what temperature must it be heated to double the average kinetic energy of its atoms? A. 155 K B. 347 K C. 310. K D. 620. K
answer: D. Average kinetic energy is directly proportional to the Kelvin temperature, so doubling the kinetic energy means doubling the Kelvin temperature: 2 × 310. K = 620. K (the factor 2 is exact, so the answer keeps three significant figures). A halves the temperature, which would halve the kinetic energy. B doubles the Celsius temperature: 310. K is 36.85 °C, twice that is 73.7 °C, or 347 K. Kinetic energy is proportional to the Kelvin temperature, not the Celsius temperature. C assumes that heating changes only the speed, not the kinetic energy. Faster atoms have more kinetic energy; that is what temperature measures.
hint: Average kinetic energy is proportional to the Kelvin temperature. What must happen to the Kelvin temperature to double the kinetic energy? Do not switch to °C.

title: Problem 10.6
question: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas? A. High pressure and low temperature B. High pressure and high temperature C. Low pressure and high temperature D. Low pressure and low temperature
answer: C. At low pressure the particles are far apart, so their own volume is a tiny fraction of the container. At high temperature they move so fast that attractions between them hardly matter. Both match the assumptions of kinetic molecular theory. A is the worst case: at high pressure the particles are crowded, and at low temperature attractions become important; this is how gases are liquefied, as with the liquid oxygen stored at hospitals. B fixes the temperature but not the crowding: at high pressure the particles' own volume still matters. D fixes the crowding but not the attractions: slow particles near the boiling point stick together.
hint: An ideal gas has particles that take up no space and do not attract each other. Which pressure keeps particles far apart, and which temperature makes attractions unimportant?

title: Problem 10.7
question: A barometer at a ranger station in Yosemite Valley, about 4,000 ft above sea level, reads 656 mmHg. What is this pressure in atmospheres? A. 1.16 atm B. 0.863 atm C. 4.99 × 10 5 atm D. 6.47 atm
answer: B. \( 656\ \text{mmHg} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{atm}}{760\ \text{mmHg}} = 0.863\ \text{atm} \) The answer makes sense: at 4,000 ft there is less air above you, so the pressure is below 1 atm. A flips the conversion factor (760/656). A pressure above 1 atm at a high elevation should be a warning sign. C multiplies by 760 instead of dividing. The mmHg units do not cancel, and no air pressure on Earth is near 500,000 atm. D divides by 101.325, the number of kilopascals in 1 atm. That factor converts kPa, not mmHg.
hint: Use 1 atm = 760 mmHg with mmHg on the bottom. Check: at 4,000 ft there is less air above you, so should the answer be above or below 1 atm?

title: Problem 10.9
question: Which is the highest pressure? A. 795 mmHg B. 106 kPa C. 15.3 psi D. 1.06 atm
answer: D. Convert each to atm and compare. A: 795 ÷ 760 = 1.046 atm. It has the biggest number, but a millimeter of mercury is a small unit. B: 106 ÷ 101.325 = 1.046 atm, the same as A. C: 15.3 ÷ 14.7 = 1.041 atm, the lowest of the four. So 1.06 atm is the highest. Never compare pressures in different units by their numbers alone.
hint: Convert every choice to the same unit (atm is easiest), then compare. A big number in a small unit can still be a smaller pressure.

title: Problem 10.11
question: In seawater, the pressure increases by about 1 atm for every 10.1 m (33 ft) of depth, on top of the 1.00 atm of air pressing on the surface. What is the total pressure on a scuba diver at a depth of 18.0 m? A. 1.78 atm B. 1.56 atm C. 2.78 atm D. 183 atm
answer: C. The water adds 18.0 m × (1 atm / 10.1 m) = 1.782 atm, and the air above the water adds 1.00 atm: \( P_\text{total} = 1.00\ \text{atm} + 18.0\ \text{m} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{atm}}{10.1\ \text{m}} = 1.00 + 1.782 = 2.78\ \text{atm} \) A counts only the water and forgets the atmosphere above it. B flips the conversion factor (10.1/18.0 + 1). Going deeper than 10.1 m must add more than 1 atm. D multiplies the depth by 10.1 m instead of dividing. The meters do not cancel, and 183 atm would crush a diver.
hint: Find the pressure from the water (depth × 1 atm per 10.1 m), then add the air pressing on the surface of the water.

title: Problem 10.14
question: A scuba diver at a depth where the pressure is 2.80 atm fills her lungs to 4.20 L from her regulator. If she held her breath while rising to the surface (1.00 atm), what volume would that air try to occupy, at constant temperature? A. 11.8 L B. 1.50 L C. 7.56 L D. 4.20 L
answer: A. Boyle's law: \( V_2 = \dfrac{P_1 V_1}{P_2} = \dfrac{(2.80\ \text{atm})(4.20\ \text{L})}{1.00\ \text{atm}} = 11.8\ \text{L} \) Lungs cannot stretch to nearly three times their volume; the expanding air could rupture them. This is why divers are trained to breathe out continuously as they ascend. B sets up Boyle's law as a ratio (or flips the pressures): 4.20 × 1.00/2.80. The pressure goes down , so the volume must go up . C multiplies the volume by the difference in pressures, 4.20 × (2.80 − 1.00). Boyle's law uses the ratio of the pressures, not their difference. D assumes the lungs are rigid. Air in a flexible container changes volume whenever the pressure on it changes.
hint: Constant temperature and moles: Boyle's law, P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>. Predict first: as the pressure drops on the way up, what happens to the volume?

title: Problem 10.16
question: A rigid steel cylinder of helium for filling balloons is at 155 atm at 21.0 °C. It is left in the bed of a pickup truck, where it warms to 48.0 °C. What is the new pressure? A. 155 atm B. 354 atm C. 142 atm D. 169 atm
answer: D. The volume and moles are constant, so use Gay-Lussac's law with Kelvin temperatures (294.15 K and 321.15 K): \( P_2 = P_1 \times \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 155\ \text{atm} \times \dfrac{321.15\ \text{K}}{294.15\ \text{K}} = 169\ \text{atm} \) Hotter gas in a rigid container means higher pressure, which is why gas cylinders are stored out of direct sun. A assumes nothing changes because the cylinder is rigid. Its volume is fixed, but the faster-moving atoms hit the walls harder, so the pressure rises. B uses Celsius temperatures (155 × 48.0/21.0). The pressure does not really more than double for a 27 °C rise. C flips the temperature ratio, so the pressure drops on heating, the wrong direction for a direct relationship.
hint: Rigid means constant volume: Gay-Lussac's law, P<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>. Convert both temperatures to kelvins; a 27 °C rise should raise the pressure only a little.

title: Problem 10.19
question: A 455 mL sample of gas is at 1.12 atm and 18.0 °C. What is its volume at 685 mmHg and 40.0 °C? A. 526 mL B. 608 mL C. 0.800 mL D. 1.26 × 10 3 mL
answer: B. Put both pressures in the same unit first: 1.12 atm × 760 mmHg/atm = 851.2 mmHg. T 1 = 291.15 K; T 2 = 313.15 K. \( V_2 = V_1 \times \dfrac{P_1}{P_2} \times \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 455\ \text{mL} \times \dfrac{851.2\ \text{mmHg}}{685\ \text{mmHg}} \times \dfrac{313.15\ \text{K}}{291.15\ \text{K}} = 608\ \text{mL} \) Predict first: the pressure drops (volume up) and the temperature rises (volume up), so the answer must be larger than 455 mL. A flips the temperature ratio. Warming a gas at lower pressure cannot shrink it below the pressure-only answer (565 mL). C divides 1.12 atm by 685 mmHg without converting. The two pressures must be in the same unit. D uses Celsius temperatures (40.0/18.0), which more than doubles the temperature effect.
hint: Put both pressures in the same unit and both temperatures in kelvins. Predict: lower pressure and higher temperature both make the volume bigger.

title: Problem 10.20
question: The Kelvin temperature of a gas sample is doubled while its pressure is tripled, with the amount of gas constant. What happens to its volume? A. It is multiplied by 6. B. It is multiplied by 2/3. C. It is multiplied by 3/2. D. It is multiplied by 1/6.
answer: B. From the combined gas law, V 2 = V 1 × (P 1 /P 2 ) × (T 2 /T 1 ) = V 1 × (1/3) × (2/1) = (2/3)V 1 . Doubling T doubles V (direct), and tripling P cuts V to a third (inverse). A treats both changes as direct. Pressure and volume are inversely related. C has both relationships upside down: it treats temperature as inverse and pressure as direct. D treats both changes as inverse. Temperature and volume are directly related.
hint: Use V<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>1</sub> × (P<sub>1</sub>/P<sub>2</sub>) × (T<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>1</sub>) with easy numbers: P<sub>1</sub> = 1, P<sub>2</sub> = 3, T<sub>1</sub> = 1, T<sub>2</sub> = 2.

title: Problem 10.23
question: How many moles of O 2 are in a 2.50 L flask at 1.85 atm and 24.0 °C? A. 0.112 mol B. 2.35 mol C. 0.190 mol D. 5.27 mol
answer: C. T = 24.0 + 273.15 = 297.2 K. \( n = \dfrac{PV}{RT} = \dfrac{(1.85\ \text{atm})(2.50\ \text{L})}{(0.082058\ \tfrac{\text{L}\cdot\text{atm}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}})(297.15\ \text{K})} = 0.190\ \text{mol} \) A divides the volume by 22.4 L/mol. That molar volume applies only at STP, and this gas is at 1.85 atm and 24.0 °C. B uses 24.0 °C for T. R is in kelvins, so T must be too. D flips the equation (RT/PV). Check the units: the answer must come out in mol, not mol −1 .
hint: One set of conditions: n = PV/RT. The gas is not at STP, so 22.4 L/mol does not apply, and T must be in kelvins.

title: Problem 10.25
question: A 1.75 L balloon holds 0.0850 mol of helium at 27.0 °C. What is the pressure inside, in mmHg? A. 909 mmHg B. 1.20 mmHg C. 81.8 mmHg D. 1.57 × 10 −3 mmHg
answer: A. With R = 0.082058, the pressure comes out in atm; convert to mmHg at the end. T = 300.15 K. \( P = \dfrac{nRT}{V} = \dfrac{(0.0850)(0.082058)(300.15)}{1.75} = 1.196\ \text{atm} \times \dfrac{760\ \text{mmHg}}{1\ \text{atm}} = 909\ \text{mmHg} \) (With R = 62.36 L·torr/(mol·K) you get the same 909 torr in one step.) B is the pressure in atm with the wrong unit attached. R = 0.082058 gives atm, not mmHg. C uses 27.0 °C for T instead of 300.15 K. D divides by 760 instead of multiplying. There are more mmHg than atm in any pressure.
hint: Find P = nRT/V with T in kelvins; with R = 0.082058 the pressure comes out in atm. Then convert atm to mmHg; there are more mmHg than atm.

title: Problem 10.27
question: Nitrous oxide (N 2 O, 44.013 g/mol) is used in dental offices. What volume does 0.375 mol of N 2 O occupy at STP? A. 59.7 L B. 0.0167 L C. 8.40 L D. 370. L
answer: C. At STP, 1 mol of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L: \( 0.375\ \text{mol} \times \dfrac{22.4\ \text{L}}{1\ \text{mol}} = 8.40\ \text{L} \) A divides 22.4 by the moles. The units would be L/mol, not L. B divides the moles by 22.4, as if converting liters to moles. D converts to grams first (0.375 mol × 44.013 g/mol = 16.5 g) and then multiplies grams by 22.4 L/mol. The molar volume multiplies moles, not grams; the molar mass is not needed here.
hint: At STP, 1 mol of any gas fills 22.4 L. Set up moles × (22.4 L / 1 mol) so moles cancel; the molar mass is not needed.

title: Problem 10.30
question: At the same temperature and pressure, the density of a gas is proportional to its molar mass. Air has an average molar mass of about 29 g/mol. If each of these gases leaked into a closed room, which would tend to collect near the floor? A. Helium, He (4.003 g/mol) B. Methane (natural gas), CH 4 (16.043 g/mol) C. Propane, C 3 H 8 (44.097 g/mol) D. Ammonia, NH 3 (17.031 g/mol)
answer: C. Propane's molar mass (44.097 g/mol) is about one and a half times that of air, so it is denser than air and settles in low places: basements, trailer floors, and pits. That is why leaking propane from a camp stove or heater is a special fire hazard. A: helium is far less dense than air; it rises, which is why helium balloons float. B: methane (16.043 g/mol) is less dense than air and rises toward the ceiling. D: ammonia (17.031 g/mol) is also lighter than air and rises.
hint: A gas whose molar mass is larger than air's (about 29 g/mol) is denser than air and sinks. Compare each molar mass with 29.

title: Problem 10.31
question: A gas has a density of 1.25 g/L at STP. What is its molar mass? A. 17.9 g/mol B. 0.0558 g/mol C. 30.6 g/mol D. 28.0 g/mol
answer: D. At STP, 1 mol occupies 22.4 L, so the mass of one mole is the mass of 22.4 L: \( M = 1.25\ \dfrac{\text{g}}{\text{L}} \times \dfrac{22.4\ \text{L}}{1\ \text{mol}} = 28.0\ \text{g/mol} \) This matches N 2 (28.014 g/mol). A divides 22.4 by the density; the units come out L²/(g·mol), not g/mol. B divides the density by 22.4; the units come out g·mol/L². No gas has a molar mass below that of hydrogen. C uses the molar volume at 25 °C (24.5 L/mol) instead of at STP. The problem says STP, so 22.4 L/mol is the right factor.
hint: Density is grams per liter, and at STP one mole fills 22.4 L. Multiply g/L by L/mol so liters cancel and g/mol remains.

title: Problem 10.33
question: Butane burns in a lighter by the reaction below. 2 C 4 H 10 (g) + 13 O 2 (g) → 8 CO 2 (g) + 10 H 2 O(g) What volume of O 2 , measured at STP, is needed to burn 0.250 mol of butane? A. 0.862 L B. 36.4 L C. 5.60 L D. 0.0725 L
answer: B. \( 0.250\ \text{mol C}_4\text{H}_{10} \times \dfrac{13\ \text{mol O}_2}{2\ \text{mol C}_4\text{H}_{10}} \times \dfrac{22.4\ \text{L}}{1\ \text{mol O}_2} = 36.4\ \text{L O}_2 \) A flips the mole ratio (2/13). Burning a fuel takes several times more moles of O 2 than moles of fuel. C skips the mole ratio and finds the volume of the butane, not of the oxygen. D divides by 22.4 instead of multiplying. Going from moles to liters at STP multiplies by 22.4 L/mol.
hint: Moles of butane, then the mole ratio of O<sub>2</sub> to butane from the coefficients, then 22.4 L/mol at STP. Burning a fuel takes more O<sub>2</sub> than fuel.

title: Problem 10.35
question: Propane burns in a backyard grill: C 3 H 8 (g) + 5 O 2 (g) → 3 CO 2 (g) + 4 H 2 O(g) What volume of O 2 is needed to burn 4.20 L of propane, with both gases measured at the same temperature and pressure? A. 12.6 L B. 0.840 L C. 21.0 L D. 4.20 L
answer: C. Both gases are at the same T and P, so the coefficients are volume ratios (Avogadro's law): \( 4.20\ \text{L C}_3\text{H}_8 \times \dfrac{5\ \text{L O}_2}{1\ \text{L C}_3\text{H}_8} = 21.0\ \text{L O}_2 \) A uses the coefficient of CO 2 (3) instead of O 2 (5). Read the ratio for the two substances in the question. B flips the ratio (1/5), so less oxygen than fuel. D skips the ratio, as if 1 L of propane used 1 L of O 2 .
hint: Same T and P, so the coefficients are volume ratios. Use the coefficients of the two substances in the question, O<sub>2</sub> and C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>.

title: Problem 10.37
question: A classic way to make oxygen in the lab is to heat potassium chlorate: 2 KClO 3 (s) → 2 KCl(s) + 3 O 2 (g) What mass of KClO 3 (122.55 g/mol) is needed to make 1.50 L of O 2 measured at STP? A. 5.47 g B. 8.21 g C. 12.3 g D. 2.75 × 10 3 g
answer: A. \( 1.50\ \text{L O}_2 \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol O}_2}{22.4\ \text{L}} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol KClO}_3}{3\ \text{mol O}_2} \times \dfrac{122.55\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mol KClO}_3} = 5.47\ \text{g} \) B skips the mole ratio, as if 1 mol KClO 3 made 1 mol O 2 . C flips the mole ratio (3/2). Each 2 KClO 3 make 3 O 2 , so fewer moles of KClO 3 are needed than moles of O 2 made. D multiplies the liters by 22.4 instead of dividing, which turns 1.50 L into "33.6 mol." To go from liters at STP to moles, divide by 22.4 L/mol.
hint: Liters of O<sub>2</sub> at STP to moles (divide by 22.4 L/mol), the mole ratio 2 KClO<sub>3</sub> : 3 O<sub>2</sub>, then the molar mass of KClO<sub>3</sub>.

title: Problem 10.39
question: An antacid tablet contains sodium bicarbonate, which fizzes in stomach acid: NaHCO 3 (s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H 2 O(l) + CO 2 (g) What volume of CO 2 , in mL, forms from 0.650 g of NaHCO 3 (84.01 g/mol) at 25.0 °C and 0.988 atm? A. 173 mL B. 16.1 mL C. 0.192 mL D. 192 mL
answer: D. n = 0.650 g ÷ 84.01 g/mol = 0.007737 mol NaHCO 3 = 0.007737 mol CO 2 (1 : 1). \( V = \dfrac{nRT}{P} = \dfrac{(0.007737)(0.082058)(298.15\ \text{K})}{0.988\ \text{atm}} = 0.192\ \text{L} = 192\ \text{mL} \) A uses 22.4 L/mol, but the gas is at 25.0 °C and 0.988 atm, not STP. B uses 25.0 °C instead of 298.15 K. C is the answer in liters with "mL" attached. R gives liters; multiply by 1000 mL/L.
hint: Grams to moles of NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, the 1 : 1 ratio to CO<sub>2</sub>, then V = nRT/P in kelvins (this is not STP). R gives liters; convert to mL.

title: Problem 10.41
question: In an anaerobic jar, a palladium catalyst makes hydrogen react with the oxygen left in the jar: 2 H 2 (g) + O 2 (g) → 2 H 2 O(l) A jar contains 0.415 L of O 2 . What volume of H 2 , measured at the same temperature and pressure, is needed to remove it all? A. 0.830 L B. 0.208 L C. 0.415 L D. 18.6 L
answer: A. Both gases are at the same T and P, so the coefficients give the volume ratio: \( 0.415\ \text{L O}_2 \times \dfrac{2\ \text{L H}_2}{1\ \text{L O}_2} = 0.830\ \text{L H}_2 \) B flips the ratio (1/2). Each O 2 needs two H 2 . C skips the ratio. D multiplies the correct volume by 22.4 L/mol, treating liters as if they were moles. A volume ratio goes straight from liters to liters.
hint: Same T and P: the coefficients are a volume ratio. How many H<sub>2</sub> does each O<sub>2</sub> need? Go straight from liters to liters.

title: Problem 10.43
question: During a dental procedure, a patient breathes a mixture that is 35.0% N 2 O and 65.0% O 2 by moles, at a total pressure of 765 mmHg. What is the partial pressure of N 2 O? A. 497 mmHg B. 268 mmHg C. 765 mmHg D. 2.68 × 10 4 mmHg
answer: B. The mole fraction is the percent divided by 100: X N 2 O = 0.350. \( P_{\text{N}_2\text{O}} = X_{\text{N}_2\text{O}} \times P_\text{total} = (0.350)(765\ \text{mmHg}) = 268\ \text{mmHg} \) A is the partial pressure of O 2 (0.650 × 765), not of N 2 O. C is the total pressure. Each gas has only its share of the total. D multiplies by 35.0 instead of 0.350. A partial pressure can never be larger than the total.
hint: Divide the percent by 100 to get the mole fraction of N<sub>2</sub>O, then multiply by the total pressure. A partial pressure is always less than the total.

title: Problem 10.46
question: Hydrogen is collected over water at 30.0 °C when the barometric pressure is 758 mmHg. The water levels inside and outside the collection tube are equal. What is the partial pressure of the H 2 ? (Water vapor pressure: 23.8 mmHg at 25 °C; 31.8 mmHg at 30 °C.) A. 758 mmHg B. 734 mmHg C. 726 mmHg D. 790. mmHg
answer: C. \( P_{\text{H}_2} = P_\text{atm} - P_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = 758 - 31.8 = 726\ \text{mmHg} \) (726.2 rounds to the ones place, set by 758.) A forgets the water vapor. The gas in the tube is "wet": the room pressure is shared by the H 2 and the water vapor. B uses the vapor pressure at 25 °C. Look up the vapor pressure at the temperature of the water. D adds the water vapor pressure instead of subtracting it. The partial pressure of one gas in a mixture is always less than the total.
hint: Subtract the vapor pressure of water at the temperature of the water (check which value that is) from the barometric pressure.

title: Problem 10.48
question: A 10.0 L tank at 25.0 °C holds a mixture of oxygen and helium at a total pressure of 5.00 atm. The partial pressure of O 2 is 1.20 atm. How many moles of O 2 are in the tank? A. 2.04 mol B. 1.55 mol C. 5.85 mol D. 0.490 mol
answer: D. To find the moles of one gas, use that gas's partial pressure in PV = nRT: \( n_{\text{O}_2} = \dfrac{P_{\text{O}_2} V}{RT} = \dfrac{(1.20\ \text{atm})(10.0\ \text{L})}{(0.082058)(298.15\ \text{K})} = 0.490\ \text{mol} \) A uses the total pressure, which gives the total moles of gas (O 2 plus He), not the moles of O 2 . B uses the partial pressure of helium (5.00 − 1.20 = 3.80 atm), so it is the moles of He. C uses 25.0 °C instead of 298.15 K.
hint: To find the moles of one gas, use that gas's own partial pressure in PV = nRT, with T in kelvins.

title: Problem 10.51
question: Helium is pumped into a rigid tank that already holds oxygen at 0.800 atm, while the temperature stays constant. What happens to the partial pressure of the O 2 ? A. It increases, because the total pressure increases. B. It decreases, because the helium pushes the oxygen molecules aside. C. It becomes equal to the partial pressure of the helium. D. It stays at 0.800 atm.
answer: D. In a mixture, each gas behaves as if it were alone in the container. The moles of O 2 , the volume, and the temperature have not changed, so the O 2 molecules hit the walls just as often as before. Only the total pressure rises, by the helium's partial pressure. (The mole fraction of O 2 does drop, but X O 2 × P total is still 0.800 atm.) A confuses the total pressure with the oxygen's share of it. B treats the gas particles as crowding each other. In an ideal gas, the particles take up almost none of the space and do not interact. C has no basis: partial pressures depend on the moles of each gas, and nothing forces them to be equal.
hint: Each gas in a mixture acts as if it were alone. Did the moles of O<sub>2</sub>, the volume, or the temperature change?

title: Problem 10.57
question: An open jar holds 0.120 mol of air at 15.0 °C. The jar is warmed to 60.0 °C; its volume does not change, and because it is open, the pressure stays equal to the room's. How many moles of air remain in the jar? A. 0.104 mol B. 0.139 mol C. 0.0300 mol D. 0.120 mol
answer: A. P and V are constant, so cross them out of P 1 V 1 /(n 1 T 1 ) = P 2 V 2 /(n 2 T 2 ), leaving n 1 T 1 = n 2 T 2 . With T 1 = 288.15 K and T 2 = 333.15 K: \( n_2 = \dfrac{n_1 T_1}{T_2} = \dfrac{(0.120\ \text{mol})(288.15\ \text{K})}{333.15\ \text{K}} = 0.104\ \text{mol} \) Warming pushes some air out of the open jar, so fewer moles remain. B treats n and T as directly related (0.120 × 333.15/288.15). More moles in a warmer, open jar of fixed size is backward. C uses Celsius temperatures (0.120 × 15.0/60.0). Gas laws need kelvins. D assumes nothing changes; that would be true only for a sealed jar, whose pressure would rise instead.
hint: P and V are constant: cross them out of the combined gas law to get n<sub>1</sub>T<sub>1</sub> = n<sub>2</sub>T<sub>2</sub>. Use kelvins; warming pushes air out of an open jar.

title: Problem 10.59
question: "A 2.50 L flask holds 0.110 mol of argon at 28.0 °C. What is the pressure in the flask?" Which equation should you use? A. PV = nRT B. P 1 V 1 /T 1 = P 2 V 2 /T 2 C. P 1 V 1 = P 2 V 2 D. P total = P 1 + P 2
answer: A. There is one volume, one amount, and one temperature, and nothing changes: no subscripts, so this is the current state of the gas. P = nRT/V = (0.110)(0.082058)(301.15) ÷ 2.50 = 1.09 atm. B and C compare a gas before and after a change; they need two values (subscripts 1 and 2) of at least one variable. D is Dalton's law for mixtures; the flask holds only argon.
hint: Look for subscripts. Is the gas changing, with before and after values, or is there just one set of conditions? Is there a mixture of gases?

title: Problem 10.63
question: A sealed flask at a total pressure of 2.00 atm contains 5 ▲ (He), 3 ● (Ne), and 2 ■ (Ar). What is the partial pressure of neon? A. 0.600 atm B. 0.667 atm C. 0.300 atm D. 1.00 atm
answer: A. There are 10 particles, 3 of them neon: X Ne = 3/10 = 0.300, and P Ne = 0.300 × 2.00 atm = 0.600 atm. B splits the pressure equally among the three gases (2.00 ÷ 3). Each gas's share depends on how many particles it has, not on how many kinds of gas there are. C is the mole fraction, 0.300, which has no units; multiply it by the total pressure. D is the partial pressure of helium (5/10 × 2.00 atm), the gas with the most particles.
hint: Count all the particles. Neon's share of the particles is its mole fraction; multiply it by the total pressure.

title: Problem 11.1
question: Which substance is most soluble in water? A. Hexane, C 6 H 14 B. Carbon tetrachloride, CCl 4 C. Glycerol, C 3 H 8 O 3 (HOCH 2 CH(OH)CH 2 OH), used in cough syrups and skin lotions D. Iodine, I 2
answer: C. Glycerol has three O–H groups, and each one hydrogen bonds with water. Like dissolves like: a polar, hydrogen-bonding solute mixes with a polar, hydrogen-bonding solvent. Glycerol and water are miscible in all proportions, which is why glycerol is easy to blend into water-based syrups and lotions. A is a hydrocarbon. It has only C and H, so it is nonpolar with only dispersion forces, and water squeezes it out into a separate layer. B is a common trap. Each C–Cl bond is polar (ΔEN = 0.5), but the four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel (Chapter 6), so the molecule is nonpolar and barely dissolves in water. D is nonpolar (two identical atoms), so it dissolves only slightly in water; it dissolves much better in nonpolar solvents.
hint: Like dissolves like. Which molecule has O–H groups that hydrogen bond with water? Molecules of only C and H, or with symmetric C–Cl bonds, are nonpolar.
new_hint: Like dissolves like: water is polar and hydrogen bonds. Check each molecule: is it polar, and can it hydrogen bond with water?

title: Problem 11.3
question: Each substance below dissolves in water. Which solution conducts electricity well? A. Glucose, C 6 H 12 O 6 B. Ethanol, CH 3 CH 2 OH C. Potassium bromide, KBr D. Urea, CH 4 N 2 O
answer: C. KBr is ionic. When it dissolves it separates into K + and Br − ions, and moving ions carry current, so KBr is a strong electrolyte . A dissolves because its O–H groups hydrogen bond with water, but the molecules stay whole. With no ions, glucose is a nonelectrolyte. B is also a molecular compound that dissolves by hydrogen bonding without forming ions. The O–H in ethanol does not break off as an ion in water. D is a molecular compound (a waste product in urine). It dissolves well by hydrogen bonding, but as whole molecules, so it does not conduct.
hint: A solution conducts only if it contains ions. Which choice is ionic (a metal with a nonmetal) rather than molecular?

title: Problem 11.5
question: The solubility of KCl is 34.2 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. At 20 °C, a student stirs 17.1 g of KCl into 50.0 g of water, and all of it dissolves with nothing left over. How should the solution be classified? A. Unsaturated, because 17.1 g is less than 34.2 g B. Saturated C. Supersaturated D. It cannot be classified without the volume of the solution
answer: B. The solubility is given per 100 g of water, but the student used only 50.0 g, half as much. Scale the amount dissolved to 100 g of water: \( \dfrac{17.1\ \text{g KCl}}{50.0\ \text{g water}} \times 100\ \text{g water} = 34.2\ \text{g KCl per 100 g water} \) That equals the solubility, so the solution holds the maximum: it is saturated. A compares 17.1 g with 34.2 g without matching the amounts of water. Half as much water holds only half as much KCl, 17.1 g. C would need more than 34.2 g per 100 g of water, held in solution by careful cooling. D is wrong because solubility tables are written per mass of water; the mass of water and the temperature are all you need.
hint: Solubility is per 100 g of water, but only 50.0 g of water was used. Scale the amount dissolved to 100 g of water before comparing.

title: Problem 11.8
question: Using the solubility table above (three salts, 0 to 80 °C), what is the greatest mass of KNO 3 that dissolves in 150. g of water at 40 °C? A. 63.9 g B. 95.9 g C. 42.6 g D. 47.4 g
answer: B. Use the solubility as a conversion factor: \( 150.\ \text{g water} \times \dfrac{63.9\ \text{g KNO}_3}{100\ \text{g water}} = 95.9\ \text{g KNO}_3 \) A is the solubility for 100 g of water. With 1.5 times as much water, 1.5 times as much KNO 3 dissolves. C divides by 1.50 instead of multiplying, as if more water held less solute. D reads the 20 °C row (31.6 g × 1.50) instead of the 40 °C row.
hint: Use the 40 °C solubility as a conversion factor (g KNO<sub>3</sub> per 100 g water) and multiply by the grams of water.

title: Problem 11.10
question: On hot, still afternoons in late summer, fish sometimes die in shallow farm ponds in the Valley. Which statement best explains why, chemically? A. Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, because the solubility of a gas decreases as temperature rises. B. Warm water holds more dissolved oxygen, and too much oxygen poisons the fish. C. Oxygen is nonpolar, so no oxygen at all can dissolve in water once it warms up. D. Heat raises the air pressure above the pond, which forces oxygen out of the water.
answer: A. Gases are always less soluble in warmer water: faster-moving gas molecules escape from the liquid more easily. A warm, shallow pond with no wind to mix in fresh air can drop below the dissolved oxygen fish need, especially at night and when algae die and decompose. B applies the rule for most solids (more soluble when hot) to a gas. Gases behave the opposite way. C goes too far. Oxygen is nonpolar, so it is only slightly soluble, but a few milligrams per liter do dissolve, and fish depend on that small amount at every temperature. D has the pressure effect backward and the cause wrong: warming does not raise the air pressure over a pond, and a higher O 2 pressure would dissolve more oxygen (Henry's law).
hint: How does temperature affect the solubility of a gas, compared with most solids? Use kinetic molecular theory: faster gas molecules escape more easily.
new_hint: How does the solubility of a gas change as water warms (Chapter 11)? Check each choice for the right trend and a correct reason.

title: Problem 11.11
question: At 25 °C, water in contact with pure oxygen at 1.00 atm dissolves 40.3 mg of O 2 per liter. At sea level, the partial pressure of O 2 in air is 0.210 atm. What is the solubility of O 2 in water in contact with air at 25 °C? A. 8.46 mg/L B. 192 mg/L C. 40.3 mg/L D. 31.8 mg/L
answer: A. Henry's law at constant temperature: \( S_2 = S_1 \times \dfrac{P_2}{P_1} = 40.3\ \tfrac{\text{mg}}{\text{L}} \times \dfrac{0.210\ \text{atm}}{1.00\ \text{atm}} = 8.46\ \tfrac{\text{mg}}{\text{L}} \) A lower O 2 pressure means less dissolved O 2 . This value is close to the dissolved oxygen measured in clean, well-mixed water at 25 °C. B divides by the pressure ratio instead of multiplying. Lowering the pressure cannot raise the solubility. C assumes pressure does not matter. For gases it matters a great deal. D uses 0.790 atm, the fraction of air that is not oxygen (mostly N 2 ). Only the O 2 partial pressure controls how much O 2 dissolves.
hint: Henry's law: S<sub>2</sub> = S<sub>1</sub> × P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>. Use only the O<sub>2</sub> partial pressure; a lower pressure means less dissolved gas.

title: Problem 11.14
question: A sports-drink mix is made by dissolving 12.4 g of sugar in 187.6 g of water. What is the mass percent of sugar? A. 6.20% B. 6.61% C. 12.4% D. 0.0620%
answer: A. The mass of solution is 12.4 g + 187.6 g = 200.0 g. \( \%\,(\text{m/m}) = \dfrac{12.4\ \text{g sugar}}{200.0\ \text{g solution}} \times 100\% = 6.20\% \) B divides by the mass of water (the solvent), 187.6 g, instead of the mass of the whole solution. C treats the grams of sugar as the percent, which is true only when the solution has a mass of exactly 100 g. D stops at the fraction, 0.0620, and then writes a percent sign without multiplying by 100%.
hint: The denominator is the whole solution: sugar plus water. Then multiply the fraction by 100%.

title: Problem 11.15
question: How many grams of NaCl are in a 1.00 L bag of 0.45% (m/v) NaCl, often called half-normal saline? A. 0.0045 g B. 4.5 g C. 450 g D. 0.45 g
answer: B. 0.45% (m/v) means 0.45 g of NaCl per 100 mL of solution. Convert the volume to mL first: 1.00 L = 1000. mL. \( 1000.\ \text{mL} \times \dfrac{0.45\ \text{g NaCl}}{100\ \text{mL}} = 4.5\ \text{g NaCl} \) Two significant figures, set by 0.45%. A check: normal saline (0.9%) has 9 g per liter, and half-normal has half as much. A plugs in 1.00 (liters) where the percent needs milliliters. C forgets to divide by 100 mL; that would be a bag that is nearly half salt. D reads 0.45% as "0.45 g per bag" (or per liter). The percent is per 100 mL.
hint: 0.45% (m/v) means 0.45 g per 100 mL. Change the liters to mL, then use the percent as a conversion factor.

title: Problem 11.19
question: A private well in the Valley tests at 18 ppb arsenic. What is this concentration in mg/L? A. 0.018 mg/L B. 18 mg/L C. 1.8 × 10 −5 mg/L D. 1.8 × 10 4 mg/L
answer: A. In water, 18 ppb ≈ 18 μg/L, and 1 mg = 1000 μg: \( 18\ \dfrac{\mu\text{g}}{\text{L}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mg}}{1000\ \mu\text{g}} = 0.018\ \dfrac{\text{mg}}{\text{L}} \) The well is above the 10 ppb drinking water limit for arsenic. B treats ppb as mg/L. In water, mg/L is ppm; ppb is a thousand times smaller. C divides by 10 6 , as if there were a million micrograms in a milligram. D multiplies by 1000 instead of dividing. Going from a small unit (μg) to a larger one (mg) must give a smaller number.
hint: In water, 1 ppb ≈ 1 μg/L. Then convert μg to mg (1 mg = 1000 μg): a larger unit means a smaller number.

title: Problem 11.21
question: A student dissolves 12.6 g of sodium bicarbonate, NaHCO 3 (84.01 g/mol), in water and fills a 250.0 mL volumetric flask to the line. What is the molarity? A. 0.600 M B. 50.4 M C. 6.00 × 10 −4 M D. 0.150 M
answer: A. \( \text{mol NaHCO}_3 = \dfrac{12.6\ \text{g}}{84.01\ \text{g/mol}} = 0.1500\ \text{mol} \qquad M = \dfrac{0.1500\ \text{mol}}{0.2500\ \text{L}} = 0.600\ M \) B divides grams by liters. That is a concentration in g/L, not molarity, which needs moles. C divides by 250.0 mL without converting to liters. D stops at the moles (0.150 mol) and never divides by the volume.
hint: Our goal is the mole: grams to moles first, then divide by the volume in liters, not mL.

title: Problem 11.24
question: What mass of KCl (74.55 g/mol) is in 40.0 mL of 0.275 M KCl? A. 0.820 g B. 820. g C. 0.0110 g D. 10.8 g
answer: A. \( 0.0400\ \text{L} \times \dfrac{0.275\ \text{mol KCl}}{1\ \text{L}} \times \dfrac{74.55\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mol}} = 0.820\ \text{g KCl} \) B multiplies by 40.0 mL without converting to liters, so the answer is 1000 times too large. C stops at moles (0.0110 mol) and labels them grams. D divides the volume by the molarity (0.0400 ÷ 0.275) instead of multiplying. Molarity times liters gives moles.
hint: Change mL to L, multiply by the molarity to get moles, then multiply by the molar mass to get grams.

title: Problem 11.27
question: A student adds 25.0 mL of 0.800 M NaOH to 175.0 mL of water and mixes. What is the molarity of the diluted NaOH? A. 0.114 M B. 0.100 M C. 6.40 M D. 0.0200 M
answer: B. The total volume is 25.0 mL + 175.0 mL = 200.0 mL, and that is V 2 : \( M_2 = \dfrac{M_1 V_1}{V_2} = \dfrac{(0.800\ M)(25.0\ \text{mL})}{200.0\ \text{mL}} = 0.100\ M \) A uses the volume of water added (175.0 mL) as V 2 . V 2 is the total final volume. C swaps the volumes. A diluted solution can never be more concentrated than the stock. D stops at the moles of NaOH (0.0250 L × 0.800 M = 0.0200 mol) and calls them a molarity.
hint: V<sub>2</sub> in M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub> is the total final volume, not the water added. Add the two volumes first.

title: Problem 11.28
question: How many milliliters of 2.50 M glucose stock are needed to prepare 200.0 mL of 30.0 mM glucose? A. 2.40 mL B. 2.40 × 10 3 mL C. 197.6 mL D. 1.67 × 10 4 mL
answer: A. Make the units match first: 30.0 mM = 0.0300 M. \( V_1 = \dfrac{M_2 V_2}{M_1} = \dfrac{(0.0300\ M)(200.0\ \text{mL})}{2.50\ M} = 2.40\ \text{mL} \) Pipet 2.40 mL of stock into a 200-mL volumetric flask and fill to the line. Check: the stock is about 83 times more concentrated, so you need about one eighty-third of the final volume. B uses 30.0 (mM) with 2.50 (M) without converting. The units do not match, so the answer is 1000 times too large, more than the final volume. C is the water needed (200.0 − 2.40 mL), not the volume of stock asked for. (Fill to the line rather than measuring water.) D swaps M 1 and M 2 (2.50 M × 200.0 mL ÷ 0.0300 M). Label the concentrated solution "1" before you plug in.
hint: Make the units match: change mM to M first. Label the concentrated stock as 1, then solve for V<sub>1</sub>.

title: Problem 11.29
question: A 5.00 mL portion of 1.20 M CaCl 2 is diluted to a total volume of 0.250 L. What is the new molarity? A. 24.0 M B. 0.0240 M C. 60.0 M D. 2.40 × 10 −5 M
answer: B. Write both volumes in the same unit: 0.250 L = 250. mL. \( M_2 = \dfrac{M_1 V_1}{V_2} = \dfrac{(1.20\ M)(5.00\ \text{mL})}{250.\ \text{mL}} = 0.0240\ M \) The volume grew 50 times, so the concentration is one-fiftieth as large. A divides 5.00 mL by 0.250 L, mixing units. A "diluted" solution 20 times stronger than the stock is the warning sign. C swaps V 1 and V 2 , which also makes the diluted solution stronger than the stock. D converts only V 1 to liters (0.00500 L) and leaves V 2 in mL. Convert both or neither.
hint: Write both volumes in the same unit before using M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>. The diluted solution must be weaker than the stock.

title: Problem 11.33
question: Barium sulfate is the insoluble white solid in the "barium" contrast that patients drink before some X-ray studies of the digestive tract. A lab makes it by precipitation: BaCl 2 (aq) + Na 2 SO 4 (aq) → BaSO 4 (s) + 2 NaCl(aq) What mass of BaSO 4 (233.39 g/mol) forms when 35.0 mL of 0.200 M BaCl 2 reacts with excess Na 2 SO 4 ? A. 7.00 × 10 −3 g B. 1.63 g C. 3.27 g D. 1.63 × 10 3 g
answer: B. \( 0.0350\ \text{L} \times \dfrac{0.200\ \text{mol BaCl}_2}{1\ \text{L}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol BaSO}_4}{1\ \text{mol BaCl}_2} \times \dfrac{233.39\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mol BaSO}_4} = 1.63\ \text{g BaSO}_4 \) A stops at moles (7.00 × 10 −3 mol) and labels them grams.
