C uses the 2 from 2 NaCl as the mole ratio. The ratio of BaSO 4 to BaCl 2 is 1 : 1. D uses 35.0 mL as if it were liters, so the answer is 1000 times too large.
hint: Volume in liters × molarity gives moles of BaCl<sub>2</sub>. Read the BaSO<sub>4</sub> : BaCl<sub>2</sub> ratio from the equation, then multiply by the molar mass.

title: Problem 11.35
question: An antacid contains magnesium hydroxide, which neutralizes stomach acid: Mg(OH) 2 (s) + 2 HCl(aq) → MgCl 2 (aq) + 2 H 2 O(l) Taking stomach acid as 0.100 M HCl, what volume of it can 0.400 g of Mg(OH) 2 (58.32 g/mol) neutralize? A. 68.6 mL B. 137 mL C. 34.3 mL D. 4.00 × 10 3 mL
answer: B. \( 0.400\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol Mg(OH)}_2}{58.32\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol HCl}}{1\ \text{mol Mg(OH)}_2} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{L}}{0.100\ \text{mol HCl}} = 0.137\ \text{L} = 137\ \text{mL} \) A skips the mole ratio (assumes 1 : 1). Each Mg(OH) 2 has two OH − and neutralizes two HCl. C flips the mole ratio (1/2 instead of 2/1). D divides grams by molarity, skipping the conversion of grams to moles.
hint: Start with the term by itself, the grams of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>. Go to moles, use the mole ratio (how many HCl per Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>?), then divide by the HCl molarity.

title: Problem 11.36
question: A student titrates an acid with NaOH, using phenolphthalein as the indicator. When should she stop adding base and record the final buret reading? A. When the solution first turns a faint pink that lasts after swirling B. When the solution turns a deep, dark pink C. When a pink color first flashes where the drop lands, even though it fades when swirled D. When the volume of base added equals the volume of acid in the flask
answer: A. Phenolphthalein is colorless in acid and pink in base. The endpoint is the first faint pink that lasts: at that point the base added has just used up the acid. B means she overshot the endpoint and added extra base, so her volume, and her answer, will be too high. C is too early. A pink flash that fades means the drop was basic only locally; once mixed, there is still acid left. Swirl and keep adding drop by drop. D confuses equal volumes with equal moles. The endpoint depends on moles and the mole ratio, not on matching volumes.
hint: Phenolphthalein turns pink once base is in excess. Which color change shows the acid is just used up throughout the flask, not only where the drop landed?

title: Problem 11.37
question: A 20.00 mL sample of HCl is titrated with 0.1100 M NaOH. The buret reads 1.35 mL at the start and 24.80 mL at the endpoint. HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H 2 O(l) What is the molarity of the HCl? A. 0.1364 M B. 0.1290 M C. 0.09382 M D. 0.06449 M
answer: B. Volume of NaOH used = 24.80 − 1.35 = 23.45 mL. \( 0.02345\ \text{L} \times \dfrac{0.1100\ \text{mol NaOH}}{1\ \text{L}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol HCl}}{1\ \text{mol NaOH}} = 2.580 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol HCl} \qquad M = \dfrac{2.580 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}}{0.02000\ \text{L}} = 0.1290\ M \) A uses the final buret reading (24.80 mL) as the volume. The volume used is final minus initial. C swaps the two volumes (0.1100 M × 20.00 mL ÷ 23.45 mL): the moles come from the NaOH volume, and you divide by the HCl volume. D uses a 2 : 1 mole ratio, as if HCl had two acidic hydrogens. HCl has one, so the ratio is 1 : 1.
hint: Volume used = final reading − initial reading. Moles of NaOH (L × M), 1 : 1 to HCl, then divide by the HCl volume in liters.

title: Problem 11.40
question: A 10.00 mL sample of sulfuric acid is titrated with 0.1500 M NaOH. The buret reads 1.12 mL at the start and 19.76 mL at the endpoint. H 2 SO 4 (aq) + 2 NaOH(aq) → Na 2 SO 4 (aq) + 2 H 2 O(l) What is the molarity of the H 2 SO 4 ? A. 0.2796 M B. 0.1398 M C. 0.1482 M D. 0.04024 M
answer: B. Volume of NaOH = 19.76 − 1.12 = 18.64 mL. \( 0.01864\ \text{L} \times \dfrac{0.1500\ \text{mol NaOH}}{1\ \text{L}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol H}_2\text{SO}_4}{2\ \text{mol NaOH}} = 1.398 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol} \qquad M = \dfrac{1.398 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}}{0.01000\ \text{L}} = 0.1398\ M \) A skips the mole ratio (assumes 1 : 1). H 2 SO 4 has two acidic hydrogens, so it uses two NaOH. C uses the final buret reading (19.76 mL) instead of the volume used. D swaps the two volumes (0.1500 M × 10.00 mL ÷ 18.64 mL, then ÷ 2): the moles come from the NaOH volume, and you divide by the acid’s volume.
hint: Find the volume used (final − initial). Moles of NaOH, then the mole ratio: how many NaOH does each H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> need? Divide by the acid's volume.

title: Problem 11.41
question: Two students each weigh exactly 0.2000 g of oxalic acid to standardize the same NaOH solution. One dissolves the solid in 25.0 mL of water; the other uses 50.0 mL. How do their endpoint volumes of NaOH compare? A. They are the same. B. The student who used 50.0 mL needs about twice as much NaOH. C. The student who used 50.0 mL needs about half as much NaOH. D. The student who used 50.0 mL needs a little less NaOH, because a more dilute acid is weaker.
answer: A. The NaOH reacts with the moles of oxalic acid, and both flasks hold the same moles (0.2000 g ÷ 90.034 g/mol). The extra water spreads the acid out but does not add or remove any of it, so the same volume of NaOH reaches the endpoint. This is why the water used to dissolve a solid known never enters the calculation. B treats the water as if it reacted with the NaOH, or as if it were the volume of the unknown. Water is not part of the balanced equation. C makes the same mistake in the other direction. D confuses concentration with amount. A more dilute acid has a lower molarity, but the total moles to neutralize are unchanged.
hint: The NaOH reacts with the moles of acid. Does the water used to dissolve the solid change the moles of oxalic acid in the flask?
new_hint: What does the NaOH actually react with: the volume of the solution or the moles of oxalic acid? Compare that quantity in the two flasks.

title: Problem 11.42
question: What is the molality of a solution made by dissolving 5.40 g of urea, CH 4 N 2 O (60.056 g/mol), in 175.0 g of water? A. 0.514 m B. 5.14 × 10 −4 m C. 0.498 m D. 30.9 m
answer: A. \( m = \dfrac{5.40\ \text{g} \div 60.056\ \text{g/mol}}{0.1750\ \text{kg water}} = \dfrac{0.08992\ \text{mol}}{0.1750\ \text{kg}} = 0.514\ m \) B divides by 175.0 g without converting to kilograms. C divides by the mass of the whole solution (5.40 + 175.0 = 180.4 g). Molality uses kilograms of solvent only. D uses grams of urea instead of moles.
hint: Molality = moles of solute ÷ kilograms of solvent. Change grams of urea to moles and grams of water to kilograms.

title: Problem 11.44
question: Which aqueous solution has the lowest freezing point? A. 0.42 m glucose B. 0.20 m KBr C. 0.15 m Na 2 SO 4 D. 0.12 m MgCl 2
answer: C. Count particles: multiply each molality by i. \( \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow 2\ \text{Na}^+ + \text{SO}_4^{2-}: \quad i\,m = 3 \times 0.15 = 0.45\ m \text{ of particles} \) The largest i × m gives the largest ΔT f , so the lowest freezing point. A has the largest molality, but glucose is a nonelectrolyte (i = 1), so it has only 0.42 m of particles. Choosing it forgets i. B: KBr gives 2 ions, 2 × 0.20 = 0.40 m of particles. D: MgCl 2 gives 3 ions, but 3 × 0.12 = 0.36 m, the fewest particles of all four.
hint: Count particles: multiply each molality by i (glucose 1; ionic solutes 2 or 3). The largest i × m gives the largest ΔT<sub>f</sub>.

title: Problem 11.46
question: By how many degrees does a 0.300 m MgCl 2 solution lower the freezing point of water (ΔT f )? A. 0.558 °C B. 1.12 °C C. 0.461 °C D. 1.67 °C
answer: D. MgCl 2 → Mg 2+ + 2 Cl − , so i = 3. \( \Delta T_f = (3)(1.86\ {}^\circ\text{C}/m)(0.300\ m) = 1.67\ {}^\circ\text{C} \) If asked for the new freezing point: \( T_f = 0.00 - 1.67 = -1.67\ {}^\circ\text{C} \). Subtract: dissolved particles always lower the freezing point, so +1.67 °C would be wrong. A forgets i, treating MgCl 2 as if it did not separate into ions. B uses i = 2, as if MgCl 2 gave one Mg and one "Cl 2 ." The two chloride ions are separate particles. C uses K b (0.512 °C/m), the boiling point constant, instead of K f (1.86 °C/m).
hint: Find i from the dissolving equation (the two chloride ions are separate particles), then ΔT<sub>f</sub> = i K<sub>f</sub> m with K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 °C/m.

title: Problem 11.48
question: Fresh cucumbers soaked in a strong salt brine for pickling become limp and shriveled. Which explanation is correct? A. Water moves out of the cucumber cells into the brine by osmosis, toward the higher solute concentration. B. Water moves from the brine into the cucumber cells by osmosis, toward the lower solute concentration. C. The salt dissolves the cell walls, so the cucumber collapses. D. No water moves, because cell membranes block water; the cucumber shrinks because the salt is heavy.
answer: A. The brine is hypertonic to the cucumber's cells. Water crosses the cell membranes from the side with fewer dissolved particles (inside the cells) to the side with more (the brine): "water follows solute." The cells lose water and the cucumber goes limp, the plant-cell version (plasmolysis) of the crenation that happens to red blood cells in a hypertonic solution. Salting meat or fish preserves it the same way, by drawing water out of bacteria too. B reverses osmosis. Water moves toward the higher solute concentration; if it moved in, the cucumber would swell. C is not what happens: salt does not dissolve the cellulose cell walls, and the shriveling is caused by water loss. D is wrong on both counts: cell membranes are semipermeable and let water through, and the weight of the salt does not shrink anything.
hint: Water follows solute: it moves across the membrane toward the side with more dissolved particles. Is the brine or the inside of the cells more concentrated?
new_hint: Which is more concentrated, the brine or the inside of the cucumber cells? Recall which way water moves across a membrane by osmosis.

title: Problem 11.49
question: A laboratory technician accidentally suspends a sample of red blood cells in sterile distilled water instead of normal saline. What happens to the cells? A. They shrink and develop spiky surfaces (crenation). B. Nothing; pure water is gentle and has no solutes to disturb the cells. C. Water flows into them, and they swell and can burst (hemolysis), because pure water is hypotonic. D. They swell, because pure water is hypertonic to the cells.
answer: C. Pure water has no dissolved particles, so it is hypotonic compared with the inside of the cells (about 290 mOsm/kg). Water flows into the cells, toward the higher solute concentration, until they swell and burst. A reverses the direction: crenation happens in a hypertonic solution, such as 3% NaCl, which pulls water out. B misses the point: it is the lack of solutes outside that drives water in. Only an isotonic solution leaves the cells unchanged. D gets the swelling right but names the wrong tonicity. A solution with fewer solutes than the cell is hypotonic.
hint: Pure water has no dissolved particles. Compared with the inside of a cell, is it hypotonic or hypertonic, and which way does water flow?

title: Problem 11.56
question: A 0.500% (m/v) KCl solution is on hand. What volume of it contains 0.200 g of KCl? A. 1.00 × 10 −3 mL B. 40.0 mL C. 2.50 mL D. 400. mL
answer: B. 0.500% (m/v) means 0.500 g KCl = 100 mL of solution. Start with the term by itself and flip the percent so grams of KCl cancel: \( 0.200\ \text{g KCl} \times \dfrac{100\ \text{mL}}{0.500\ \text{g KCl}} = 40.0\ \text{mL} \) A multiplies by the percent instead of dividing (0.200 × 0.500 ÷ 100). The units do not cancel, and a volume smaller than a drop cannot hold 0.200 g of a 0.5% solute. C divides the percent by the mass (0.500 ÷ 0.200), which leaves out the 100 mL that the percent is based on. D treats 0.500% as 0.500 g per liter instead of per 100 mL, so the answer is ten times too large.
hint: 0.500% (m/v) means 0.500 g KCl per 100 mL. Start with the term by itself, the grams of KCl, and flip the percent so grams cancel.

title: Problem 11.59
question: 40.0 mL of 0.150 M BaCl 2 is mixed with 25.0 mL of 0.200 M Na 2 SO 4 . What mass of BaSO 4 (233.39 g/mol) precipitates? BaCl 2 (aq) + Na 2 SO 4 (aq) → BaSO 4 (s) + 2 NaCl(aq) A. 1.40 g B. 1.17 g C. 2.57 g D. 0.583 g
answer: B. Both solutions come with a volume and a molarity, so this is a limiting-reactant problem. Find the BaSO 4 each reactant could make: \( 0.0400\ \text{L} \times 0.150\ \tfrac{\text{mol BaCl}_2}{\text{L}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol BaSO}_4}{1\ \text{mol BaCl}_2} = 6.00 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol} \qquad 0.0250\ \text{L} \times 0.200\ \tfrac{\text{mol Na}_2\text{SO}_4}{\text{L}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol BaSO}_4}{1\ \text{mol Na}_2\text{SO}_4} = 5.00 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol} \) Na 2 SO 4 makes less, so it is limiting: 5.00 × 10 −3 mol × 233.39 g/mol = 1.17 g . (1.00 × 10 −3 mol of BaCl 2 is left over.) A uses the BaCl 2 , which is in excess. The smaller amount of product is the answer. C adds the two amounts together. Each formula unit of BaSO 4 needs one of each reactant, so the reactants are not added. D uses a 1 : 2 ratio between Na 2 SO 4 and BaSO 4 . The 2 in the equation belongs to NaCl, not BaSO 4 .
hint: Both solutions come with V and M, so find the moles of BaSO<sub>4</sub> each reactant could make. The smaller amount is what forms; then use the molar mass.

title: Problem 11.60
question: What volume of 0.200 M HCl can 0.150 g of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH) 2 (74.09 g/mol), neutralize? Ca(OH) 2 (s) + 2 HCl(aq) → CaCl 2 (aq) + 2 H 2 O(l) A. 10.1 mL B. 20.2 mL C. 5.06 mL D. 750. mL
answer: B. Start with the term by itself, the 0.150 g, on the side whose amount you know: \( 0.150\ \text{g Ca(OH)}_2 \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol}}{74.09\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol HCl}}{1\ \text{mol Ca(OH)}_2} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{L}}{0.200\ \text{mol HCl}} = 0.0202\ \text{L} = 20.2\ \text{mL} \) A skips the mole ratio (1 : 1). Each Ca(OH) 2 has two OH − and neutralizes two HCl. C flips the mole ratio (1/2 instead of 2/1). D divides grams by molarity, skipping the conversion of grams to moles; it is also far too large a volume for a fraction of a gram of base.
hint: Start with the grams of Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>: grams to moles, the mole ratio (how many HCl per Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>?), then divide by the HCl molarity.

title: Problem 11.61
question: Which aqueous solution has the lowest freezing point? A. 0.20 m glucose B. 0.10 m Ca(C 2 H 3 O 2 ) 2 C. 0.12 m NaCl D. 0.080 m FeCl 3
answer: D. Count particles, then multiply by molality: FeCl 3 → Fe 3+ + 3 Cl − , i = 4, and 4 × 0.080 = 0.32 m of particles, the most of the four. A: glucose stays whole (i = 1), so 0.20 m of particles. Its molality is the largest, but its particle count is the smallest. B: Ca(C 2 H 3 O 2 ) 2 gives Ca 2+ + 2 C 2 H 3 O 2 − , i = 3: 0.30 m, close but less than 0.32 m. C: NaCl gives 2 ions: 0.24 m.
hint: Count particles: find i for each solute (acetate stays together) and multiply by its molality. The largest i × m freezes lowest.

title: Problem 11.63
question: A student titrates HCl with NaOH using phenolphthalein. Which statement is correct? A. At the endpoint, the flask contains no ions. B. The endpoint comes just after the equivalence point, when a slight excess of OH − turns the indicator pink. C. The equivalence point is reached when equal volumes of acid and base have been mixed. D. A starting buret reading of 0.50 mL means the buret holds only 0.50 mL of NaOH.
answer: B. The reaction in the flask is H + (aq) + OH − (aq) → H 2 O(l). At the equivalence point the moles of OH − added match the moles of H + ; the next fraction of a drop leaves OH − in excess, and the indicator changes color. That color change is the endpoint. A: Na + and Cl − are still dissolved; only H + and OH − combine to make water. C: the moles match by the balanced equation; the volumes are equal only if the two molarities happen to be equal (for a 1 : 1 reaction). D: a buret tells how much has been dispensed. 0.50 mL is how far the level sits below the zero mark.
hint: Think through H<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>O. Which ions are left in the flask? What makes phenolphthalein change color? What does a buret reading measure?

title: Problem 12.1
question: Which observation shows that a solution is basic ? A. It turns blue litmus paper red. B. It stays colorless when phenolphthalein is added. C. It turns red cabbage indicator green. D. It fizzes when a piece of chalk (calcium carbonate) is dropped in.
answer: C. Red cabbage indicator turns blue, green, or yellow in basic solutions; green means roughly pH 9 to 11. A is the acid test ("BRA": blue turns red in acid). A base turns red litmus blue ; this choice swaps the colors. B describes an acidic or neutral solution. Phenolphthalein turns pink only in base. D is a property of acids: acid + carbonate makes CO 2 gas. A base does not fizz with a carbonate.
hint: Recall the base colors: red litmus turns blue, phenolphthalein turns pink, red cabbage turns blue, green, or yellow. Which choice gives a base color? Watch for swapped litmus colors.
new_hint: For each choice, name the indicator and recall its color in acid and in base (BRA for litmus). Which kind of solution makes chalk fizz?

title: Problem 12.4
question: Some effervescent antacid tablets contain potassium bicarbonate, KHCO 3 . Which set of products forms when KHCO 3 reacts with hydrochloric acid? A. KCl(aq) + H 2 CO 3 (aq), and nothing else B. KCl(aq) + H 2 O(l) + CO 2 (g) C. KCl(aq) + H 2 (g) + CO 2 (g) D. KCl(aq) + H 2 O(l), with no gas
answer: B. Acid + bicarbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide: KHCO 3 (s) + HCl(aq) → KCl(aq) + H 2 O(l) + CO 2 (g) Check: 1 K, 2 H, 1 C, 3 O, and 1 Cl on each side. The CO 2 is the fizz you see in the glass. A stops halfway. H 2 CO 3 forms first but breaks down into H 2 O and CO 2 , so it is not written as a product. C mixes in the acid + metal reaction. H 2 forms when an acid reacts with an active metal, not with a bicarbonate. D leaves out the CO 2 . Any carbonate or bicarbonate releases CO 2 gas with an acid; that is why the tablet fizzes.
hint: Acid + bicarbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Remember that H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> breaks down, and H<sub>2</sub> comes only from active metals.
new_hint: Swap partners first: what forms from H<sup>+</sup> and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>? Then use the unstable-products table to see what that product becomes.

title: Problem 12.6
question: The surface of healthy skin is usually around pH 5, while many ordinary bar soaps are around pH 9 to 10. Which statement is correct? A. Skin's surface is basic, so it would turn red litmus blue. B. The soap is acidic, because it removes oils from the skin. C. A drop of phenolphthalein on wet soap lather would stay colorless. D. The soap is basic, so it would turn red litmus paper blue.
answer: D. A pH above 7 is basic, and bases turn red litmus blue. (The slippery feel of soap is another base property.) This is the reason soaps for sensitive skin are often formulated closer to skin's own pH. A reverses the classification. A pH near 5 is mildly acidic (the "acid mantle"), so skin would turn blue litmus red , not red litmus blue. B confuses what soap does with its pH. Removing oils is not an acid property; a pH of 9 to 10 is basic. C has the indicator backward. Phenolphthalein turns pink above about pH 8, so it would turn pink in the lather.
hint: Classify each pH first: below 7 acidic, above 7 basic. Then check each indicator statement: BRA for litmus, pink above about pH 8 for phenolphthalein.

title: Problem 12.8
question: Which statement is the Brønsted–Lowry definition of a base? A. A substance that donates a proton (H + ) B. A substance that produces OH − ions when it dissolves in water C. A substance that accepts a proton (H + ) D. Any substance whose formula contains hydrogen
answer: C. Brønsted–Lowry bases are proton acceptors ("BAD": bases accept, acids donate). A is the Brønsted–Lowry definition of an acid . B is the Arrhenius definition of a base. It is narrower: it misses bases such as NH 3 that contain no hydroxide. D is a common trap. NH 3 and CH 4 both contain H, and neither donates it in water; having H atoms does not decide anything.
hint: Brønsted–Lowry definitions are about a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) moving between substances. Two choices mention a proton: which one describes an acid? One choice is the older Arrhenius definition.
new_hint: Brønsted–Lowry definitions are about a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) moving between substances. Recall what an acid does with the proton; a base does the opposite. Which choice is the older Arrhenius definition?

title: Problem 12.10
question: What is the conjugate base of the ammonium ion, NH 4 + ? A. NH 5 2+ B. NH 4 C. NH 2 − D. NH 3
answer: D. To make a conjugate base, remove one H + : one fewer H, and the charge goes down by 1, from +1 to 0. NH 4 + − H + = NH 3 . A adds an H + . That is the direction for a conjugate acid, and NH 4 + does not actually accept another proton. B removes the charge without removing the H. A proton carries the +1 charge with it. C removes two protons. Conjugates differ by exactly one H + ; NH 2 − is the conjugate base of NH 3 , not of NH 4 + .
hint: A conjugate base has exactly one fewer H and a charge one lower than its acid.

title: Problem 12.12
question: In the reaction below, which two species form a conjugate acid–base pair? NH 4 + (aq) + H 2 O(l) ⇄ NH 3 (aq) + H 3 O + (aq) A. NH 4 + and H 2 O B. NH 4 + and NH 3 C. H 2 O and NH 3 D. NH 4 + and H 3 O +
answer: B. NH 4 + donates a proton and becomes NH 3 ; the two differ by exactly one H + . (The other pair is H 2 O and H 3 O + .) A pairs the two reactants. They are the acid and the base of the forward reaction, not partners; a conjugate pair always has one member on each side. C pairs species that differ by more than one H + (different elements, too). Water's partner here is H 3 O + . D pairs the two acids, one from each side. A pair is an acid with its own conjugate base.
hint: A conjugate pair has one member on each side of the arrow, and the two differ by exactly one H<sup>+</sup>.

title: Problem 12.16
question: Which of these is a strong acid? A. HF, hydrofluoric acid B. H 3 PO 4 , phosphoric acid C. HC 2 H 3 O 2 , acetic acid D. HClO 4 , perchloric acid
answer: D. HClO 4 is one of the six strong acids on the green sheet (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO 3 , HClO 4 , H 2 SO 4 ), so it ionizes completely in water. A is weak. HCl, HBr, and HI are strong, but HF is not, even though fluorine is in the same group. B is weak. Having three H atoms does not make an acid strong; strength is about how completely it ionizes, and H 3 PO 4 is not on the list. C is weak: the acid in vinegar is mostly intact molecules in water.
hint: Only six common acids are strong; recall the green-sheet list. Having more H atoms, or a halogen, does not make an acid strong.

title: Problem 12.17
question: Which statement best describes a 0.10 M solution of lactic acid, HC 3 H 5 O 3 ? A. [H 3 O + ] = 0.10 M, because each lactic acid molecule gives one H + . B. Most of the lactic acid stays as intact HC 3 H 5 O 3 molecules, so [H 3 O + ] is much less than 0.10 M. C. It contains no H 3 O + at all, because lactic acid is weak. D. It has the same [H 3 O + ] as 0.10 M HCl, because the two concentrations are equal.
answer: B. Lactic acid is not on the strong-acid list, so it is weak: only a small fraction of its molecules donate a proton at any moment. HC 3 H 5 O 3 (aq) + H 2 O(l) ⇄ H 3 O + (aq) + C 3 H 5 O 3 − (aq) A treats a weak acid as if it ionized completely. That shortcut, [H 3 O + ] = acid molarity, works only for strong acids. C goes too far the other way. A weak acid ionizes slightly , not zero; the solution is still acidic. D confuses concentration with strength. Equal molarities do not mean equal ionization: the HCl is all ions, the lactic acid mostly molecules.
hint: Is lactic acid on the strong-acid list? A weak acid ionizes only slightly, not zero, and not completely.
new_hint: Is lactic acid on the green-sheet strong-acid list? How much of a weak acid ionizes, compared with a strong acid?

title: Problem 12.19
question: A particle picture of a 0.1 M acid, HX, in water shows 10 intact HX molecules, 2 H 3 O + ions, and 2 X − ions (water molecules not shown). Which acid could HX be? A. HNO 2 , nitrous acid B. HNO 3 , nitric acid C. HCl, hydrochloric acid D. HBr, hydrobromic acid
answer: A. Most of the acid is still intact molecules, so HX ionizes only slightly: it is a weak acid. Of the choices, only HNO 2 is weak. B is strong. A picture of 0.1 M HNO 3 would show only H 3 O + and NO 3 − ions and no HNO 3 molecules. (Watch the subscript: HNO 3 is strong, HNO 2 is weak.) C is strong and would show only ions. D is strong and would show only ions.
hint: Most of the HX is still intact molecules. Is that a strong or a weak acid? Then find the choice that is not on the strong list.

title: Problem 12.21
question: Which equation is written correctly? A. HF(aq) + H 2 O(l) → H 3 O + (aq) + F − (aq) B. HNO 3 (aq) + H 2 O(l) ⇄ H 3 O + (aq) + NO 3 − (aq) C. Sr(OH) 2 (aq) → Sr 2+ (aq) + 2 OH − (aq) D. NH 3 (aq) + H 2 O(l) → NH 4 + (aq) + OH − (aq)
answer: C. Sr(OH) 2 is a strong base, so it gets a single arrow, and each formula unit releases two OH − . Mass and charge balance (+2 and 2 × −1 = 0). A uses a single arrow for a weak acid. HF ionizes only slightly, so it needs a double arrow. B uses a double arrow for a strong acid. HNO 3 ionizes completely, so it gets a single arrow. D uses a single arrow for a weak base. Ammonia accepts protons from water only to a small extent.
hint: Classify each substance as strong or weak first: strong gets a single arrow, weak a double arrow. Then check that each equation balances.

title: Problem 12.24
question: Which statement about pure water at 25 °C is true? A. It contains no ions at all, because it is neutral. B. [H 3 O + ] = [OH − ] = 1.0 × 10 −7 M. C. [H 3 O + ] = [OH − ] = 1.0 × 10 −14 M. D. [H 3 O + ] = 1.0 × 10 −7 M, but [OH − ] = 0, because only acids make ions.
answer: B. Water autoionizes, H 2 O + H 2 O ⇄ H 3 O + + OH − , making one of each ion. In pure water the two are equal, and their product is K w : (1.0 × 10 −7 )(1.0 × 10 −7 ) = 1.0 × 10 −14 . A mixes up "neutral" with "no ions." Neutral means the two ion concentrations are equal ; pure water has a tiny but real amount of each. C uses K w itself as each concentration. 1.0 × 10 −14 is the product of the two. D forgets that autoionization makes the ions in pairs: every H 3 O + formed leaves an OH − behind.
hint: Write water's autoionization: each H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> forms with one OH<sup>−</sup>. The two equal concentrations multiply to give K<sub>w</sub>; what must each one be?

title: Problem 12.25
question: A grapefruit juice has [H 3 O + ] = 6.4 × 10 −4 M. What is [OH − ]? A. 6.4 × 10 −18 M B. 6.4 × 10 −4 M C. 1.6 × 10 3 M D. 1.6 × 10 −11 M
answer: D. \( [\text{OH}^-] = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{6.4 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.6 \times 10^{-11}\ M \) Check: [H 3 O + ] is above 10 −7 M (acidic), so [OH − ] must be below it, and it is. A multiplies K w by [H 3 O + ] instead of dividing. B assumes the two concentrations are equal. They are equal only in neutral water. C divides 1 by 6.4 × 10 −4 , leaving out K w . No real water solution has 1600 M of anything.
hint: Divide K<sub>w</sub> by [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>]. Then check: an acidic juice must have [OH<sup>−</sup>] below 10<sup>−7</sup> M.

title: Problem 12.27
question: Which solution is basic? A. [H 3 O + ] = 2.0 × 10 −5 M B. [OH − ] = 5.0 × 10 −9 M C. [H 3 O + ] = 7.1 × 10 −10 M D. [OH − ] = 1.0 × 10 −7 M
answer: C. 7.1 × 10 −10 M is smaller than 1.0 × 10 −7 M, so [H 3 O + ] is below neutral and [OH − ] is above it: [OH − ] = 1.0 × 10 −14 ÷ 7.1 × 10 −10 = 1.4 × 10 −5 M. A is acidic: 2.0 × 10 −5 is larger than 10 −7 (watch the negative exponents). B is a trap: it gives [OH − ], but 5.0 × 10 −9 M is less than 10 −7 M, so the solution is acidic ([H 3 O + ] = 2.0 × 10 −6 M). Seeing OH − does not make a solution basic; the comparison does. D is neutral: [OH − ] = [H 3 O + ] = 1.0 × 10 −7 M.
hint: Compare each value with 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M, and note whether it is [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] or [OH<sup>−</sup>]. Basic means [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] below 10<sup>−7</sup> M.

title: Problem 12.29
question: What is [H 3 O + ] in 0.0035 M Ca(OH) 2 ? A. 1.4 × 10 −12 M B. 2.9 × 10 −12 M C. 7.0 × 10 −3 M D. 7.0 × 10 −17 M
answer: A. Ca(OH) 2 → Ca 2+ + 2 OH − , so [OH − ] = 2 × 0.0035 M = 0.0070 M. \( [\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{7.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.43 \times 10^{-12} = 1.4 \times 10^{-12}\ M \) B forgets to double: it uses [OH − ] = 0.0035 M. Each Ca(OH) 2 releases two OH − . C is [OH − ], not [H 3 O + ]. The question asks for the other ion. D multiplies K w by [OH − ] instead of dividing.
hint: Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> releases two OH<sup>−</sup> per formula unit, so find [OH<sup>−</sup>] first. Then divide K<sub>w</sub> by it; the question asks for H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>.

title: Problem 12.32
question: A few pellets of NaOH are dissolved in a liter of pure water at 25 °C. What happens to the ion concentrations? A. [OH − ] and [H 3 O + ] both increase. B. [OH − ] increases, [H 3 O + ] decreases, and their product stays 1.0 × 10 −14 . C. [OH − ] increases, and [H 3 O + ] becomes zero. D. [OH − ] increases, and [H 3 O + ] stays at 1.0 × 10 −7 M.
answer: B. K w = [H 3 O + ][OH − ] stays 1.0 × 10 −14 in every water solution at 25 °C, so the two concentrations move like a seesaw: when the base raises [OH − ], [H 3 O + ] must fall. A would make the product grow past K w . The extra OH − combines with H 3 O + to make water, so [H 3 O + ] goes down. C goes too far. Every water solution contains both ions; a basic solution has a very small [H 3 O + ], not zero. D ignores K w . If [H 3 O + ] stayed at 10 −7 M, the product would be larger than 1.0 × 10 −14 .
hint: K<sub>w</sub> = [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>] stays the same in every water solution at 25 °C. Think of a seesaw: if one goes up, what must the other do?
new_hint: Does K<sub>w</sub> = [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>] change when a base dissolves at 25 °C? If [OH<sup>−</sup>] goes up, what must happen to keep the product fixed?

title: Problem 12.33
question: What is the pH of 0.0042 M HNO 3 ? A. −2.38 B. 2.4 C. 2.38 D. 11.62
answer: C. HNO 3 is a strong acid, so [H 3 O + ] = 0.0042 M = 4.2 × 10 −3 M. \( \text{pH} = -\log(4.2 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.3767\ldots = 2.38 \) Two significant figures in 4.2 give two decimal places. Check: the concentration is between 10 −3 and 10 −2 M, so the pH is between 2 and 3. A uses pH = log[H 3 O + ] and drops the minus sign in the definition. Ordinary pH values are positive. B has the wrong number of decimal places. A two-significant-figure concentration needs two decimal places in the pH. D is 14.00 − 2.38, the pOH. An acid must have a pH below 7.
hint: HNO<sub>3</sub> is strong, so [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] equals its molarity. Take −log, and count significant figures in the concentration for the decimal places.

title: Problem 12.35
question: Pickling lime, calcium hydroxide, is used in many Valley kitchens to soak corn for masa and tortillas (nixtamalization). What is the pH of a 0.0040 M Ca(OH) 2 solution? A. 11.90 B. 11.60 C. 2.10 D. 11.9
answer: A. Ca(OH) 2 → Ca 2+ + 2 OH − , so [OH − ] = 2 × 0.0040 M = 0.0080 M. \( \text{pOH} = -\log(0.0080) = 2.0969\ldots = 2.10 \qquad \text{pH} = 14.00 - 2.10 = 11.90 \) B forgets to double [OH − ]: −log(0.0040) = 2.40, and 14.00 − 2.40 = 11.60. C is the pOH. For a base, subtract the pOH from 14.00 at the end. D has the right value but the wrong number of decimal places. 0.0080 has two significant figures, so the pH needs two decimal places: 11.90.
hint: Each Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> gives two OH<sup>−</sup>. Find [OH<sup>−</sup>], take −log for the pOH, subtract from 14.00, and watch the decimal places.

title: Problem 12.36
question: A cup of black coffee has pH 5.12. What is [H 3 O + ]? A. 1.3 × 10 5 M B. 1.3 × 10 −9 M C. 5.12 × 10 −6 M D. 7.6 × 10 −6 M
answer: D. \( [\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-5.12} = 7.585\ldots \times 10^{-6} = 7.6 \times 10^{-6}\ M \) Two decimal places in 5.12 give two significant figures. Check: a pH between 5 and 6 means [H 3 O + ] between 10 −6 and 10 −5 M, and it is. A uses 10 +5.12 , dropping the minus sign. The concentration must be a small number. B uses 10 −(14 − pH) = 10 −8.88 . That is [OH − ]; 14 − pH gives the pOH, not the pH. C just copies the pH digits in front of a power of ten. A pH is an exponent; you need the 10 x key to undo it.
hint: Undo the pH with the 10<sup>x</sup> key: [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>−pH</sup>. Two decimal places in the pH give two significant figures.

title: Problem 12.38
question: A lemonade has pH 3.5. Tooth enamel begins to dissolve below the critical pH of 5.5. How many times greater is [H 3 O + ] in the lemonade than in a liquid at the critical pH? A. 2 times B. 100 times C. 1.6 times D. 20 times
answer: B. Each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H 3 O + ]. The lemonade is 5.5 − 3.5 = 2 pH units lower: \( \dfrac{10^{-3.5}}{10^{-5.5}} = 10^{5.5 - 3.5} = 10^{2} = 100 \) A treats pH as a simple count: it takes the difference, 2, as the factor. A difference of 2 pH units is a factor of 10 × 10. C divides the two pH values (5.5 ÷ 3.5 = 1.6). pH values are exponents, so their ratio means nothing. D multiplies 10 by the difference of 2. Each unit multiplies by another 10.
hint: Each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>]. Find the pH difference, then raise 10 to that power.

title: Problem 12.40
question: A rainwater sample has [H 3 O + ] = 4.80 × 10 −5 M. What is its pH, reported to the correct number of decimal places? A. 4.319 B. 4.32 C. 4.3 D. −4.319
answer: A. \( \text{pH} = -\log(4.80 \times 10^{-5}) = 4.3187\ldots = 4.319 \) 4.80 has three significant figures (the trailing zero after the decimal point counts), so the pH gets three decimal places. The 4 before the decimal point comes from the power of ten and is not counted. B has only two decimal places, as if the concentration had two significant figures. C has only one decimal place. D uses log instead of −log.
hint: Count the significant figures in 4.80 × 10<sup>−5</sup> (does the trailing zero count?). That is the number of decimal places the pH gets.

title: Problem 12.43
question: A student says, "0.010 M lactic acid has pH 2.00, the same as 0.010 M HCl." Which statement about the pH of 0.010 M lactic acid is correct? A. It is exactly 2.00, because [H 3 O + ] equals the acid's molarity. B. It is less than 2.00, because lactic acid is a larger molecule. C. It is greater than 2.00 (but below 7), because lactic acid ionizes only slightly. D. It is 12.00, because a weak acid makes a basic solution.
answer: C. Lactic acid is weak, so [H 3 O + ] is much less than 0.010 M. A smaller [H 3 O + ] means a higher pH, so the pH is above 2.00, while the solution is still acidic. A treats the weak acid as fully ionized. [H 3 O + ] = molarity holds only for strong acids, such as the HCl. B has no basis: the size of the molecule does not raise [H 3 O + ]. A pH below 2.00 would need more H 3 O + than a fully ionized acid gives, which is impossible here. D confuses "weak" with "basic." A weak acid is still an acid; it just raises [H 3 O + ] less. (12.00 is 14.00 − 2.00, a pOH-style slip.)
hint: Is lactic acid strong or weak? A weak acid makes less H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> than its molarity; does less H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> mean a higher or a lower pH?
new_hint: Is lactic acid strong or weak? Compare the [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] it makes with that of 0.010 M HCl, then decide which way the pH moves.

title: Problem 12.44
question: Which mixture is a buffer? A. HCl and NaCl B. NH 3 and NaOH C. HNO 2 and NaNO 3 D. HCN and KCN
answer: D. HCN (hydrocyanic acid) is a weak acid, and KCN supplies CN − , its conjugate base. The two differ by exactly one H + . A is a strong acid with its salt. Cl − is too weak a base to take back protons, so nothing in the mixture can neutralize added acid. B is a weak base with a strong base, not with its conjugate acid. NH 3 's partner would be NH 4 + (from NH 4 Cl), and nothing here neutralizes added base. C is a near miss: HNO 2 is weak, but NO 3 − (nitrate) is not its conjugate base. The partner of HNO 2 is NO 2 − (nitrite), from NaNO 2 .
hint: A buffer needs a weak acid with its own conjugate base (the same formula, one H<sup>+</sup> less). Cross out strong acids first, then check each partner.

title: Problem 12.46
question: In the blood's buffer of carbonic acid (H 2 CO 3 ) and bicarbonate (HCO 3 − ), which species neutralizes a small amount of added OH − ? A. H 2 CO 3 B. HCO 3 − C. Na + D. CO 2 gas leaving through the lungs
answer: A. Added base is neutralized by the acid partner: H 2 CO 3 (aq) + OH − (aq) → HCO 3 − (aq) + H 2 O(l) B is the base partner; it neutralizes added acid . Choosing it mixes up which partner reacts. C is a spectator ion. It neither donates nor accepts protons. D has the role of CO 2 backward for this case. Exhaling CO 2 removes acid (it is how added acid is finally cleared); it does not neutralize added base.
hint: Added OH<sup>−</sup> needs something that can donate a proton to it. Which species in the blood buffer is the acid partner, and which is the base partner?

title: Problem 12.49
question: A student mixes hydrochloric acid with sodium chloride and calls the mixture a buffer. What is the best reason it is not one? A. NaCl is not a salt. B. HCl is a weak acid, so it cannot neutralize added base. C. Cl − is too weak a base to take a proton back, so nothing in the mixture can neutralize added acid. D. A buffer must contain only bases.
answer: C. A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base. HCl is completely ionized, and its "conjugate base" Cl − does not accept protons, so added acid simply adds to [H 3 O + ] and the pH falls. A is false: NaCl is the classic salt, a base's cation (Na + ) with an acid's anion (Cl − ). B has HCl's strength backward. HCl is a strong acid (on the list), and a strong acid does neutralize added base; the missing piece is a partner to neutralize added acid. D is false: a buffer contains an acid partner and a base partner, one for each kind of addition.
hint: Check what a buffer needs: a weak acid plus its conjugate base. Is HCl weak, and can its anion take back a proton to neutralize added acid?
new_hint: A buffer needs a weak acid plus its conjugate base. Which part neutralizes added acid, and which neutralizes added base? Test HCl and Cl<sup>−</sup> against those two jobs.

title: Problem 12.56
question: What is the conjugate base of the dihydrogen phosphate ion, H 2 PO 4 − ? A. HPO 4 2− B. PO 4 3− C. H 3 PO 4 D. HPO 4 −
answer: A. A conjugate base is one rung down the proton ladder: remove one H + (one H, and the charge goes down by 1). H 3 PO 4 ↔ H 2 PO 4 − ↔ HPO 4 2− ↔ PO 4 3− . B removes two protons, two rungs down. A conjugate is always one H + away. C adds a proton: H 3 PO 4 is the conjugate acid of H 2 PO 4 − . D removes the H but forgets to change the charge. Removing H + takes a positive charge away, so −1 becomes −2.
hint: A conjugate base is one rung down the proton ladder: one fewer H, and the charge goes down by 1.

title: Problem 12.58
question: A cleaning solution has pH 11.80. What is [H 3 O + ]? A. 6.3 × 10 11 M B. 1.6 × 10 −12 M C. 6.3 × 10 −3 M D. 1.80 × 10 −11 M
answer: B. [H 3 O + ] = 10 −11.80 = 1.58… × 10 −12 = 1.6 × 10 −12 M. Two decimal places in 11.80 give two significant figures. A high pH must mean a very small [H 3 O + ]. A drops the minus sign: 10 +11.80 . No solution can be hundreds of billions of moles per liter; a huge answer means a missing (−). C is [OH − ], found from pOH = 14.00 − 11.80 = 2.20. The question asks for [H 3 O + ]. D copies the digits of the pH into scientific notation instead of taking the antilog. The pH is an exponent, not a coefficient.
hint: Use [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>−pH</sup> with the 10<sup>x</sup> key. A high pH must mean a very small [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>].

title: Problem 12.59
question: 0.73 g of strontium hydroxide, Sr(OH) 2 (121.63 g/mol), is dissolved in enough water to make 500. mL of solution. What is the pH? A. 12.38 B. 12.08 C. 1.62 D. 9.38
answer: A. Map it out: g → mol Sr(OH) 2 → mol OH − → [OH − ] → pOH → pH. Sr(OH) 2 → Sr 2+ + 2 OH − . \( 0.73\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol}}{121.63\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol OH}^-}{1\ \text{mol}} = 0.01200\ \text{mol OH}^- \qquad [\text{OH}^-] = \dfrac{0.01200\ \text{mol}}{0.500\ \text{L}} = 0.0240\ M \) pOH = −log(0.02401) = 1.62; pH = 14.00 − 1.62 = 12.38 (two decimal places for two significant figures in 0.73 g). B forgets the 2 OH − per formula unit: [OH − ] = 0.0120 M gives pOH 1.92 and pH 12.08. C is the pOH. For a base, subtract from 14.00 at the end. D divides by 500 instead of 0.500 L (mL not converted to liters), so [OH − ] comes out 1000 times too small.
hint: Map it out: g → mol Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> → mol OH<sup>−</sup> (two per formula unit) → [OH<sup>−</sup>] in mol/L → pOH → pH.

title: Problem 12.61
question: Which pair would make a buffer if mixed in roughly equal amounts? A. HClO 4 and NaClO 4 B. H 2 CO 3 and Na 2 CO 3 C. HC 2 H 3 O 2 and KC 2 H 3 O 2 D. NH 4 Cl and NaCl
answer: C. Acetic acid is a weak acid, and potassium acetate supplies its conjugate base, C 2 H 3 O 2 − ; K + is a spectator. The two differ by exactly one H + . A: HClO 4 is a strong acid, so ClO 4 − is a negligible base. Crossed out first. B: H 2 CO 3 and CO 3 2− differ by two H + . The partner of H 2 CO 3 is HCO 3 − (NaHCO 3 ). D: NH 4 + is a weak acid, but its partner NH 3 is missing; NaCl adds only spectator ions.
hint: Cross out any pair with a strong acid. Then check that the two species differ by exactly one H<sup>+</sup> and that both partners are present.

title: Problem 12.62
question: Which compound acts as a base in water? A. Lactic acid, CH 3 CH(OH)COOH B. Methylamine, CH 3 NH 2 C. Ethyl acetate, CH 3 COOCH 2 CH 3 D. Methanol, CH 3 OH
answer: B. Methylamine is an amine: the lone pair on its nitrogen accepts a proton, CH 3 NH 2 + H 2 O ⇄ CH 3 NH 3 + + OH − . A has a –COOH group, so it is an acid (the –OH on the middle carbon is an alcohol group). C is an ester: no acidic H and no amine nitrogen, so it is neither. D is an alcohol. Its –OH is covalently bonded to carbon, not a hydroxide ion, so it is neither.
hint: Look for the functional group: –COOH is an acid, an amine nitrogen is a base, and alcohols and esters are neither.
new_hint: Name the functional group in each compound. Which of those groups did Chapter 12 call acidic, which basic, and which neither?

title: Problem 13.1
question: Nitric oxide from car exhaust reacts with ozone in the air: NO(g) + O 3 (g) → NO 2 (g) + O 2 (g) In a flask of the two gases, the molecules collide billions of times per second, yet only a small fraction of those collisions form products. Why? A. The molecules can react only when they collide with a catalyst, and the flask has none. B. At room temperature gas molecules are not moving, so they collide only when the flask is shaken. C. A collision forms products only if the molecules hit with the right orientation and with at least the activation energy. D. As soon as a few NO 2 molecules form, the reaction reaches equilibrium and the collisions stop.
answer: C. Collision theory says an effective collision needs two things: the right orientation (the right atoms touching, so the right bond can break and form) and enough energy to reach at least E a . Most collisions miss on one or both counts, and the molecules simply bounce apart unchanged. A is wrong because a catalyst is not required. It only lowers the activation energy so that more collisions succeed; many reactions run without one. B is wrong because gas particles are always moving (Chapter 10). Even at room temperature they collide constantly. D mixes up two ideas. Collisions never stop, and at equilibrium (Section 13.2) the forward and reverse reactions keep running at equal rates.
hint: Recall what collision theory says an effective collision needs. Which choice states that, and which choices contradict how gas particles and equilibrium behave?

title: Problem 13.3
question: On an energy diagram, the reactants sit at 75 kJ, the top of the hill is at 160 kJ, and the products sit at 10 kJ. What is the activation energy of the forward reaction? A. 150 kJ B. 85 kJ C. 160 kJ D. 65 kJ
answer: B. Activation energy is always measured from the reactants up to the top of the hill: E a = 160 kJ − 75 kJ = 85 kJ. A measures from the products (160 − 10). That is the hill for the reverse reaction, not the forward one. C reads the height of the hill from the bottom of the graph (zero) instead of from the reactants. D is the size of ΔH (10 − 75 = −65 kJ, an exothermic reaction), the difference between reactants and products, not the hill.
hint: Activation energy is always measured from the reactants up to the top of the hill, not from zero and not from the products.

title: Problem 13.5
question: A student drops marble chips (calcium carbonate) into hydrochloric acid and watches the bubbles of carbon dioxide: CaCO 3 (s) + 2 HCl(aq) → CaCl 2 (aq) + H 2 O(l) + CO 2 (g) Which change makes the bubbling slower ? A. Warming the acid from 20 °C to 40 °C B. Using a few large chips instead of many small chips of the same total mass C. Using 2.0 M HCl instead of 1.0 M HCl D. Grinding the chips into a powder before adding them
answer: B. The reaction happens only where acid touches the surface of the solid. A few large chips expose much less surface area than many small chips of the same mass, so fewer CaCO 3 units are available to collide with the acid each second, and the reaction slows. A speeds the reaction up: hotter particles collide more often and harder, and more collisions have at least E a . C speeds it up: more H + ions per liter means more collisions with the solid per second. D speeds it up a great deal: a powder has far more surface area than chips.
hint: Three of the changes speed the reaction up. Which one reduces how much of the solid's surface can touch the acid?
new_hint: Go through the rate factors: temperature, concentration, and surface area. For each choice, does the change speed the reaction up or slow it down?

title: Problem 13.8
question: Fine dust from almond hulling, grain handling, or flour milling can explode if it is stirred into the air and meets a spark, but a solid pile of the same material only smolders. Which statement best explains the difference? A. The dust has far more surface area, so far more of the fuel is exposed to collisions with O 2 at the same time. B. Grinding a material into dust changes it into a new substance with a lower activation energy. C. Dust particles are hotter than a solid pile because they float in warm air. D. A cloud of dust contains more total fuel than a pile of the same mass.
answer: A. Breaking a solid into tiny particles exposes an enormous surface area. Each particle is surrounded by air, so huge numbers of fuel–O 2 collisions happen at once, and the burning spreads through the cloud almost instantly. In a pile, only the outside surface touches air. B is wrong because grinding is a physical change. The dust is the same substance with the same activation energy; there is simply much more of it exposed. C is wrong because the dust starts at the same temperature as its surroundings. The spark, not the dust, supplies the activation energy. D is wrong because the problem compares the same mass of material. The amount of fuel is the same; only how much of it can collide with oxygen at once is different.
hint: Grinding is a physical change. Which rate factor changes when a solid becomes a fine dust?

title: Problem 13.11
question: Which statement is true for every reaction at chemical equilibrium? A. The concentrations of the reactants and products are equal. B. The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped. C. The forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction. D. The forward and reverse rates are equal, so the concentrations stay constant.
answer: D. Equilibrium is defined by equal rates. Because each species is made as fast as it is used up, there is no net change, and the concentrations stay constant: equal rates, constant amounts. A is the most common trap. The concentrations are constant, but they are usually not equal; the mixture can be mostly products, mostly reactants, or a fair amount of both. B is wrong because equilibrium is dynamic. Both reactions keep running; they just run at the same rate. C describes a reaction that is still approaching equilibrium from the reactant side, not one that has reached it.
hint: Equilibrium is defined by rates, not amounts: equal rates, constant amounts.
new_hint: Is equilibrium defined by amounts or by rates? Do the reactions stop, and does “constant” mean the same as “equal”?

title: Problem 13.12
question: A sealed bottle of sparkling water has been sitting on a shelf for a week, and the pressure inside has stopped changing: CO 2 (g) ⇄ CO 2 (aq) Which statement about the bottle is correct? A. No CO 2 molecules move between the gas space and the water anymore. B. All of the CO 2 has dissolved in the water. C. CO 2 molecules dissolve in the water and escape from it at the same rate. D. The concentration of CO 2 in the water is equal to the concentration of CO 2 in the gas space.
answer: C. This is a dynamic equilibrium (a physical one: the CO 2 changes phase, not identity). Molecules are constantly dissolving and escaping, but at the same rate, so the amount in each phase, and so the pressure, stays constant. A says the rates are zero. At equilibrium the rates are equal, not zero. B is wrong because there is still CO 2 gas in the space above the water; that gas is what keeps the pressure up. D confuses constant with equal. The two concentrations stay constant, but nothing makes them the same number.
hint: The pressure stopped changing, so the bottle is at dynamic equilibrium. Have the processes stopped, or are they running at equal rates? Constant does not mean equal.
new_hint: The pressure stopped changing, so the bottle is at equilibrium. What is still happening at the molecular level at equilibrium? Does constant mean equal?

title: Problem 13.14
question: A reversible reaction is started in a sealed flask with only reactants. On a graph of rate versus time, which description of the reverse rate is correct? A. It starts high and falls to zero at equilibrium. B. It starts at zero, rises, and levels off at the same value as the forward rate. C. It stays at zero until equilibrium is reached, then jumps up to match the forward rate. D. It starts at zero and keeps rising until it is larger than the forward rate.
answer: B. With no products at the start, the reverse reaction cannot happen, so its rate is zero. As products build up, more reverse collisions happen and the reverse rate rises, while the forward rate falls. At equilibrium the two curves meet and stay level together. A describes the forward rate's shape, and even the forward rate does not reach zero; it levels off. C is wrong because the reverse reaction starts as soon as the first product molecules form; it rises gradually, not in a jump. D is wrong because once the rates are equal there is no net change, so nothing pushes the reverse rate any higher.
hint: With only reactants at the start, the reverse reaction has no products to collide. How does its rate change as products build up, and where does it end?

title: Problem 13.16
question: Water evaporates both from an open pot on a counter and from a capped bottle that is half full. Which can reach a liquid–vapor equilibrium, H 2 O(l) ⇄ H 2 O(g)? A. Only the open pot, because the vapor has room to spread out B. Both, because evaporation happens in both containers C. Neither, because evaporation is a physical change, not a chemical reaction D. Only the capped bottle, because it is a closed system
answer: D. In the capped bottle, vapor collects above the liquid and some of it condenses back. Soon molecules evaporate and condense at the same rate, and the amount of vapor stays constant. In the open pot, the vapor drifts away, so condensation cannot keep up, and the water eventually evaporates completely. A has it backward: letting the vapor escape is exactly what prevents equilibrium. B is wrong because evaporation alone is not equilibrium; the reverse process, condensation, has to keep pace, and that needs a closed system. C is wrong because physical changes such as evaporation and dissolving can reach dynamic equilibrium too, as long as the system is closed.
hint: Equilibrium needs the reverse process, condensation, to keep pace. Where can water vapor collect and condense instead of drifting away? Equilibrium needs a closed system.
new_hint: Equilibrium needs the reverse process, condensation, to keep pace with evaporation. In which container can the vapor collect above the liquid?

title: Problem 13.18
question: Nitrosyl chloride breaks down into nitric oxide and chlorine: 2 NOCl(g) ⇄ 2 NO(g) + Cl 2 (g) Which is the equilibrium constant expression? A. \( K = \dfrac{[\text{NOCl}]^2}{[\text{NO}]^2[\text{Cl}_2]} \) B. \( K = \dfrac{[\text{NO}][\text{Cl}_2]}{[\text{NOCl}]} \) C. \( K = \dfrac{[\text{NO}]^2[\text{Cl}_2]}{[\text{NOCl}]^2} \) D. \( K = \dfrac{2[\text{NO}][\text{Cl}_2]}{2[\text{NOCl}]} \)
answer: C. Products over reactants, with each coefficient as an exponent: NO and NOCl each have a coefficient of 2, and Cl 2 has 1 (not written). A is upside down: reactants over products. B leaves out the exponents, as if every coefficient were 1. D multiplies by the coefficients instead of raising to their powers. (The 2's would also cancel, giving B again.)
hint: Products over reactants, with each coefficient as an exponent (not a multiplier).

title: Problem 13.19
question: Hydrogen gas reduces magnetite, an iron ore, to iron metal: Fe 3 O 4 (s) + 4 H 2 (g) ⇄ 3 Fe(s) + 4 H 2 O(g) Which is the equilibrium constant expression? A. \( K = \dfrac{[\text{H}_2\text{O}]^4}{[\text{H}_2]^4} \) B. \( K = \dfrac{[\text{Fe}]^3[\text{H}_2\text{O}]^4}{[\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4][\text{H}_2]^4} \) C. \( K = \dfrac{1}{[\text{H}_2]^4} \) D. \( K = \dfrac{[\text{H}_2]^4}{[\text{H}_2\text{O}]^4} \)
answer: A. Fe 3 O 4 and Fe are pure solids, so they are left out. Water here is a gas (g), not a liquid, so it stays in. Products over reactants, coefficients as exponents. B includes the two solids. Their concentrations do not change, so they never appear in K. C drops the water as if it were a liquid. Always read the phase label: H 2 O(g) stays in; H 2 O(l) would be left out. D is upside down: reactants over products.
hint: Circle the phase labels and cross out (s) and (l). Then write products over reactants with exponents. Is the water here a liquid or a gas?

title: Problem 13.21
question: A reaction has this equilibrium constant expression: \( K = \dfrac{[\text{NO}]^2[\text{O}_2]}{[\text{NO}_2]^2} \) Which balanced equation does it belong to? A. 2 NO(g) + O 2 (g) ⇄ 2 NO 2 (g) B. 2 NO 2 (g) ⇄ 2 NO(g) + O 2 (g) C. NO 2 (g) ⇄ NO(g) + O 2 (g) D. 2 NO 2 (g) ⇄ 2 NO(g) + 2 O(g)
answer: B. The species on top (NO and O 2 ) are the products, the species on the bottom (NO 2 ) is the reactant, and the exponents are the coefficients: 2 NO 2 ⇄ 2 NO + O 2 . Check that it balances: 2 N and 4 O on each side. A is the reverse reaction. Its K would be the reciprocal, [NO 2 ] 2 / ([NO] 2 [O 2 ]). C is not balanced (2 O on the left, 3 on the right), and its K would have no exponents. D has O atoms instead of O 2 molecules, so its K would contain [O] 2 , not [O 2 ].
hint: The species on top are the products and those on the bottom are the reactants; the exponents are the coefficients. Check that the equation balances.

title: Problem 13.22
question: At a certain high temperature, an equilibrium mixture for the reaction below contains [CO] = 0.0400 M, [H 2 O] = 0.0500 M, [CO 2 ] = 0.0600 M, and [H 2 ] = 0.0600 M. CO(g) + H 2 O(g) ⇄ CO 2 (g) + H 2 (g) What is K? A. 0.556 B. 1.33 C. 0.00360 D. 1.80
answer: D. All four species are gases, and every coefficient is 1: \( K = \dfrac{[\text{CO}_2][\text{H}_2]}{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2\text{O}]} = \dfrac{(0.0600)(0.0600)}{(0.0400)(0.0500)} = \dfrac{0.00360}{0.00200} = 1.80 \) Three significant figures in each concentration give three in K. K is close to 1, so the mixture has sizable amounts of both reactants and products, as the numbers show. A is reactants over products, 0.00200 ÷ 0.00360. That is K for the reverse reaction. B adds the concentrations, (0.0600 + 0.0600) ÷ (0.0400 + 0.0500), instead of multiplying them. C stops after the numerator and never divides by the reactants.
hint: Write K (every coefficient is 1): multiply the products on top, multiply the reactants on the bottom, then divide.

title: Problem 13.24
question: Solid ammonium hydrogen sulfide is placed in a sealed flask and partly breaks down into two gases: NH 4 HS(s) ⇄ NH 3 (g) + H 2 S(g) At equilibrium, [NH 3 ] = [H 2 S] = 0.0110 M, and some solid is still present. What is K? A. 1.21 × 10 −4 B. 0.0220 C. 8.26 × 10 3 D. 0.0110
answer: A. The solid is left out, so K is just the product of the two gas concentrations: \( K = [\text{NH}_3][\text{H}_2\text{S}] = (0.0110)(0.0110) = 1.21 \times 10^{-4} \) B adds the two concentrations instead of multiplying them. C is 1 ÷ (1.21 × 10 −4 ), the expression turned upside down, as if the gases were reactants. D uses only one of the two products.
hint: Leave the solid out. What is left is just the two gas concentrations, multiplied together.

title: Problem 13.26
question: At 25 °C, the reaction 2 H 2 (g) + O 2 (g) ⇄ 2 H 2 O(g) has K of about 10 80 . Yet a balloon filled with a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen can sit for years without making any noticeable water, until a spark sets it off. Which statement explains this? A. K is so large that the reaction is already complete inside the balloon. B. K tells how far the reaction goes at equilibrium, not how fast it gets there; with a high activation energy, the reaction is extremely slow until a spark supplies the energy. C. A K of 10 80 means the reactants are strongly favored, so no water forms. D. The balloon is already at equilibrium, because the concentrations of H 2 and O 2 are not changing.
answer: B. The size of K (Section 13.3) and the rate (Section 13.1) answer different questions. A huge K says that if the mixture reaches equilibrium, it will be almost all water. The activation energy decides how quickly that happens, and for H 2 and O 2 at room temperature it is so high that almost no collisions succeed. A spark gives some molecules enough energy, the heat released sets off the rest, and the balloon explodes. A contradicts the problem: the balloon contains almost no water, so the reaction has not happened. C reads K backward. A K much greater than 1 favors products . D is wrong because nothing changing is not enough: an equilibrium mixture for this K would be almost all water. The mixture is unchanged because the reaction is too slow to be seen, not because it has reached equilibrium.
hint: K tells how far a reaction goes, not how fast. Which idea from Section 13.1 controls how fast?
new_hint: What question does K answer, and what question does rate answer (Section 13.1)? Which one explains why nothing happens until a spark?

title: Problem 13.28
question: Nitric oxide and bromine are at equilibrium with nitrosyl bromide in a sealed flask: 2 NO(g) + Br 2 (g) ⇄ 2 NOBr(g) More Br 2 is added, and the temperature is kept constant. What happens? A. The equilibrium shifts left, toward the added Br 2 ; K does not change. B. The equilibrium shifts right; K does not change. C. The equilibrium shifts right, and K increases. D. Nothing happens, because the system was already at equilibrium.
answer: B. Add → away: Br 2 is a reactant, so the system shifts away from it, to the right. The extra Br 2 means more forward collisions, so for a while the forward reaction runs faster, using up some Br 2 and NO and making more NOBr. The temperature did not change, so K stays the same; the concentrations rearrange until their ratio equals the same K again. A shifts toward the added substance. Adding pushes the system away from it. C has the right direction, but only a temperature change changes K. D is wrong because adding Br 2 disturbs the equilibrium. Le Chatelier's principle is about exactly that: how an equilibrium responds to a stress.
hint: Is Br<sub>2</sub> a reactant or a product, and which way does adding it push the system? Did this stress change the temperature?

title: Problem 13.31
question: In simplified form, hemoglobin carries oxygen by the equilibrium Hb(aq) + O 2 (aq) ⇄ HbO 2 (aq). In a leg muscle during a long run, cells use O 2 quickly, so the O 2 concentration there is low. What happens to the equilibrium in the red blood cells passing through that muscle? A. It shifts left, so HbO 2 releases O 2 to the muscle. B. It shifts right, because the muscle needs more oxygen. C. It does not shift, because hemoglobin is a catalyst. D. It shifts right, because removing O 2 pushes the system away from O 2 .
answer: A. The working muscle removes O 2 . Take → toward: the system shifts toward O 2 , to the left. HbO 2 breaks apart and releases its oxygen right where it is being used. In the lungs, where O 2 is high, the same equilibrium shifts right and hemoglobin loads up again. B gives a reason from biology ("the muscle needs it"), not from the equilibrium. Shifting right would make hemoglobin hold on to more oxygen, the opposite of delivery. C is wrong because hemoglobin is a reactant in this equilibrium, not a catalyst; it is bound and released, not left unchanged on the side. D swaps the rules. Removing a substance pulls the system toward it; adding one pushes the system away.
hint: The muscle removes O<sub>2</sub>. Take → Toward: which side of the equation is O<sub>2</sub> on?

title: Problem 13.33
question: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin more than 200 times more tightly than oxygen does. One way to picture the competition between them is this equilibrium: HbCO(aq) + O 2 (aq) ⇄ HbO 2 (aq) + CO(aq) A person with carbon monoxide poisoning is given a high concentration of oxygen. According to Le Chatelier's principle, why does this help? A. O 2 is a catalyst that breaks the bond between hemoglobin and CO. B. Adding O 2 shifts the equilibrium left, toward the added O 2 . C. Adding O 2 raises the value of K, so less HbCO is present at equilibrium. D. Adding O 2 shifts the equilibrium right, releasing CO from hemoglobin and forming HbO 2 .
answer: D. O 2 is a reactant here. Add → away: a large excess of O 2 pushes the system to the right, so hemoglobin trades its CO for O 2 , and the freed CO is breathed out. Because CO binds so tightly, a lot of O 2 is needed to drive this shift, which is why high-concentration oxygen (sometimes in a hyperbaric chamber) is used. A is wrong because O 2 appears in the equation as a reactant; a catalyst would not, and a catalyst would not shift the equilibrium anyway. B shifts toward the added substance. Adding pushes the system away from it. C is wrong because only temperature changes K. Adding O 2 changes a concentration, and the system shifts until the ratio equals the same K. (Context only; CO poisoning is an emergency, treated by medical professionals.)
hint: O<sub>2</sub> is a reactant in this equilibrium. Add → Away: which way does adding a lot of it push the system? Remember that only temperature changes K.

title: Problem 13.34
question: Mateo Herrera, the irrigation technician with asthma from the chapter opener, is in the first hour of an asthma attack and is breathing fast. Which describes the effect on the blood equilibrium below? CO 2 (aq) + H 2 O(l) ⇄ H 2 CO 3 (aq) ⇄ H + (aq) + HCO 3 − (aq) A. It shifts left; [H + ] decreases; blood pH rises. B. It shifts right; [H + ] increases; blood pH falls. C. It shifts left; [H + ] decreases; blood pH falls. D. It does not shift, because water is a pure liquid and is left out of K.
answer: A. Fast breathing blows off CO 2 faster than his cells make it, so CO 2 is removed. Take → toward: the system shifts left, toward CO 2 . H + combines with HCO 3 − to replace the lost CO 2 , so [H + ] drops, and a lower [H + ] means a higher pH (Chapter 12): a mild respiratory alkalosis, as in his blood gas in Section 13.4. B is the direction for CO 2 building up (hypoventilation), not for fast breathing that removes it. C gets the shift and [H + ] right but the pH backward. Fewer H + ions means a less acidic blood, so the pH goes up. D misuses the solid-and-liquid rule. Water is left out of K, but the stress here is a change in CO 2 , which is dissolved (aq) and is in the equilibrium. (The case is for learning chemistry only; it is not treatment advice.)
hint: Fast breathing removes CO<sub>2</sub>. Use Take → Toward, then follow [H<sup>+</sup>]: does less H<sup>+</sup> mean a higher or a lower pH?

title: Problem 13.35
question: Tooth enamel is in equilibrium with its ions in saliva: Ca 5 (PO 4 ) 3 OH(s) ⇄ 5 Ca 2+ (aq) + 3 PO 4 3− (aq) + OH − (aq) A dental hygiene patient sips lemon water all day. The H + from the citric acid reacts with OH − to form water. What happens to the enamel equilibrium? A. No shift, because H + does not appear in the equation. B. It shifts right, toward the removed OH − , so enamel dissolves (demineralization). C. It shifts left, away from the added H + , so enamel rebuilds. D. No shift, because hydroxyapatite is a solid and solids are left out of K.
answer: B. H + (aq) + OH − (aq) → H 2 O(l) removes OH − , a product. Take → toward: the equilibrium shifts right, and more hydroxyapatite dissolves to replace the lost OH − . Sipping all day keeps the enamel shifted toward demineralization for hours at a time. A misses the indirect stress. H + is not in the equation, but it removes OH − , which is. C treats H + as if it were a product in this equation. It is not; its effect comes only through removing OH − . D misreads the rule. Adding or removing the solid causes no shift, but removing an aqueous ion does. Here the solid is the thing that dissolves.
hint: H<sup>+</sup> is not in the equation, but it reacts with OH<sup>−</sup>, which is. Is OH<sup>−</sup> being added or taken away?

title: Problem 13.37
question: Nitric oxide reacts with oxygen to form brown nitrogen dioxide: 2 NO(g) + O 2 (g) ⇄ 2 NO 2 (g)    ΔH = −114 kJ The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is raised. What happens? A. The equilibrium shifts right, and K increases. B. The equilibrium shifts left, and K decreases. C. The equilibrium shifts left, and K does not change. D. Nothing shifts; a temperature change only makes the reactions faster.
answer: B. ΔH is negative (exothermic), so heat is a product : 2 NO + O 2 ⇄ 2 NO 2 + heat. Raising the temperature adds heat. Add → away: the system shifts left, less NO 2 is present, and because temperature is the one stress that changes K, K decreases. A puts heat on the wrong side, as if the reaction were endothermic. C has the right direction but treats temperature like a concentration change. Temperature changes the value of K itself. D is half true: heating does speed up both reactions, but not by the same factor, so the equilibrium position moves too.
hint: ΔH is negative, so heat is a product. Raising the temperature adds heat: Add → Away. Temperature is the one stress that changes K.
new_hint: When ΔH is negative, is heat a reactant or a product? Which way does adding heat push the system? Which kind of stress is the one that changes K?

title: Problem 13.38
question: A sealed glass tube holds an equilibrium mixture of colorless N 2 O 4 and brown NO 2 , N 2 O 4 (g) ⇄ 2 NO 2 (g). At 50 °C the gas is dark brown; in an ice bath at 0 °C it is pale, almost colorless. What can you conclude? A. The forward reaction is endothermic, and K is larger at 50 °C than at 0 °C. B. The forward reaction is exothermic, because heating makes the mixture release brown gas. C. K is the same at both temperatures; only the concentrations changed. D. At 0 °C the reactions are too slow for any NO 2 to form, so the tube is not at equilibrium.
answer: A. Heating makes more NO 2 , so heating shifts the system right. Adding heat pushes the system away from the heat term, so heat must be on the left, a reactant: the forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH positive). More product at the higher temperature means K is larger at 50 °C. B confuses "making more product" with "releasing heat." Shifting right when heated means the forward reaction absorbs heat. C is wrong because the concentrations changed when only the temperature changed, which can only happen if K changed. D is wrong because cold slows the reactions but does not stop them. Given time, the tube reaches equilibrium at 0 °C too; that equilibrium just has very little NO 2 .
hint: Heating made more brown NO<sub>2</sub>, so heating shifted the system right. With Add → Away, which side must heat be on? Then, more product means what for K?

title: Problem 13.40
question: Oxygen binding to hemoglobin releases heat: Hb(aq) + O 2 (aq) ⇄ HbO 2 (aq) + heat Hard-working muscle is slightly warmer than the rest of the body. What does the extra warmth do to this equilibrium in the muscle? A. It shifts right, so hemoglobin holds its oxygen more tightly. B. Nothing, because temperature changes only the rate, not the equilibrium. C. It shifts left and K decreases, so hemoglobin releases more O 2 where it is needed. D. It shifts left, but K does not change, because the body's temperature is controlled.
answer: C. Heat is a product here (the binding is exothermic). Warming adds heat. Add → away: the system shifts left, HbO 2 gives up O 2 , and K for binding gets smaller. This is one of the reasons active muscle, which is warmer and makes more CO 2 and acid, receives more oxygen. A puts the shift toward the heat that was added, as if adding a product pulled the system toward it. B is wrong because temperature changes both the rates and the equilibrium; it is the one stress that changes K. D has the right direction, but any change in temperature, even a small, local one, changes K.
hint: Heat is a product here. Which way does adding heat push the system? Which kind of stress is the one that changes K?

title: Problem 13.41
question: Phosphorus pentachloride breaks down at high temperature: PCl 5 (g) ⇄ PCl 3 (g) + Cl 2 (g) The volume of the container is decreased at constant temperature. Which way does the equilibrium shift? A. Left, toward the side with fewer moles of gas B. Right, toward the side with more moles of gas C. No shift, because K does not change D. Right, because the higher pressure makes more PCl 5 molecules collide and break apart
answer: A. Count moles of gas: 1 on the left, 1 + 1 = 2 on the right. A smaller volume raises the pressure, and the system relieves it by shifting toward fewer gas particles, to the left, making more PCl 5 . B has the rule backward. Squeezing shifts toward fewer moles of gas; expanding shifts toward more. C is true about K but wrong about the shift. Squeezing changes the concentrations so that their ratio no longer equals K, and the system shifts to restore it. D treats the squeeze as if it sped up only the forward reaction. Crowding the gases together speeds up the reverse reaction, which needs PCl 3 and Cl 2 to collide, even more, so the net shift is toward fewer moles of gas, to the left.
hint: Count moles of gas on each side. A smaller volume (higher pressure) shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas.
new_hint: Count moles of gas on each side. Does a smaller volume (higher pressure) favor the side with more or fewer moles of gas?

title: Problem 13.43
question: A rigid steel tank holds an equilibrium mixture for the Haber process, N 2 (g) + 3 H 2 (g) ⇄ 2 NH 3 (g). Argon gas is pumped in, which raises the total pressure, while the volume and temperature stay the same. What happens? A. The equilibrium shifts right, toward fewer moles of gas, because the pressure went up. B. The equilibrium shifts left, away from the added gas. C. Nothing shifts, because the concentrations of N 2 , H 2 , and NH 3 did not change. D. K increases, because the total pressure is higher.
answer: C. Argon is an inert gas: it is not in the equation. In a rigid tank the volume is fixed, so the moles per liter of N 2 , H 2 , and NH 3 are unchanged, the ratio still equals K, and there is no shift. A applies the volume rule where it does not fit. The "fewer moles of gas" rule works when the volume changes, which changes every concentration in the reaction; here the volume did not change. B treats argon as if it were a product. Add → away applies only to substances in the equilibrium. D is wrong because only temperature changes K.
hint: Argon is not in the equation, and the volume is fixed. Did the concentration (mol/L) of N<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>, or NH<sub>3</sub> change?

title: Problem 13.44
question: In red blood cells, the enzyme carbonic anhydrase catalyzes CO 2 (aq) + H 2 O(l) ⇄ H 2 CO 3 (aq). Which statement about the enzyme is correct? A. It makes the reaction reach equilibrium faster in both directions, without changing the equilibrium amounts or K. B. It shifts the equilibrium toward H 2 CO 3 , because it speeds up the forward reaction. C. It increases K, so more H 2 CO 3 is present at equilibrium. D. It is used up as the reaction runs, so red blood cells must keep making more of it.
answer: A. A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the forward and the reverse reactions, so it speeds both up by the same factor. Equilibrium is reached much sooner, but the equilibrium mixture and K are the same. That lets the blood switch quickly between making H 2 CO 3 in the tissues and releasing CO 2 in the lungs, in whichever direction the conditions push. B forgets that the enzyme speeds up the reverse reaction just as much as the forward one, so neither direction wins. C is wrong because only temperature changes K; a catalyst changes the path, not the starting and ending points. D is wrong because a catalyst comes out of the reaction unchanged and is used over and over.
hint: A catalyst lowers the hill for both the forward and the reverse reactions. Does it change how fast equilibrium is reached, where it ends up, or both?

title: Problem 13.46
question: Limewater is a saturated solution of calcium hydroxide with some undissolved solid at the bottom of the bottle: Ca(OH) 2 (s) ⇄ Ca 2+ (aq) + 2 OH − (aq) A student adds another spoonful of solid Ca(OH) 2 and stirs, keeping the temperature constant. What happens to the concentration of OH − in the solution? A. It increases, because adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium right. B. It stays the same, because adding a pure solid causes no shift. C. It decreases, because the system shifts toward the added solid. D. It doubles, because twice as much solid is now present.
answer: B. A pure solid does not appear in K = [Ca 2+ ][OH − ] 2 , so adding more of it does not change the ratio, and nothing shifts. The solution was already saturated; the extra solid simply sits on the bottom. A applies "add → away" to a solid. The rule applies only to species that appear in K, gases and aqueous species. C moves toward the added substance, which is backward even for species that do count. D assumes the dissolved amount depends on how much solid is present. A saturated solution holds a fixed amount at a given temperature, however much extra solid is underneath.
hint: Does a pure solid appear in K? Adding something that is not in the expression cannot change the ratio.
new_hint: Does a pure solid appear in the K expression? If adding the solid changed [OH<sup>−</sup>], what would that do to the value of the expression?

title: Problem 13.53
question: In a two-tub water-transfer model of equilibrium, a 500 mL beaker moves water forward from the "reactant" tub and a 100 mL beaker moves water back from the "product" tub. After many rounds, the water levels stop changing. Which statement is true at that point? A. The reactant tub is empty, because the forward beaker is five times larger. B. Both beakers carry the same volume of water per trip, and the product tub holds more water. C. Both tubs hold the same volume of water. D. Water has stopped moving between the tubs.
answer: B. The levels stop changing only when each forward trip is matched by an equal reverse trip: equal rates. The large forward beaker favors the product tub, so the product tub ends up with more water, but the reactant tub is not empty; once it is shallow, the big beaker cannot fill. A forgets the reverse direction. As the product tub fills, the small beaker carries a full load back every trip, so the reactant tub never runs dry. C confuses equal rates with equal amounts . At equilibrium the amounts are constant, not equal. D describes a static stop. Equilibrium is dynamic: both beakers keep moving water, at the same rate.
hint: The levels stop changing when each forward trip is matched by a reverse trip: equal rates. Do equal rates mean equal amounts?

title: Problem 13.55
question: Iron(III) ions and thiocyanate ions are at equilibrium with the red complex ion: Fe 3+ (aq) + SCN − (aq) ⇄ FeSCN 2+ (aq, red) A student stirs a few crystals of potassium nitrate, KNO 3 , into the red solution. What happens? A. The solution turns deeper red, because a salt was added. B. The color fades, because adding a substance shifts the system left. C. Nothing changes, because neither K + nor NO 3 − is part of the equilibrium. D. The solution turns deeper red, because NO 3 − is a common ion.
answer: C. Write the dissociation first: KNO 3 (s) → K + (aq) + NO 3 − (aq). Neither ion appears in the equilibrium, so both are spectators, and there is no shift and no color change. A treats every added salt as a stress. Only an ion that appears in the equation (a common ion) causes a shift. B applies "add → away" to a substance that is not in the equation at all. D misnames NO 3 − . A common ion is one already in the equilibrium; nitrate is not. (Adding iron(III) nitrate would deepen the red, but because of its Fe 3+ , not its nitrate.)
hint: Write the dissociation of KNO<sub>3</sub> first. Does either ion appear in the equilibrium?

title: Problem 13.57
question: Hydrogen sulfide, the rotten-egg gas, burns in oxygen: 2 H 2 S(g) + 3 O 2 (g) ⇄ 2 SO 2 (g) + 2 H 2 O(g) The volume of the container is doubled at constant temperature. Which way does the equilibrium shift? A. Right, because a larger volume always favors products. B. Left, toward the side with more moles of gas. C. Right, toward the side with fewer moles of gas. D. No shift, because volume is not a stress.
answer: B. Doubling the volume lowers the pressure. Count moles of gas: left, 2 + 3 = 5; right, 2 + 2 = 4. Lower pressure shifts toward more moles of gas, which is the left side here. A has no basis: a larger volume favors whichever side has more moles of gas, which can be either side. C has the rule backward. Fewer moles of gas is the answer for a smaller volume (higher pressure). D is wrong for gas reactions with different numbers of moles of gas on each side; volume changes the pressure, and the system responds.
hint: Doubling the volume lowers the pressure. Count moles of gas on each side, and shift toward the side with more.
